topics.name: NEE city case study: Rio de Janeiro
Uneven development and reducing the gap
Resource management: food, water and energy in the UK

questions.q: Which type of plate margin is formed where two plates move away from each other?
ms: Constructive (divergent) margins form where plates pull apart and magma rises to fill the gap, e.g. the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
questions.tip: Learn the three AQA terms: constructive, destructive, conservative. 'Collision' is a type of destructive margin, not a separate answer here.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a conservative plate margin?
options: Oceanic plate subducts beneath continental plate
Two continental plates collide to form fold mountains
Plates slide past each other with no crust created or destroyed
Plates move apart and new crust forms
ms: At a conservative margin plates move sideways past each other (e.g. San Andreas Fault). Friction causes earthquakes but there are no volcanoes.
questions.tip: Students lose marks by saying volcanoes form at conservative margins. They do not, because no magma is produced.

questions.q: Why does the oceanic plate sink beneath the continental plate at a destructive margin?
options: It is older than the continental plate
ms: Oceanic crust is denser (basaltic) than continental crust (granitic), so it is subducted.
questions.tip: Use the word 'denser'. 'Heavier' is weaker because it is density that matters.

questions.q: The Nepal earthquake of 25 April 2015 had a magnitude of:
ms: The Gorkha (Nepal) earthquake was magnitude 7.8. Chile 2010 was 8.8.
questions.tip: Don't mix up your HIC and LIC case study figures. Chile was the bigger quake but had far fewer deaths.

questions.q: Approximately how many people died in the Chile earthquake of February 2010?
ms: Around 500 people died in Chile (magnitude 8.8), compared with almost 9,000 in Nepal 2015.
questions.tip: 230,000 is Haiti 2010, a common mix-up. Be precise with your own case studies.

questions.q: Which of these is the best explanation for why Chile 2010 had far fewer deaths than Nepal 2015 despite a larger magnitude?
options: Chile's earthquake did not cause a tsunami
Chile has strict building codes and well-funded, well-practised emergency services
ms: Chile is a richer country with earthquake-resistant building regulations and trained emergency services, so fewer buildings collapsed and response was faster.
questions.tip: Always link the difference in effects to level of development (wealth, preparation, building quality).

questions.q: Which of these is a PRIMARY effect of an earthquake?
ms: Primary effects happen immediately due to the ground shaking, e.g. buildings collapsing. The others are secondary effects.
questions.tip: Primary = caused directly by the shaking or eruption. Secondary = results from the primary effects, often later.

questions.q: Give two reasons why people continue to live in areas at risk from tectonic hazards.
questions.answer: Fertile volcanic soils for farming; geothermal energy; tourism income; jobs/family ties; confidence in prediction and protection.
ms: 1 mark for each valid reason, max 2. E.g. volcanic soils are fertile (1); geothermal energy can be produced (1); tourism brings jobs and income (1); people have always lived there / family ties (1); they believe monitoring and building design protects them (1); they cannot afford to move (1).
Do not accept 'they like it there' without a reason.
questions.tip: Give two different reasons. Two farming points (soil and crops) only score once.

questions.q: Explain how monitoring and prediction can reduce the effects of volcanic eruptions.
questions.answer: Instruments such as tiltmeters detect ground swelling, seismometers detect small earthquakes as magma rises, and gas sensors measure rising sulphur dioxide. This gives warning so people can be evacuated in time, reducing deaths.
ms: 1 mark per valid point, with extra marks for development. E.g. seismometers detect increased small earthquakes as magma rises (1); tiltmeters/GPS detect the volcano bulging (1); gas emissions such as sulphur dioxide increase before eruptions (1); satellites detect heat (thermal imaging) (1).
Development marks: this gives warning time (1) so people can be evacuated before the eruption, reducing deaths and injuries (1); valuable possessions/livestock can be moved (1).
Max 2 if only methods listed with no explanation of how they reduce effects.
questions.tip: The question asks how they REDUCE EFFECTS. Every method must link to warning and evacuation.

questions.q: Explain why earthquakes occur at destructive plate margins.
questions.answer: The denser oceanic plate is subducted under the continental plate. Friction causes the plates to stick, pressure builds up and is suddenly released as the plates jerk, sending seismic waves out from the focus.
ms: Oceanic plate is denser and subducts beneath continental plate (1).
Plates get stuck due to friction (1).
Pressure/stress builds up over time (1).
Pressure is suddenly released as plates slip, sending out seismic waves / shock waves from the focus (1).
questions.tip: Use the sequence: stuck, pressure builds, sudden release. Missing the build-up step is the most common reason for losing a mark.

questions.q: Using a named example, describe the secondary effects of an earthquake in a lower income country (LIC).
questions.answer: Nepal 2015: landslides and avalanches (including on Mount Everest) blocked roads and killed people; around 3 million people were left homeless and lived in temporary shelters; damage to historic sites in Kathmandu reduced tourism income; rebuilding cost billions of dollars.
ms: 1 mark per valid secondary effect, with development marks for detail. E.g. landslides blocked roads, slowing aid (1+1); avalanche on Mount Everest killed climbers at base camp (1); millions left homeless lived in temporary shelters into the monsoon/winter (1); loss of tourism income because UNESCO heritage sites in Kathmandu were damaged (1+1); disease risk from lack of clean water (1).
Max 2 if no named example. Do not credit primary effects (deaths from collapsing buildings) unless clearly linked to a secondary effect.
questions.tip: Secondary effects only. Many students list deaths from building collapse, which is a primary effect and earns nothing.

questions.q: Compare the effects of, and responses to, a tectonic hazard in two areas of contrasting levels of wealth.
questions.answer: Chile 2010 (HIC, M8.8): about 500 deaths, quick response, power and water restored to most people within days, rebuilding plan and national appeal. Nepal 2015 (LIC, M7.8): almost 9,000 deaths, about 3 million homeless, response relied heavily on international aid, landslides slowed rescue. Effects were worse in Nepal because of poorer building quality, weaker infrastructure and less money for response.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Named HIC and LIC events with dates and magnitudes. Chile: M8.8, 27 Feb 2010, around 500 deaths, tsunami damaged coastal towns, Concepción area badly affected, emergency services responded fast, most power/water restored within around 10 days, national appeal raised money, government housing reconstruction plan. Nepal: M7.8, 25 April 2015, almost 9,000 deaths, about 3 million homeless, Kathmandu heritage sites destroyed, landslides and Everest avalanche, aid from UK, India, China and NGOs, rescue helicopters, slow access to rural areas, rebuilding slow. Direct comparison words needed (whereas, however, in contrast) for Level 3. Explanation linked to wealth, building codes, preparedness, infrastructure.
questions.tip: This is a COMPARE question. Writing two separate case studies with no comparison words caps you at Level 2.

questions.q: 'Planning is the most effective way to reduce the risk from tectonic hazards.' To what extent do you agree with this statement? (9 marks + 3 SPaG)
questions.answer: Planning (evacuation drills, emergency kits, hazard mapping, land-use zoning) is highly effective and cheap, e.g. drills in Chile and Japan. But it works best combined with protection (earthquake-resistant buildings, which explain Chile's low death toll of about 500 at M8.8) and monitoring/prediction (useful for volcanoes, not earthquakes). In LICs like Nepal, lack of money limits all three. Judgement: planning is essential but protection may be more effective for earthquakes, because buildings kill people, not the shaking itself.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): Thorough knowledge and understanding. Detailed, well-balanced evaluation that considers both sides. Detailed, accurate place-specific case study evidence (named places, facts, figures). Reaches a clear, substantiated judgement that answers 'to what extent' / 'how far'.

Level 2 (4-6 marks): Reasonable knowledge and understanding. Partly balanced evaluation, may favour one side. Some case study detail but it is general or patchy. A judgement is given but only partly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Limited knowledge. Simple, unbalanced points with little evaluation. Little or no case study evidence. No clear judgement.

SPaG (3 marks): High performance 3 = accurate spelling and punctuation, grammar controls meaning, wide range of geographical terms used precisely. Intermediate 2 = considerable accuracy, good range of terms. Threshold 1 = reasonable accuracy, some terms used.

Indicative content: Planning: hazard maps restrict building in high-risk zones; evacuation routes; emergency drills (Japan has a national disaster prevention day on 1 September); emergency supplies. Strengths: cheap, suitable for LICs. Limits: relies on people following plans, cannot stop buildings collapsing. Protection: reinforced buildings, cross-bracing, rubber shock absorbers, rolling counterweights; Chile's building codes kept deaths to about 500 at M8.8 compared with almost 9,000 in Nepal at M7.8. Monitoring/prediction: tiltmeters, gas sensors, seismometers give warning for volcanoes; earthquakes cannot be reliably predicted. Judgement depends on hazard type and wealth of country.
questions.tip: Use all four strategies (monitoring, prediction, protection, planning) and come down on one side. Case study evidence is needed for Level 3.

questions.q: Explain why the effects of tectonic hazards are often greater in LICs than in HICs.
questions.answer: LICs have poorer quality buildings without earthquake-resistant design, so more collapse; less money for monitoring and emergency services; weaker infrastructure slows rescue; poorer healthcare means injuries become deaths; many people live in dense informal settlements.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Building quality (no building codes or not enforced, unreinforced brick/mud). Less monitoring and warning. Fewer trained emergency services and equipment. Poor roads and rural access (landslides in Nepal blocked roads). Limited healthcare, clean water so disease spreads. Dense urban populations in squatter settlements. Reliance on foreign aid, slower recovery. HICs: insurance, money to rebuild. Use of Nepal vs Chile figures for Level 3.
questions.tip: Use 'which means' chains. A list of differences with no explanation stays in Level 1.

questions.q: Define the term 'natural hazard'.
questions.answer: A natural event or process that poses a threat to people and property.
ms: A natural process/event (1) that threatens people or property (both needed for the mark).
questions.tip: A volcano erupting on an uninhabited island is not a hazard. The threat to people is essential.

questions.q: State two factors that affect hazard risk.
questions.answer: Population growth/urbanisation, poverty, farming in hazard areas, climate change.
ms: 1 mark each, max 2: urbanisation / high population density (1); poverty / poor housing (1); farming in at-risk areas e.g. floodplains or volcanic slopes (1); climate change increasing frequency/intensity of some hazards (1).
questions.tip: Factors that change risk, not types of hazard.

questions.q: At approximately what latitude is the high pressure belt that separates the Hadley and Ferrel cells?
ms: Air sinks at about 30° N and S, creating high pressure. This is where most hot deserts are found.
questions.tip: Low pressure at 0° and 60°, high pressure at 30° and the poles. Learn the pattern.

questions.q: What is the minimum sea surface temperature generally needed for a tropical storm to form?
ms: Tropical storms need warm ocean water of at least about 26-27°C to supply heat energy and moisture.
questions.tip: Some textbooks quote 26.5°C. Either is fine but be consistent.

questions.q: Why do tropical storms not form directly on the equator (between 0° and 5°)?
options: The Coriolis effect is too weak to make the storm spin
ms: The Coriolis effect, caused by Earth's rotation, is almost zero at the equator, so the air does not start to spin.
questions.tip: Remember the 5-30° belt and the reason (Coriolis).

questions.q: Which part of a tropical storm has calm conditions and sinking air?
ms: In the eye, cool air sinks, so it is calm and often clear. The eyewall around it has the strongest winds and heaviest rain.
questions.tip: Don't confuse the eye (calm) with the eyewall (most violent).

questions.q: Typhoon Haiyan struck the Philippines in:
ms: Haiyan made landfall on 8 November 2013. August 2005 is Hurricane Katrina.
questions.tip: Know the date, the country and the worst-hit city (Tacloban).

questions.q: Which surface wind is formed as air moves from the subtropical high pressure belt towards the equator?
ms: Air flows at the surface from high pressure at 30° to low pressure at the equator. These are the trade winds, deflected by the Coriolis effect.
questions.tip: The UK is in the westerlies, which blow from 30° towards 60°.

questions.q: Which statement about the possible effect of climate change on tropical storms is most accurate?
options: Climate change has no possible effect on tropical storms
Warmer oceans may increase storm intensity and the area where they can form
Storms will only form at the equator
Storms will become less intense as oceans warm
ms: Higher sea temperatures provide more energy, so storms may become more intense and could form over a wider latitude range. Frequency may not increase.
questions.tip: Scientists are more confident about intensity rising than frequency rising. Saying 'more storms' without qualification is weak.

questions.q: Describe the global distribution of tropical storms.
questions.answer: They form over warm tropical oceans between about 5° and 30° north and south of the equator, e.g. the Caribbean, the western Pacific near the Philippines, and the Bay of Bengal.
ms: Between 5° and 30° N and S of the equator / in the tropics (1).
Over oceans, named example of area e.g. Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, western Pacific, Indian Ocean / Bay of Bengal (1).
Allow: not found in the South Atlantic / not on the equator (1).
questions.tip: Distribution means WHERE. Don't explain why they form unless asked.

questions.q: Explain how a tropical storm forms.
questions.answer: Warm ocean (over 27°C) heats air, which rises rapidly, creating low pressure. Rising air cools and condenses, releasing heat which powers the storm. The Coriolis effect makes it spin. Cool air sinks in the centre forming the eye. It loses energy over land or cooler water.
ms: Ocean water at least 26-27°C heats the air above (1).
Warm moist air rises rapidly creating low pressure / more air is drawn in (1).
Rising air cools and condenses forming cumulonimbus clouds, releasing heat energy (latent heat) which powers the storm (1).
Coriolis effect causes the system to spin (1). Allow: cool air sinks in the centre to form the eye (1).
questions.tip: Sequence matters. Include condensation releasing heat; it is what keeps the storm going.

questions.q: Using a named tropical storm, describe its primary effects.
questions.answer: Typhoon Haiyan, Philippines, November 2013: winds of over 300 km/h and a storm surge of around 5 m flattened Tacloban, where around 90% of the city was destroyed. Around 6,300 people died, and over a million houses were damaged or destroyed.
ms: Named storm and place (needed for full marks).

1 mark per accurate primary effect with development: e.g. about 6,300 deaths (1); storm surge up to around 5 m flooded coastal areas (1); around 90% of Tacloban destroyed (1); Tacloban airport terminal badly damaged (1); over 1 million houses damaged or destroyed (1); power lines and crops destroyed (1).
Do not credit secondary effects (looting, disease, food shortages).
questions.tip: Primary only. Looting in Tacloban and rice shortages are secondary.

questions.q: Explain how the global atmospheric circulation produces low pressure and high rainfall at the equator.
questions.answer: The sun's rays are concentrated at the equator so the ground is heated intensely. Warm air rises, creating low pressure. Rising air cools and condenses to form clouds, giving heavy convectional rainfall.
ms: Intense heating at the equator because the sun is overhead (1).
Warm air rises, giving low pressure at the surface (1).
Rising air cools, condenses and forms clouds/rain (1).
questions.tip: Name the cell if you can (Hadley cell) and use the word 'condenses'.

questions.q: Using a named example, explain how the immediate and long-term responses to a tropical storm helped people.
questions.answer: Haiyan 2013: immediate responses included the UK sending HMS Daring and aircraft, the US military helping clear Tacloban airport, field hospitals, food, water and emergency shelters. Long-term: 'cash for work' schemes paid people to clear debris, rebuilding of homes with stronger designs, more cyclone shelters, mangrove replanting and no-build zones along the coast.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Immediate: evacuation of around 800,000 people before landfall; international aid including UK (HMS Daring) and US military; airport reopened to fly in supplies; emergency shelters, food, water, medical teams; NGOs such as Red Cross and Plan International. Long-term: UN and other agencies funded recovery; 'cash for work'; rebuilding homes to stronger standards; new storm shelters; no-build zones in coastal areas; mangroves replanted to absorb storm surge; rice and coconut farming rebuilt. Must explain HOW each helped (saved lives, restored income, reduced future risk).
questions.tip: Split into immediate and long-term clearly. Level 3 needs place-specific detail, not generic 'aid was sent'.

questions.q: 'The secondary effects of tropical storms are more serious than the primary effects.' Using a named example, to what extent do you agree? (9 marks + 3 SPaG)
questions.answer: Haiyan: primary effects were severe (around 6,300 deaths, 90% of Tacloban destroyed, 5 m storm surge). Secondary effects were also severe and longer lasting: about 4 million people displaced, shortages of food and water, looting, disease risk, loss of income as crops (rice, coconut) were destroyed, outbreaks of violence. Judgement could argue secondary effects affected more people for longer, but primary effects caused most deaths.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): Thorough knowledge and understanding. Detailed, well-balanced evaluation that considers both sides. Detailed, accurate place-specific case study evidence (named places, facts, figures). Reaches a clear, substantiated judgement that answers 'to what extent' / 'how far'.

Level 2 (4-6 marks): Reasonable knowledge and understanding. Partly balanced evaluation, may favour one side. Some case study detail but it is general or patchy. A judgement is given but only partly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Limited knowledge. Simple, unbalanced points with little evaluation. Little or no case study evidence. No clear judgement.

SPaG (3 marks): High performance 3 = accurate spelling and punctuation, grammar controls meaning, wide range of geographical terms used precisely. Intermediate 2 = considerable accuracy, good range of terms. Threshold 1 = reasonable accuracy, some terms used.

Indicative content: Primary: wind over 300 km/h, storm surge around 5 m, about 6,300 deaths, over a million houses damaged/destroyed, airport damaged, power cut. Secondary: around 4 million displaced, 14 million affected, food and water shortages, looting in Tacloban, disease from contaminated water, loss of crops and fishing boats damaging livelihoods, rice prices rose, slow rebuilding. Judgement: 'serious' can be measured by deaths (primary), number affected and duration (secondary), economic cost. Best answers define seriousness and argue consistently.
questions.tip: Define what 'serious' means in your answer (deaths? people affected? how long it lasts?), then judge. That is what gets Level 3.

questions.q: Explain how planning can reduce the effects of tropical storms.
questions.answer: Evacuation plans and routes allow people to leave before landfall; storm shelters give protection; education and drills mean people know what to do; emergency supplies are stored in advance. In the Philippines around 800,000 people were evacuated before Haiyan.
ms: 1 mark per method, plus development: e.g. evacuation routes and plans (1) allow people to move away from coast before storm surge (1); storm shelters built on stilts/raised ground (1) protect people who can't leave (1); education and drills (1) so people respond quickly to warnings (1); stockpile food, water, medicines (1).
Do not credit protection measures (sea walls, building design) or prediction unless linked to planning.
questions.tip: Planning is not the same as protection or prediction. Keep to plans, drills, shelters, evacuation.

questions.q: Describe two features of the structure of a tropical storm.
questions.answer: The eye is a calm, clear centre of sinking air about 10-50 km across. The eyewall surrounding it has the strongest winds, towering cumulonimbus clouds and heaviest rain.
ms: 1 mark each for two features described: eye, calm sinking air, low pressure (1); eyewall, strongest winds and heaviest rain (1); spiralling rain bands (1); large size, several hundred km across (1).
questions.tip: Describe, don't just name.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of extreme weather in the UK?
ms: A heatwave is extreme because it is well outside the normal range. The UK recorded 40.3°C at Coningsby, Lincolnshire, on 19 July 2022.
questions.tip: Extreme weather means much more severe than usual. Normal seasonal weather does not count.

questions.q: Which two rivers flooded the Somerset Levels in winter 2013-14?
ms: The Rivers Parrett and Tone burst their banks. Both were later dredged as part of the response.
questions.tip: Naming the rivers adds place-specific detail that pushes answers into Level 3.

questions.q: Which village on the Somerset Levels was cut off by the 2014 floods, so residents had to use boats?
ms: Muchelney was cut off for weeks. Boscastle (2004) and Cockermouth (2009) were different flood events; Mappleton is on the Holderness coast.
questions.tip: Mixing up UK case studies is a common way to lose credibility in a 6 or 9 marker.

questions.q: Which human factor is thought to have made the Somerset Levels floods worse?
options: Rivers had not been dredged for about 20 years, so they held less water
The Bridgwater tidal barrier stopped water draining
The area had recently been urbanised with new towns
Too many trees were planted on the levels
ms: Lack of dredging allowed silt to build up, reducing channel capacity. The Bridgwater tidal barrier was a later response, not a cause.
questions.tip: Separate physical causes (rainfall, high tides, low flat land) from human causes (no dredging).

questions.q: Describe two types of extreme weather that affect the UK.
questions.answer: Flooding from heavy or prolonged rainfall, e.g. Somerset 2014; heatwaves and drought, e.g. 40°C in July 2022. Also gales/storms, snow and ice.
ms: 1 mark for each type with a brief description or example, max 2. Accept: heavy rainfall/flooding, drought, heatwave, strong winds/storms, heavy snow, thunderstorms, cold spells.
Do not accept tropical storms/hurricanes hitting the UK.
questions.tip: Describe means say what it is like. A single word earns less than a short description with an example.

questions.q: Explain the causes of the Somerset Levels floods in 2014.
questions.answer: Physical: a series of Atlantic depressions brought very heavy, prolonged rain in December 2013 and January 2014, one of the wettest periods on record. The levels are low-lying and flat, and high tides stopped rivers draining to the sea. Human: rivers had not been dredged for around 20 years so were clogged with silt.
ms: Series of low pressure systems/depressions from the Atlantic (1).
Very heavy, prolonged rainfall: one of the wettest winters/Januarys on record, saturating the ground (1).
Low-lying, flat land close to sea level so water drains slowly / high tides and storm surges in the Bristol Channel prevented rivers draining (1).
Rivers Parrett and Tone not dredged for about 20 years, so silt reduced their capacity (1).
questions.tip: Mix physical and human causes. Saying only 'it rained a lot' gets 1 mark at most.

questions.q: Describe the social and economic effects of the Somerset Levels floods.
questions.answer: Social: around 600 homes flooded, Muchelney cut off, residents evacuated, people suffered stress. Economic: around 6,900 hectares of farmland flooded, over 1,000 livestock evacuated, roads closed and the main railway line between Bridgwater and Taunton disrupted, local businesses lost trade.
ms: Social: over 600 homes flooded (1); villages such as Muchelney cut off, residents needed boats (1); people evacuated / power cut (1).

Economic: around 6,900 hectares of farmland under water (1); farmers had to move over 1,000 livestock / lost income (1); roads closed and the Bridgwater to Taunton railway disrupted, costing businesses (1); total cost estimated in the tens of millions of pounds (1).
Max 3 if only social or only economic effects given.
questions.tip: Two effect types are asked for, so cover both. Use figures if you know them.

questions.q: Evaluate the management responses to the Somerset Levels floods.
questions.answer: A £100 million 20-year Flood Action Plan was produced. About 8 km of the Rivers Parrett and Tone were dredged, river banks were raised and strengthened, some roads were raised, and a tidal barrier was planned for Bridgwater. Dredging was popular locally and removed silt, but critics argue it is expensive, needs repeating and may not stop flooding from such extreme rainfall. The plan should reduce risk but cannot remove it.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Responses: Somerset Levels and Moors Flood Action Plan (20 years, around £100 million); dredging about 8 km of the Parrett and Tone (began March 2014); raising and strengthening banks; pumping stations upgraded; raising roads such as the one to Muchelney; tidal barrier for Bridgwater; homes flood-proofed. Evaluation: dredging popular with farmers but some experts say benefits are limited and silt returns; very high cost; protecting farmland vs homes; long time to complete. Judgement needed for Level 3.
questions.tip: Evaluate means weigh up strengths and weaknesses then judge. Describing responses alone stays at Level 2.

questions.q: Assess the evidence that weather in the UK is becoming more extreme.
questions.answer: Evidence for: record UK temperature of 40.3°C in July 2022; several of the UK's warmest years have been since 2000; record-breaking winter rainfall in 2013-14 and storms such as those in 2015-16 and 2020. Evidence against: the UK has always had extreme events (1953 floods, 1976 drought), the record is short, and one event does not prove a trend. Overall evidence suggests extremes are increasing, linked to climate change.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: For: 2022 heatwave (40.3°C at Coningsby, first time over 40°C); Somerset Levels 2014 wettest winter; Storm Desmond 2015; Beast from the East 2018; Met Office statistics show warmest years mostly since 2000. Against: historic extremes (1953 North Sea flood, 1976 drought, 1987 Great Storm); natural variability; limited length of reliable records. Judgement required.
questions.tip: Use 'assess' like 'evaluate': show both sides and a judgement backed by named events.

questions.q: Explain why the low-lying Somerset Levels are at risk of flooding.
questions.answer: The land is flat and close to (or below) sea level, so water drains away slowly. Rivers are tidal near the coast, so high tides can stop water flowing out to sea. Clay soils have low permeability, so water lies on the surface.
ms: Low-lying / near sea level so gradient is gentle and water drains slowly (1).
High tides in the Bristol Channel/Severn Estuary can block rivers from draining (1).
Impermeable clay soils / saturated ground means surface runoff (1). Allow: rivers silted up / historically drained wetland.
questions.tip: Link each feature to WHY it causes flooding.

questions.q: State the highest temperature ever recorded in the UK.
questions.answer: 40.3°C at Coningsby, Lincolnshire, on 19 July 2022.
ms: 40.3°C (1). Allow 'just over 40°C in July 2022'.
questions.tip: A precise figure shows the UK is experiencing more extreme weather.

questions.q: Suggest two ways people can reduce the impact of flooding on their homes.
questions.answer: Fit flood gates or boards on doors, move electrical sockets higher up walls, use tiled floors instead of carpet, keep sandbags.
ms: 1 mark each, max 2: flood boards/gates (1); raise sockets/boilers (1); tiled floors (1); sandbags (1); sign up for flood warnings (1); move valuables upstairs (1).
questions.tip: Keep to individual household actions when that's what is asked.

questions.q: Which of these is a natural cause of climate change?
ms: Orbital changes alter the amount of solar energy reaching Earth over long timescales. The others are human causes.
questions.tip: Natural causes: orbital changes, solar output, volcanic eruptions. Learn all three.

questions.q: Ice cores provide evidence for climate change because:
options: Trapped air bubbles show past carbon dioxide levels and temperature
They show annual growth rings of trees
They show the dates of historical paintings
ms: Air bubbles trapped in ice preserve past atmospheric gases; ice cores from Antarctica go back about 800,000 years.
questions.tip: Tree rings and ice cores are both proxy evidence. Know what each one actually shows.

questions.q: How do large volcanic eruptions usually affect global temperature in the short term?
options: They warm the Earth by releasing heat
They cool the Earth because ash and sulphur dioxide block sunlight
They permanently raise temperatures by several degrees
ms: Ash and sulphur aerosols reflect solar radiation. Mount Pinatubo (1991) cooled global temperatures by about 0.5°C for around a year or two.
questions.tip: The effect is short-term cooling, not long-term warming.

questions.q: Which is an example of ADAPTATION to climate change rather than mitigation?
ms: Adaptation means responding to the effects of climate change. Mitigation means reducing the causes (cutting greenhouse gas emissions or removing them).
questions.tip: Mitigation = reduce the cause. Adaptation = cope with the effects. This distinction is tested every year.

questions.q: Outline two pieces of evidence for climate change.
questions.answer: Global temperature records since about 1850 show warming of over 1°C; sea level has risen by about 20 cm since 1900; glaciers and Arctic sea ice are shrinking; ice cores show CO₂ link with temperature.
ms: 1 mark per valid piece of evidence, max 2: e.g. global temperature data / thermometer records (1); ice cores (1); tree rings (1); shrinking glaciers or Arctic sea ice (1); sea level rise (1); paintings/diaries showing past climate e.g. frost fairs (1); seasonal changes such as earlier flowering (1).
questions.tip: Outline asks for brief points. Two distinct pieces of evidence, not two examples of the same one.

questions.q: Explain how human activities are causing climate change.
questions.answer: Burning fossil fuels for energy and transport releases CO₂. Deforestation removes trees that absorb CO₂ and releases carbon when burned. Agriculture, especially cattle and rice, releases methane. These gases enhance the greenhouse effect, trapping more heat.
ms: Burning fossil fuels in power stations/cars releases carbon dioxide (1).
Deforestation reduces CO₂ absorption and burning releases CO₂ (1).
Agriculture: cattle and rice paddies release methane (1).
More greenhouse gases trap more heat / enhanced greenhouse effect so global temperature rises (1).
questions.tip: You need the mechanism (enhanced greenhouse effect) to get full marks, not just a list of activities.

questions.q: Describe the possible effects of climate change on people and the environment.
questions.answer: Environment: sea level rise floods coastal areas, coral bleaching, species extinction, melting ice. People: more extreme weather damages homes, crops fail from drought, water shortages, low-lying countries such as Bangladesh and the Maldives at risk, diseases such as malaria spread to new areas.
ms: 1 mark per valid effect with extra mark for development. Environment: rising sea levels flood low-lying coasts (1); ice caps and glaciers melt (1); coral bleaching (1); habitat loss and species extinction (1).

People: crop yields fall in some areas, food shortages (1); water shortages (1); more frequent extreme weather (1); millions displaced from low-lying areas e.g. Bangladesh/Maldives (1); spread of diseases e.g. malaria (1).
Max 3 if only people or only environment.
questions.tip: Use 'may' or 'possible'. Effects are predictions, not certainties.

questions.q: Explain how managing climate change involves both mitigation and adaptation.
questions.answer: Mitigation reduces the causes: alternative energy such as wind and solar, carbon capture and storage, planting trees, and international agreements like the Paris Agreement (2015) to keep warming well below 2°C. Adaptation responds to effects: changing farming (drought-resistant crops, irrigation), managing water supply (reservoirs, water meters), and reducing sea level rise risk (flood barriers, raising buildings). Both are needed because some warming is already locked in.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Mitigation: renewables, nuclear, carbon capture and storage, afforestation, international agreements (Kyoto 1997, Paris 2015, aim to limit to 1.5°C). Adaptation: agricultural changes (new crops, irrigation), water management (desalination, hosepipe bans, reservoirs), coastal defence (Thames Barrier, Maldives raised islands/sea walls). Link explaining why both needed for Level 3.
questions.tip: Clearly label which strategies are mitigation and which are adaptation.

questions.q: 'International agreements are the most effective way of managing climate change.' To what extent do you agree? (9 marks + 3 SPaG)
questions.answer: Agreements like the Paris Agreement (2015) set targets for almost every country to keep warming well below 2°C, so they tackle a global problem. But targets are voluntary and countries may not meet them; the USA left in 2020, rejoined in 2021 and withdrew again from 2025. Alternative energy, carbon capture and tree planting actually cut emissions, and adaptation protects people now. Judgement: agreements are vital to coordinate action but are only effective if backed by real national strategies.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): Thorough knowledge and understanding. Detailed, well-balanced evaluation that considers both sides. Detailed, accurate place-specific case study evidence (named places, facts, figures). Reaches a clear, substantiated judgement that answers 'to what extent' / 'how far'.

Level 2 (4-6 marks): Reasonable knowledge and understanding. Partly balanced evaluation, may favour one side. Some case study detail but it is general or patchy. A judgement is given but only partly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Limited knowledge. Simple, unbalanced points with little evaluation. Little or no case study evidence. No clear judgement.

SPaG (3 marks): High performance 3 = accurate spelling and punctuation, grammar controls meaning, wide range of geographical terms used precisely. Intermediate 2 = considerable accuracy, good range of terms. Threshold 1 = reasonable accuracy, some terms used.

Indicative content: For: climate change is global so needs global action; Paris 2015 nearly 200 countries; targets drive national laws (UK net zero by 2050). Against: pledges not legally binding; countries can withdraw; emissions still rising globally; poorer countries argue they need to develop. Other strategies: renewables (UK wind power growth), carbon capture (still small scale and expensive), afforestation, adaptation. Judgement needed.
questions.tip: Compare the named strategy against others. A Level 3 answer argues which is MOST effective, not just whether one works.

questions.q: Explain how natural factors can cause climate change.
questions.answer: Milankovitch cycles: changes in Earth's orbit (eccentricity about 100,000 years), tilt and wobble change how much solar energy Earth gets, causing glacial and interglacial periods. Solar output varies with sunspot activity, e.g. the Maunder Minimum (1645-1715) during the Little Ice Age. Large volcanic eruptions release ash and sulphur dioxide which reflect sunlight and cool the Earth for a year or two, e.g. Pinatubo 1991.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Orbital changes: eccentricity (around 100,000 year cycle), axial tilt (around 41,000 years), precession/wobble (around 26,000 years). Solar output: sunspots, Maunder Minimum linked to Little Ice Age. Volcanic activity: Pinatubo 1991 cooled by about 0.5°C; Tambora 1815 'year without a summer' 1816. Level 3 explains mechanism and timescale.
questions.tip: Explain how each one changes the energy reaching or leaving the Earth.

questions.q: Explain how the greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm.
questions.answer: Short-wave radiation from the sun passes through the atmosphere and heats the Earth's surface. The surface gives off long-wave radiation. Greenhouse gases such as CO₂ and methane absorb some of this and re-radiate it, trapping heat in the atmosphere.
ms: Short-wave solar radiation passes through the atmosphere (1).
Earth's surface emits long-wave (infrared) radiation (1).
Greenhouse gases absorb/trap some long-wave radiation, warming the atmosphere (1).
questions.tip: Short-wave in, long-wave out. Getting these the wrong way round loses marks.

questions.q: Give the name of the period from about 1300 to 1870 when the UK and Europe were colder than average.
questions.answer: The Little Ice Age.
ms: Little Ice Age (1).
questions.tip: Frost fairs on the frozen River Thames are evidence from this period.

questions.q: Which organisms break down dead plant and animal matter, returning nutrients to the soil?
ms: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead material and release nutrients, which plants then take up.
questions.tip: Decomposers are key to nutrient cycling. Name examples (fungi, bacteria) for extra credit.

questions.q: In a food chain, what is a producer?
options: An animal that eats other animals
A green plant that makes its own food by photosynthesis
ms: Producers convert the sun's energy into food through photosynthesis.
questions.tip: Energy enters an ecosystem through producers.

questions.q: In a small pond ecosystem, the number of herons that eat frogs falls sharply. What is the most likely short-term effect?
options: Frog numbers rise, so insect numbers may fall
ms: With fewer predators, frogs increase. More frogs eat more insects, so insect numbers may fall. Change in one component affects others.
questions.tip: Follow the knock-on chain at least two steps. That is how you show interdependence.

questions.q: Which global biome is mainly found around 30° N and S of the equator?
ms: Sinking air at about 30° creates high pressure and very little rainfall, so hot deserts form there.
questions.tip: Link biome location to the global atmospheric circulation.

questions.q: Define the term 'ecosystem'.
questions.answer: A community of plants and animals (biotic) interacting with each other and with their physical environment (abiotic), such as soil, water and climate.
ms: Community of living organisms / plants and animals (1).
Interacting with the non-living (abiotic) environment, e.g. climate, soil, water (1).
questions.tip: You need both the living and non-living parts.

questions.q: Using a named example of a small-scale UK ecosystem, explain how its components are interdependent.
questions.answer: A freshwater pond: plants (reeds, algae) photosynthesise using sunlight and provide oxygen and food for insects and snails. These are eaten by frogs and fish, which are eaten by herons. When organisms die, decomposers such as bacteria return nutrients to the water and mud, which plants use to grow.
ms: Named small-scale ecosystem e.g. a pond, hedgerow or Epping Forest woodland (needed for full marks).
Producers rely on abiotic factors (sunlight, water, nutrients) (1).
Food chain/web link: consumers depend on producers for food (1).
Predator-prey link with named organisms (1).
Decomposers return nutrients to soil/water for producers (nutrient cycling) (1).
questions.tip: Interdependence means 'depend on each other'. Show links in both directions, not just a food chain.

questions.q: Explain how nutrient cycling works in an ecosystem.
questions.answer: Plants take nutrients from the soil to grow. When plants and animals die or drop leaves, litter builds up. Decomposers break it down, returning nutrients to the soil to be used again.
ms: Plants absorb nutrients from the soil (1).
Dead organisms/leaf fall form litter (1).
Decomposers break down litter and return nutrients to the soil (1).
questions.tip: Name the three stores if you can: biomass, litter, soil.

questions.q: Describe the global distribution of tropical rainforests and hot deserts.
questions.answer: Tropical rainforests are found along the equator, between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, e.g. the Amazon, Congo Basin and South-East Asia. Hot deserts are found around 30° N and S, e.g. the Sahara in North Africa, the Thar in India/Pakistan and much of central Australia.
ms: Rainforests along/near the equator (1), named example e.g. Amazon, Congo, Indonesia/Malaysia (1).
Hot deserts around 15-30° N and S / near the tropics (1), named example e.g. Sahara, Thar, Kalahari, Australian deserts (1).
questions.tip: Use latitude and named continents, not vague terms like 'in hot places'.

questions.q: Explain how a change to one component of an ecosystem can affect other components.
questions.answer: Example: farmers adding fertiliser runs off into a pond, so algae grow rapidly (eutrophication). Algae block light, so other plants die. Bacteria decomposing dead material use up oxygen, so fish die. Fewer fish means fewer herons. Another example: removing hedgerows reduces habitat and food for birds and insects.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Any change (natural or human): fertiliser run-off and eutrophication; draining a pond; removing a predator; hedgerow removal; drought; new species introduced. Level 3 needs a clear chain of at least three linked effects across biotic and abiotic components, ideally using a named small-scale ecosystem.
questions.tip: Build a chain: change, then effect 1, which leads to effect 2, which leads to effect 3.

questions.q: Explain how climate influences the characteristics of global ecosystems.
questions.answer: Temperature and rainfall control which plants can grow. Near the equator, high temperatures (around 27°C) and over 2,000 mm of rain give dense rainforest with high biodiversity. At 30° the sinking air brings little rain (under 250 mm), so deserts have sparse, drought-adapted plants. Cold tundra has short growing seasons, so only low plants grow.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Climate is controlled by global circulation: low pressure at equator (rainforest), high pressure at 30° (deserts), cold polar air (tundra), temperate (UK deciduous forest, seasonal). Vegetation, soil and animal adaptations follow climate. Level 3 links climate figures to ecosystem features.
questions.tip: Use figures for temperature and rainfall and link them to vegetation.

questions.q: Using a food web, explain what is meant by a primary consumer.
questions.answer: An animal that eats producers (plants), e.g. a snail or caterpillar, gaining energy from them.
ms: Eats plants/producers (1).
Valid example e.g. rabbit, snail, insect, caterpillar (1).
questions.tip: Primary = first level of consumer = herbivore.

questions.q: State two characteristics of the tundra biome.
questions.answer: Very cold with long winters, low precipitation, permafrost, short growing season, low plants such as mosses and lichens.
ms: 1 mark each, max 2: very cold/below freezing for most of the year (1); low precipitation (1); permafrost (1); short growing season (1); low-growing plants, mosses and lichens, no trees (1).
questions.tip: Tundra is cold, not hot. Students confuse it with savanna.

questions.q: Which layer of the tropical rainforest is made up of the tallest trees, up to around 50 m, that stick out above the main canopy?
ms: Emergents rise above the canopy. Many have buttress roots to support them.
questions.tip: Learn the layers top to bottom: emergents, canopy, under canopy, shrub layer, forest floor.

questions.q: Why are tropical rainforest soils (latosols) usually infertile?
options: Heavy rain leaches nutrients and plants take them up quickly
The soil is frozen for part of the year
ms: Nutrients are held mainly in the biomass. Heavy rain washes (leaches) nutrients down and plants absorb any that are released quickly.
questions.tip: Decomposition is FAST in the hot, wet climate. Saying it is slow is a classic error.

questions.q: Which is the biggest single cause of deforestation in the Amazon rainforest?
ms: Clearing land for cattle pasture is the biggest cause in the Brazilian Amazon. In Malaysia, palm oil plantations are a major cause.
questions.tip: Match causes to your case study. Don't use Malaysia's palm oil for the Amazon or vice versa.

questions.q: Malaysia is one of the world's largest producers of which crop, linked to rainforest clearance?
ms: Malaysia is the world's second largest producer of palm oil (after Indonesia). Large areas of forest, especially in Sabah and Sarawak, have been cleared for plantations.
questions.tip: Use the regions Sabah and Sarawak (Borneo) to make your case study place-specific.

questions.q: Describe two characteristics of the tropical rainforest climate.
questions.answer: Hot all year, around 27°C, with a small annual range. Very wet, over 2,000 mm of rain per year, with heavy convectional rainfall most afternoons.
ms: High temperatures all year, around 26-28°C / small temperature range (1).
High rainfall, over 2,000 mm per year / rain almost every day (1).
Allow: humid; no distinct seasons.
questions.tip: Give figures where you can. 'Hot and wet' alone is basic.

questions.q: Explain two ways plants have adapted to the tropical rainforest environment.
questions.answer: Drip tips on leaves let heavy rain run off quickly so leaves don't rot or grow algae. Buttress roots support tall emergent trees in shallow soils. Lianas climb trees to reach sunlight. Epiphytes grow on branches to get light and take nutrients from the air and rain.
ms: 1 mark for adaptation + 1 mark for explanation, x2. Drip tips (1) shed water to prevent rotting/algae (1). Buttress roots (1) support tall trees in shallow soil (1). Lianas (1) use trees to climb to sunlight (1). Epiphytes (1) live on branches to reach light (1). Thin smooth bark (1) as no need for insulation, stops plants climbing (1).
questions.tip: Each adaptation needs its reason linked to the environment.

questions.q: Using a named example, describe the economic and environmental impacts of deforestation.
questions.answer: Malaysia: economic benefits include jobs and export income from palm oil and timber, and the Bakun Dam in Sarawak produces HEP. Environmental impacts include loss of habitats (threatening orangutans), soil erosion, river silting, and increased CO₂ emissions from burning.
ms: Named example needed for full marks (Malaysia or Amazon).
Economic: jobs and income from logging/palm oil/cattle (1); export earnings for the country (1); HEP from dams e.g. Bakun Dam, Sarawak (1); loss of future income from tourism (1).
Environmental: loss of habitat and biodiversity e.g. orangutans (1); soil erosion and river silting (1); CO₂ released, contributing to climate change (1).
Max 3 if only economic or only environmental.
questions.tip: Cover both economic and environmental impacts, with at least one positive economic one.

questions.q: Explain how the tropical rainforest can be managed sustainably.
questions.answer: Selective logging removes only some mature trees so the forest regenerates. Replanting replaces trees cut down. Ecotourism earns money while keeping the forest. International agreements such as debt-for-nature swaps reduce debt in return for protection. Conservation and education raise awareness. Laws and protected areas restrict damaging activities.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Selective logging (helicopter removal reduces damage); replanting/afforestation; ecotourism (local guides, small groups, profits to locals); international agreements (CITES, hardwood regulations, FSC certification); debt reduction / debt-for-nature swaps (e.g. USA and Costa Rica); conservation areas/national parks; education. Level 3 explains how each balances economic use with keeping the forest for future generations.
questions.tip: Sustainable means meeting present needs without harming future generations. Use the word and show HOW each method does this.

questions.q: 'The benefits of deforestation outweigh the costs.' Using a named example, to what extent do you agree? (9 marks + 3 SPaG)
questions.answer: Malaysia: deforestation has brought jobs, export income from palm oil and timber, HEP from the Bakun Dam and roads to remote areas, supporting development. However, costs include loss of biodiversity (orangutans), indigenous people losing land, soil erosion, river pollution, and CO₂ emissions. Many benefits go to large companies, while the costs are long-term and global. Judgement: costs outweigh benefits unless it is managed sustainably.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): Thorough knowledge and understanding. Detailed, well-balanced evaluation that considers both sides. Detailed, accurate place-specific case study evidence (named places, facts, figures). Reaches a clear, substantiated judgement that answers 'to what extent' / 'how far'.

Level 2 (4-6 marks): Reasonable knowledge and understanding. Partly balanced evaluation, may favour one side. Some case study detail but it is general or patchy. A judgement is given but only partly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Limited knowledge. Simple, unbalanced points with little evaluation. Little or no case study evidence. No clear judgement.

SPaG (3 marks): High performance 3 = accurate spelling and punctuation, grammar controls meaning, wide range of geographical terms used precisely. Intermediate 2 = considerable accuracy, good range of terms. Threshold 1 = reasonable accuracy, some terms used.

Indicative content: Malaysia: palm oil (second largest producer), logging, mineral extraction (tin), HEP (Bakun Dam in Sarawak flooded a large area of forest and displaced thousands of indigenous people), roads, population pressure and resettlement schemes. Amazon alternative: cattle ranching, soya, Trans-Amazonian Highway (opened 1972), Carajás mine, Belo Monte dam. Benefits: jobs, export income, energy, development. Costs: biodiversity loss, indigenous displacement, soil erosion, climate change, flooding. Judgement on who benefits and timescale.
questions.tip: Level 3 needs named regions (Sarawak, Sabah), named projects and a final judgement that weighs short-term vs long-term.

questions.q: Explain why tropical rainforests have such high biodiversity.
questions.answer: The hot, wet climate all year gives a long growing season with no winter, so plants grow quickly and provide plenty of food. The forest's layers create many different habitats and niches. Rainforests are very old and stable, giving time for species to evolve. Fast nutrient cycling supports rapid growth.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Constant high temperatures and rainfall (27°C, 2,000 mm+); year-round growing season; vertical layering gives multiple niches; high primary productivity; stable ancient environment for evolution; interdependence (pollinators, seed dispersers). Rainforests cover a small part of the land surface but hold over half of the world's plant and animal species.
questions.tip: Explain WHY: link climate and structure to the number of species.

questions.q: Explain why tropical rainforests are important for the planet.
questions.answer: They store huge amounts of carbon, helping reduce climate change. They contain over half of the world's species, many used for medicines. They regulate the water cycle and local climate, and are home to indigenous people.
ms: 1 mark per valid reason, max 3: carbon store / absorb CO₂ (1); biodiversity / genetic resources (1); medicines (1); water cycle and rainfall regulation (1); home to indigenous tribes (1); resources e.g. timber, food (1).
questions.tip: Give three distinct reasons, not three versions of 'they absorb CO₂'.

questions.q: Give two causes of deforestation in Malaysia.
questions.answer: Palm oil plantations, commercial logging, energy (HEP dams e.g. Bakun), mineral extraction (tin), road building, settlement and population growth.
ms: 1 mark each, max 2: palm oil/commercial farming (1); logging (1); HEP, e.g. Bakun Dam (1); mining, e.g. tin (1); roads (1); settlement/resettlement and population pressure (1).
questions.tip: Match causes to the case study you're using.

questions.q: Hot deserts are usually defined as receiving less than how much rainfall per year?
ms: Deserts receive less than 250 mm of rainfall per year.
questions.tip: 2,000 mm is the rainforest figure. Don't swap them.

questions.q: Why do hot deserts have a very large daily (diurnal) temperature range?
options: Clear skies mean heat is quickly lost at night
ms: Without cloud cover, the sun heats the ground strongly during the day, but heat escapes quickly at night.
questions.tip: The answer is cloud cover, not winds.

questions.q: Which large irrigation canal has allowed farming to expand in the Thar Desert?
ms: The Indira Gandhi Canal in Rajasthan brings water from the Punjab rivers, allowing crops such as wheat and cotton.
questions.tip: This is the key fact for 'opportunities: farming' in the Thar case study.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of using appropriate technology to reduce desertification in the Sahel?
options: Placing lines of stones (bunds/magic stones) along contours
Drilling deep boreholes with diesel pumps
ms: Stone lines slow runoff, so water soaks in and soil is trapped. They are cheap, use local materials and need simple skills.
questions.tip: Appropriate technology = cheap, local materials, easy to maintain.

questions.q: Which is a HUMAN cause of desertification?
options: Reduced rainfall due to climate variation
ms: Overgrazing removes vegetation, exposing soil to wind and water erosion. Rainfall changes are physical causes (though climate change is partly human-caused).
questions.tip: Remember the human causes: overgrazing, over-cultivation, fuelwood removal, population growth.

questions.q: Describe one way animals have adapted to hot desert conditions.
questions.answer: Camels have humps that store fat which can be used for energy when food is scarce, and wide feet to stop them sinking into sand. Fennec foxes have large ears to lose heat and are nocturnal.
ms: 1 mark for adaptation, 1 for explanation. E.g. camel's hump stores fat (1) used for energy when food is scarce (1); long eyelashes (1) protect from sand (1); nocturnal (1) avoids daytime heat (1); fennec fox big ears (1) lose heat (1).
questions.tip: The second mark is always for explaining HOW the adaptation helps survival.

questions.q: Explain how plants are adapted to survive in hot deserts.
questions.answer: Cacti store water in thick stems and have spines instead of leaves to reduce water loss through transpiration. Long roots (e.g. mesquite) reach deep groundwater. Waxy coatings reduce water loss. Some seeds lie dormant for years and germinate quickly after rain.
ms: 2 x (adaptation + explanation). E.g. spines instead of leaves (1) reduce transpiration (1); thick waxy skin (1) reduces water loss (1); long tap roots (1) reach deep water (1); shallow widespread roots (1) absorb rain quickly (1); stems store water (1); seeds dormant until rain (1).
questions.tip: Use 'transpiration'. It is the key term examiners look for.

questions.q: Using a named example, describe the development opportunities in a hot desert.
questions.answer: Thar Desert (India/Pakistan): mineral extraction such as gypsum, feldspar and limestone; energy, e.g. large wind farms near Jaisalmer and strong solar potential; farming using irrigation from the Indira Gandhi Canal (wheat, cotton); tourism such as camel safaris and desert festivals around Jaisalmer.
ms: Named desert needed for full marks.

1 mark per opportunity, with development for named detail: mineral extraction e.g. gypsum, limestone, feldspar, kaolin (1+1); energy, wind (Jaisalmer Wind Park) and solar (1+1); farming with Indira Gandhi Canal irrigation (1+1); tourism, Jaisalmer, camel safaris, Desert Festival (1+1).
questions.tip: Name specific minerals and places. 'Tourism' alone gets 1 mark; 'camel safaris from Jaisalmer' gets 2.

questions.q: Using a named example, describe the challenges of developing a hot desert.
questions.answer: Thar Desert: extreme temperatures, often over 45°C in summer, make working outside hard; water supply is limited and evaporation from the canal is high; inaccessibility, as poor roads and moving sand dunes make transport difficult; salinisation of soils from irrigation.
ms: 1 mark per challenge plus development: extreme temperatures (1) make work and farming hard / high evaporation (1); water supply is scarce (1) and canals lose water by evaporation (1); inaccessibility / few roads (1) because sand dunes shift and distances are long (1); salinisation from irrigation reduces crop yields (1).
Named desert needed for full marks.
questions.tip: Challenges are the problems of developing the area, not just 'it is hot'.

questions.q: Explain the causes of desertification.
questions.answer: Population growth increases demand for food and fuel. Overgrazing by too many animals removes vegetation; over-cultivation exhausts soil; fuelwood collection removes trees whose roots held the soil. Exposed soil is eroded by wind and rain. Climate change brings lower, less reliable rainfall and higher evaporation, drying soils.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Human: population growth, overgrazing, over-cultivation, removal of fuelwood. Physical: climate change, reduced and unreliable rainfall, higher temperatures and evaporation. Soil erosion is the key mechanism: without plant cover and roots, soil is blown or washed away. Level 3 links causes together (population growth leads to overgrazing which leads to erosion), ideally with Sahel examples.
questions.tip: Show how the causes link together through a chain to soil erosion.

questions.q: 'Desertification can only be reduced through large-scale projects.' To what extent do you agree? (9 marks + 3 SPaG)
questions.answer: Large-scale projects such as the Great Green Wall across the Sahel aim to restore land across a whole region. However, many of the most successful strategies are small-scale and use appropriate technology: stone lines and bunds in Burkina Faso, tree planting by communities, water harvesting and soil management such as leaving land fallow. These are cheap and involve local people. Judgement: small-scale strategies are often more effective and sustainable, although large projects can coordinate action.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): Thorough knowledge and understanding. Detailed, well-balanced evaluation that considers both sides. Detailed, accurate place-specific case study evidence (named places, facts, figures). Reaches a clear, substantiated judgement that answers 'to what extent' / 'how far'.

Level 2 (4-6 marks): Reasonable knowledge and understanding. Partly balanced evaluation, may favour one side. Some case study detail but it is general or patchy. A judgement is given but only partly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Limited knowledge. Simple, unbalanced points with little evaluation. Little or no case study evidence. No clear judgement.

SPaG (3 marks): High performance 3 = accurate spelling and punctuation, grammar controls meaning, wide range of geographical terms used precisely. Intermediate 2 = considerable accuracy, good range of terms. Threshold 1 = reasonable accuracy, some terms used.

Indicative content: Large-scale: Great Green Wall (planned 8,000 km tree belt across Africa, launched 2007), progress slow and patchy. Small-scale: water management (drip irrigation, small dams, water harvesting); tree planting (shelter belts, roots bind soil, fuelwood); soil management (crop rotation, fallow, compost); appropriate technology (magic stones/stone lines, zai pits, solar cookers reducing fuelwood use). Judgement on cost, local ownership, maintenance, scale of problem.
questions.tip: Argue both sides with named schemes, then decide.

questions.q: Explain how the Thar Desert's physical characteristics create both opportunities and challenges.
questions.answer: High sunshine and clear skies give opportunities for solar energy, and strong winds support wind farms near Jaisalmer. Underlying rocks provide minerals. However, extreme heat and low rainfall mean water is scarce and crops need irrigation, which leads to salinisation; shifting sand dunes make building roads difficult.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Physical features: low rainfall (less than 250 mm in the west), high temperatures, clear skies, strong winds, sand dunes, mineral deposits. Opportunities: solar/wind, minerals, tourism based on landscape. Challenges: water supply, extreme temperatures, inaccessibility, salinisation. Level 3 explicitly links each physical feature to an opportunity or challenge.
questions.tip: Every point should start from a physical feature and show the link.

questions.q: Describe the climate of a hot desert.
questions.answer: Very low rainfall (under 250 mm a year), very hot days often over 40°C, but cold nights, giving a high daily temperature range.
ms: Low rainfall, under 250 mm/year (1).
Hot days with cold nights / high diurnal range (1).
questions.tip: Mention the cold nights; it shows deeper understanding.

questions.q: Define 'desertification'.
questions.answer: The process by which land in dry areas becomes more like desert, as it becomes drier and loses vegetation and soil.
ms: Land degradation in dry/semi-arid areas turning land into desert (1).
questions.tip: Desertification happens on desert fringes, e.g. the Sahel, not in the middle of the Sahara.

questions.q: Which type of wave has a strong backwash and erodes the coastline?
ms: Destructive waves are tall and frequent (around 10-14 per minute) with a backwash stronger than the swash, so they remove material.
questions.tip: Constructive = strong swash, builds beaches. Destructive = strong backwash, erodes.

questions.q: Which process of erosion involves rocks and pebbles being thrown at the cliff by waves?
ms: Abrasion is when material carried by waves is thrown against the cliff, wearing it away like sandpaper.
questions.tip: Attrition is rocks hitting EACH OTHER, getting smaller and rounder. Don't mix them up.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of the formation of a stack?
ms: A crack is widened into a cave, caves on either side of a headland join to form an arch, the arch roof collapses leaving a stack, which erodes into a stump.
questions.tip: Use Old Harry (stack) and Old Harry's Wife (stump) at Handfast Point near Swanage as the named example.

questions.q: At Swanage Bay, the bays have formed in which rock type?
ms: Swanage Bay is cut into softer sands and clays, while the resistant chalk forms Ballard Point/Handfast Point and limestone forms Peveril Point and Durlston Head.
questions.tip: Headlands and bays form on discordant coastlines with alternating hard and soft rock.

questions.q: Spurn Head, at the southern end of the Holderness coast, is an example of a:
ms: Spurn Head is a spit formed by longshore drift carrying material south, extending across the mouth of the Humber estuary.
questions.tip: Spits grow where the coastline changes direction. Mention the hooked end caused by changing wind direction.

questions.q: Why did the coastal defences at Mappleton cause increased erosion further south, for example at Cowden?
options: Tourists damaged the cliffs further south
The groynes trapped sediment, so less material reached beaches down-drift
The rock armour reflected wave energy south
The sea wall made the cliffs taller
ms: Two rock groynes trapped sand moving south by longshore drift. Beaches down-drift were starved of sediment, so cliffs there eroded faster.
questions.tip: This 'terminal groyne syndrome' is the key evaluation point for Mappleton.

questions.q: Which coastal management strategy involves allowing an area to flood naturally to create salt marsh?
ms: Managed retreat (coastal realignment) lets the sea flood low-value land, creating marsh that absorbs wave energy, e.g. at Medmerry, West Sussex.
questions.tip: Learn the hard engineering, soft engineering and managed retreat categories and an example of each.

questions.q: What is the name for the process by which material is moved along a beach in a zig-zag pattern?
ms: Swash moves material up the beach at the angle of the prevailing wind; backwash pulls it straight back down under gravity, so it zig-zags along the coast.
questions.tip: Mention prevailing wind and gravity when explaining it.

questions.q: Describe the difference between hydraulic power and solution.
questions.answer: Hydraulic power is the force of waves hitting the cliff, forcing air and water into cracks and breaking rock apart. Solution is when chemicals in seawater dissolve soluble rocks such as chalk and limestone.
ms: Hydraulic power: force of water/air compressed into cracks breaking rock (1).
Solution: rock dissolved by weak acids in seawater, e.g. limestone/chalk (1).
questions.tip: Describe each process precisely.

questions.q: Explain the formation of a wave-cut platform.
questions.answer: Destructive waves erode the base of a cliff between high and low tide by hydraulic power and abrasion, forming a wave-cut notch. The notch gets deeper until the overhanging cliff collapses. The cliff retreats and the process repeats, leaving a gently sloping rocky platform exposed at low tide.
ms: Erosion at the base of the cliff between high and low tide, by hydraulic power/abrasion (1).
Forms a wave-cut notch (1).
Cliff above becomes unsupported and collapses (1).
Repeated, so the cliff retreats inland leaving a flat rocky platform exposed at low tide (1).
questions.tip: Name erosion processes and the notch. Draw a sequence in your head: notch, overhang, collapse, retreat.

questions.q: Explain how a spit is formed.
questions.answer: Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast. Where the coastline changes direction, for example at a river mouth, material is deposited and builds out into the sea. Changes in wind direction can curve the end, forming a hook. Salt marsh forms in the sheltered area behind. Example: Spurn Head.
ms: Longshore drift transports sediment along the coast (1).
Coastline changes direction so material is deposited in sheltered/calmer water (1).
Deposition builds up a ridge extending out to sea (1).
Change in wind/wave direction creates a curved/hooked end; or salt marsh forms behind (1). Allow named example e.g. Spurn Head, Hurst Castle Spit.
questions.tip: Don't forget the change in coastline direction; it is why deposition happens there.

questions.q: Explain why the Holderness coast erodes so rapidly.
questions.answer: The cliffs are made of soft boulder clay (till) left by glaciers, which is easily eroded and slumps when wet. Long fetch across the North Sea produces powerful destructive waves. Narrow beaches give little protection because longshore drift carries sediment south. It is one of the fastest eroding coastlines in Europe, losing around 1.8 m per year on average.
ms: Soft boulder clay/till cliffs (1) that are easily eroded and slump when saturated (1).
Powerful destructive waves from the North Sea / long fetch from the north east (1).
Narrow beaches/longshore drift removes sediment south, so cliffs are not protected (1). Allow: average around 1.8 m a year / one of fastest eroding coasts in Europe (1).
questions.tip: Geology and waves are both needed. Use the term 'boulder clay'.

questions.q: Using a named example, evaluate a coastal management scheme.
questions.answer: Mappleton, Holderness (1991): about £2 million spent on two rock groynes and rock armour along the cliff base. Benefits: protected the village and the B1242 road; the beach widened. Costs: groynes trapped sediment so erosion increased to the south, e.g. at Cowden, where farmland and properties were lost. Judgement: successful locally but has moved the problem down the coast.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Mappleton: 1991, about £2 million, two rock groynes made of granite from Norway, rock armour at cliff foot, protected the village and the main coastal road (B1242). Down-drift effects: Cowden Farm and cliffs south eroding faster, conflict with landowners. Alternative Swanage: groynes replaced, beach nourishment, sea wall. Level 3 must judge success using economic, social, environmental criteria.
questions.tip: Evaluate = success AND failure, then judge. Use the scheme's date, cost and named down-drift places.

questions.q: 'Hard engineering is the best way to protect the coastline.' Using examples, to what extent do you agree? (9 marks + 3 SPaG)
questions.answer: Hard engineering (sea walls, rock armour, groynes, gabions) gives strong, immediate protection to valuable places, e.g. Mappleton's rock groynes and armour protected the village and road. But it is expensive (sea walls can cost thousands of pounds per metre), can look unnatural, and can move erosion elsewhere (Cowden). Soft engineering such as beach nourishment at Swanage and managed retreat at Medmerry work with nature and are cheaper long term but need maintenance or sacrifice land. Judgement: hard engineering is best only where land value is high.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): Thorough knowledge and understanding. Detailed, well-balanced evaluation that considers both sides. Detailed, accurate place-specific case study evidence (named places, facts, figures). Reaches a clear, substantiated judgement that answers 'to what extent' / 'how far'.

Level 2 (4-6 marks): Reasonable knowledge and understanding. Partly balanced evaluation, may favour one side. Some case study detail but it is general or patchy. A judgement is given but only partly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Limited knowledge. Simple, unbalanced points with little evaluation. Little or no case study evidence. No clear judgement.

SPaG (3 marks): High performance 3 = accurate spelling and punctuation, grammar controls meaning, wide range of geographical terms used precisely. Intermediate 2 = considerable accuracy, good range of terms. Threshold 1 = reasonable accuracy, some terms used.

Indicative content: Hard: sea walls (curve reflects waves; expensive, high maintenance), groynes (trap longshore drift, starve down-drift beaches), rock armour (cheap-ish, can be unattractive), gabions. Soft: beach nourishment and reprofiling (e.g. Swanage, natural look but must be repeated), dune regeneration. Managed retreat: Medmerry (2013, created intertidal habitat, protected around 350 homes). Judgement linked to cost-benefit analysis and Shoreline Management Plans (hold the line, advance, managed realignment, no active intervention).
questions.tip: Bring in cost-benefit analysis and named schemes. Level 3 judgement often depends on the value of what is being protected.

questions.q: Using a named example, explain how geology influences the formation of coastal landforms.
questions.answer: Swanage, Dorset: a discordant coastline where hard chalk and limestone alternate with soft sands and clays. The soft rock erodes faster, forming Swanage Bay and Studland Bay; the resistant chalk forms the headland of Handfast Point and limestone forms Durlston Head. Faults in the chalk headland have been widened into caves, arches and stacks such as Old Harry.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
