Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Discordant coastline (rock bands at right angles to the coast). Differential erosion. Swanage Bay (soft Wealden clays and sands), Studland Bay, Handfast Point and Ballard Point (chalk), Peveril Point and Durlston Head (Purbeck/Portland limestone). Old Harry stack and Old Harry's Wife stump. Faults/joints as weaknesses. Contrast with Lulworth Cove/concordant coast is credit-worthy.
questions.tip: Use 'discordant' and 'differential erosion'. Name headlands and bays.

questions.q: Explain how mass movement affects cliffs on the coast.
questions.answer: Heavy rain saturates cliffs such as boulder clay, making them heavier and reducing friction. Material then moves downhill under gravity by sliding, slumping (rotational movement) or rockfall. This makes the cliff retreat.
ms: Rain saturates the cliff, adding weight and lubricating it (1).
Material moves downhill under gravity (1).
Named type e.g. slumping (rotational slip), sliding, rockfall (1).
questions.tip: Mass movement is driven by gravity. Say this explicitly.

questions.q: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of beach nourishment.
questions.answer: Advantages: makes the beach wider so it absorbs wave energy, looks natural and benefits tourism, relatively cheap compared with sea walls. Disadvantages: sand is washed away so it must be repeated regularly; taking sand from the seabed elsewhere can harm marine habitats.
ms: Advantages: wider beach absorbs wave energy (1); natural appearance / good for tourism (1); cheaper than hard engineering (1).
Disadvantages: needs constant maintenance as material is removed by waves (1); dredging can damage seabed ecosystems (1); ongoing cost (1). Max 3 for one side.
questions.tip: Both sides are needed for 4 marks.

questions.q: State two features of a constructive wave.
questions.answer: Low height, long wavelength, low frequency (6-8 per minute), strong swash and weak backwash, so they deposit material.
ms: 1 mark each, max 2: low height (1); long wavelength (1); 6-8 waves per minute (1); swash stronger than backwash (1); builds up beaches (1).
questions.tip: Swash stronger than backwash is the most important feature.

questions.q: Name one landform of coastal erosion and one landform of coastal deposition.
questions.answer: Erosion: cave, arch, stack, stump, wave-cut platform, headland. Deposition: beach, spit, bar, sand dune.
ms: Erosion landform e.g. headland, bay, cave, arch, stack, stump, cliff, wave-cut platform (1).
Deposition landform e.g. beach, spit, bar, sand dune (1).
questions.tip: Bays are usually counted as erosion features.

questions.q: What is the name for a deep, steep-sided armchair-shaped hollow formed by glacial erosion?
ms: A corrie (also called a cirque or cwm) forms where snow collects in a north-facing hollow and rotational slip deepens it. Red Tarn on Helvellyn is a corrie lake.
questions.tip: Corrie lakes are called tarns. Use Red Tarn as the example.

questions.q: Which glacial erosion process involves rocks freezing onto the base of the glacier and being pulled away?
ms: In plucking, meltwater freezes onto rock; when the glacier moves it pulls pieces out. This leaves jagged surfaces.
questions.tip: Abrasion = rocks embedded in the ice scrape the bedrock (smooth). Plucking = pulls rock out (jagged).

questions.q: Striding Edge in the Lake District is an example of:
ms: Striding Edge is a knife-edge ridge between two corries, Red Tarn and Nethermost Cove, leading to Helvellyn.
questions.tip: Arête = two corries back-to-back. Pyramidal peak = three or more corries.

questions.q: Windermere, England's largest natural lake, is an example of a:
ms: Windermere is a ribbon lake: long and narrow, formed where the glacier eroded softer rock more deeply in the trough. It is about 18 km long.
questions.tip: Ribbon lakes form in troughs; tarns form in corries.

questions.q: Which landform is a smooth, elongated hill of till, with the steep end facing the direction the ice came from?
ms: Drumlins are egg-shaped mounds of till, with a blunt stoss end facing up-glacier and a tapered lee end. Found in the Eden Valley in Cumbria.
questions.tip: Roche moutonnée is a rock outcrop with a smooth upstream side and jagged downstream side; a drumlin is made of till.

questions.q: Why do corries in the UK mostly face north or north-east?
options: North-facing slopes get less sun, so snow stays longer and builds into ice
Prevailing winds blow from the north
The rock is softer on the north side
ms: In the Northern Hemisphere north-facing hollows are shaded, so snow accumulates and compacts into glacial ice instead of melting.
questions.tip: Link aspect to temperature and snow accumulation.

questions.q: Which of these is a land use conflict in the Lake District?
ms: Slate quarrying (e.g. Honister) provides jobs but brings noise, lorries and visual scars, conflicting with conservation and tourism in a National Park.
questions.tip: Other key conflicts: farming vs walkers, forestry, water supply (Thirlmere, Haweswater), tourism vs residents.

questions.q: Describe how freeze-thaw weathering breaks down rock.
questions.answer: Water enters cracks in rock during the day. At night it freezes and expands by about 9%, putting pressure on the rock. Repeated freezing and thawing widens the crack until pieces break off, forming scree.
ms: Water gets into cracks and freezes at night (1).
Ice expands (by about 9%), widening the crack; repeated over time until rock breaks off (1).
questions.tip: Mention repetition. One freeze does not break the rock.

questions.q: Explain how a corrie is formed.
questions.answer: Snow collects in a north-facing hollow and compacts into ice. The ice moves in a circular motion called rotational slip. Plucking steepens the back wall and abrasion deepens the base. A rock lip forms at the front where erosion is less. When the ice melts, water may collect to form a tarn, e.g. Red Tarn.
ms: Snow accumulates in a hollow (often north-facing) and compresses into ice (1).
Rotational slip / circular movement of the ice (1).
Plucking steepens the backwall and abrasion deepens the floor (1).
Lip forms at the front; after melting, a tarn may form, e.g. Red Tarn (1).
questions.tip: Name both erosion processes and where each acts.

questions.q: Explain the formation of a U-shaped valley (glacial trough).
questions.answer: A glacier moves down an existing V-shaped river valley. Because it is large and powerful it erodes the sides and floor by plucking and abrasion, making the valley wider, deeper and straighter. Interlocking spurs are cut off to form truncated spurs. When the ice melts a wide flat floor with steep sides remains, often with a misfit stream and ribbon lake.
ms: Glacier occupies a former V-shaped river valley (1).
Erodes sides and floor by abrasion and plucking, widening and deepening it (1).
Interlocking spurs are cut off, forming truncated spurs / straightened valley (1).
Leaves steep sides and flat floor; may contain ribbon lake or misfit stream / hanging valleys (1).
questions.tip: Start from the V-shaped valley; that's the starting point examiners want.

questions.q: Describe the difference between lateral and terminal moraine.
questions.answer: Lateral moraine is a ridge of material deposited along the sides of the glacier, from scree falling onto the edges. Terminal moraine is a ridge of material deposited at the furthest point (snout) the glacier reached.
ms: Both are deposited ridges of unsorted material/till (1).
Lateral: along the sides of the valley/glacier (1).
Terminal: at the snout / maximum extent of the glacier (1).
questions.tip: Use 'snout' for terminal and 'sides' for lateral.

questions.q: Explain the economic activities that take place in glaciated upland areas such as the Lake District.
questions.answer: Tourism: around 18 million visitors a year come for walking, climbing and water sports on lakes such as Windermere. Farming: thin soils and steep slopes suit sheep farming (Herdwick sheep). Forestry: conifer plantations like Grizedale. Quarrying: slate at Honister. Water supply: reservoirs such as Thirlmere and Haweswater supply Manchester.
ms: 1 mark per activity with extra mark for explaining why it suits the area or named detail: tourism (1) attracted by scenery/lakes (1); sheep farming (1) because of steep slopes and thin soils (1); forestry (1) on land unsuitable for crops (1); quarrying of slate (1) e.g. Honister (1); water supply/reservoirs (1) e.g. Thirlmere (1).
questions.tip: Explain why the landscape supports the activity.

questions.q: Using a named example, explain the effects of tourism on a glaciated upland area and how they are managed.
questions.answer: Lake District: around 18 million visitors a year. Positive: tourism supports jobs and businesses. Negative: footpath erosion on popular routes such as Helvellyn; traffic congestion on narrow roads, especially around Windermere and Ambleside; house prices rise because of second homes; pollution and litter. Management: footpaths repaired with stone pitching by Fix the Fells; park-and-ride and Windermere lake ferries; the 10 knot (about 11.5 mph) speed limit on Windermere, enforced from 2005, reduced noise and erosion from speedboats.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Lake District National Park (designated 1951, World Heritage Site 2017). Visitors: around 18 million a year. Impacts: footpath erosion, traffic congestion (most visitors arrive by car), second homes/house prices, seasonal jobs, conflict between water users. Management: Fix the Fells path repairs (stone pitching), Windermere 10 knot speed limit (enforced from 2005), car parks and park-and-ride, public transport such as boat and bus links, education. Level 3 evaluates success.
questions.tip: Name the area AND specific locations within it (Windermere, Helvellyn).

questions.q: 'Tourism brings more benefits than problems to glaciated upland areas.' Using a named example, to what extent do you agree? (9 marks + 3 SPaG)
questions.answer: Lake District: tourism brings around 18 million visitors and supports thousands of jobs, keeping rural services open. But it causes footpath erosion, traffic congestion, high house prices from second homes, seasonal low-paid work, and pollution. Management such as Fix the Fells and the Windermere speed limit reduces problems. Judgement: benefits outweigh problems if managed well, but local people may feel the costs most.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): Thorough knowledge and understanding. Detailed, well-balanced evaluation that considers both sides. Detailed, accurate place-specific case study evidence (named places, facts, figures). Reaches a clear, substantiated judgement that answers 'to what extent' / 'how far'.

Level 2 (4-6 marks): Reasonable knowledge and understanding. Partly balanced evaluation, may favour one side. Some case study detail but it is general or patchy. A judgement is given but only partly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Limited knowledge. Simple, unbalanced points with little evaluation. Little or no case study evidence. No clear judgement.

SPaG (3 marks): High performance 3 = accurate spelling and punctuation, grammar controls meaning, wide range of geographical terms used precisely. Intermediate 2 = considerable accuracy, good range of terms. Threshold 1 = reasonable accuracy, some terms used.

Indicative content: Lake District: about 18 million visitors per year, tourism is the main source of local employment, money spent supports shops, cafés, outdoor centres. Problems: path erosion (Helvellyn, Scafell Pike), congestion and parking, second homes and holiday lets raising house prices so locals priced out, seasonal and low-paid jobs, litter, conflict with farmers (gates, dogs worrying sheep). Management: Fix the Fells, speed limit on Windermere (10 knots, enforced from 2005), park and ride, education. Judgement for whom (tourists, residents, environment) and over what time.
questions.tip: Think about WHO benefits and who loses. That is the route to a balanced Level 3 judgement.

questions.q: Explain how glacial deposition creates distinctive landforms.
questions.answer: When glaciers melt they drop unsorted material called till. Ridges of moraine form at the sides (lateral), where two glaciers meet (medial), and at the snout (terminal). Drumlins form when ice moulds till into streamlined mounds. Erratics are large boulders carried long distances and left on different rock types.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, accurate knowledge. Clear, developed explanation with linked chains of reasoning (because... which means...). Specific place detail used where the question asks for an example.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge with some explanation. Some points developed, but chains of reasoning are partial. Example used in a general way.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic, simple points listed with little or no explanation. Little or no relevant example.

Indicative content: Till is unsorted, angular material. Moraines: lateral, medial, terminal, ground. Drumlins: blunt stoss end faces up-ice, tapered lee end, formed as ice moves over and moulds till (e.g. Eden Valley, Ribblehead). Erratics: large boulders of a different rock type from the bedrock they rest on, e.g. Norber erratics in the Yorkshire Dales. Level 3 explains processes (melting, loss of energy, carrying and moulding).
questions.tip: Explain the processes, not just a list of landform names.

questions.q: Explain why glaciers transport material that is unsorted.
questions.answer: Glaciers carry material of all sizes in, on and under the ice. Because ice is solid, it does not sort sediment by size the way water does. When the ice melts, everything is dropped together.
ms: Ice carries material of all sizes on/in/under the glacier (1).
Ice is solid so does not sort by size/weight (1).
When melting, material is deposited all together as till (1).
questions.tip: Contrast with rivers, which sort material by size as energy falls.

questions.q: Give two pieces of evidence that the Lake District was once covered by glaciers.
questions.answer: Corries such as Red Tarn, arêtes such as Striding Edge, U-shaped valleys and ribbon lakes such as Windermere, hanging valleys, erratics, drumlins.
ms: 1 mark each for named/described glacial landforms, max 2. Allow named Lake District examples.
questions.tip: Named examples make the answer place-specific.

questions.q: On an OS map, a four-figure grid reference gives:
options: The exact location of a point to 10 m
The northings first, then the eastings
The grid square, using the eastings then the northings at its bottom-left corner
ms: Read along the corridor (eastings) first, then up the stairs (northings), using the lines meeting at the bottom-left corner of the square.
questions.tip: Eastings before northings: 'along the corridor and up the stairs'.

questions.q: On a 1:50,000 map, how many kilometres does 1 cm represent?
ms: 1 cm represents 50,000 cm = 500 m = 0.5 km.
questions.tip: On 1:50,000 maps a grid square (2 cm) is 1 km. On 1:25,000 a grid square (4 cm) is 1 km.

questions.q: On a 1:25,000 map, two churches are 7.2 cm apart. What is the real distance?
questions.tip: Convert cm to km by dividing by 100,000.

questions.q: Contour lines that are very close together show:
ms: Closely spaced contours mean height changes quickly over a short distance, so the slope is steep.
questions.tip: Wide spacing = gentle slope. Use contour spacing to describe relief.

questions.q: The median of these daily rainfall values (mm) is: 12, 15, 9, 20, 14, 10, 18
ms: In order: 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 18, 20. The middle (4th) value is 14.
questions.tip: Always put values in order before finding the median.

questions.q: The number of visitors to a café rose from 450 to 540. What is the percentage increase?
questions.tip: Divide by the ORIGINAL value, not the new one. 90 ÷ 540 gives 16.7%, a common mistake.

questions.q: For the data set 3, 7, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, which statement is correct?
ms: Sum 62 ÷ 7 = 8.857, so 8.9; median is the 4th value, 8; mode 7; range 15 − 3 = 12.
questions.tip: Check each statistic separately; distractors often get one right.

questions.q: In a set of 11 ordered values (2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 15, 18, 21), what is the interquartile range?
ms: Lower quartile is the 3rd value (5), upper quartile the 9th value (15). IQR = 15 − 5 = 10.
questions.tip: For n values, LQ is at (n+1)/4 and UQ at 3(n+1)/4. Range (19) is not the IQR.

questions.q: Which type of graph is best for showing how average monthly temperature and rainfall vary through the year?
options: Climate graph (bar chart for rainfall, line graph for temperature)
ms: A climate graph combines rainfall bars with a temperature line on the same 12-month axis.
questions.tip: Know which graph suits which data: choropleth for shading areas, scatter for correlation.

questions.q: A scatter graph shows that as GDP per head increases, deaths from earthquakes fall. This is:
ms: As one variable increases the other decreases, which is a negative correlation.
questions.tip: Correlation does not prove causation. Say 'suggests a relationship'.

questions.q: On a map, the spot height in the grid square where easting 42 meets northing 17 at its bottom-left corner is in which four-figure grid square?
ms: 4217 (1). Do not accept 1742.
questions.tip: Eastings first, then northings.

questions.q: A cliff on the Holderness coast retreats at an average of 1.8 m per year. How far would it retreat in 25 years? Show your working.
ms: Answer 45 m with units (1).
questions.tip: Show the calculation so you can get the method mark even with an arithmetic slip.

questions.q: Monthly rainfall (mm) in a rainforest location is: 260, 290, 310, 280, 180, 90, 60, 40, 70, 120, 180, 220. Calculate the total annual rainfall and the range.
questions.answer: Total 2,100 mm. Range 310 − 40 = 270 mm.
ms: Total annual rainfall = 2,100 mm (1).
Range = 270 mm (1). Units needed for both marks.
questions.tip: Range is highest minus lowest, given as one number, not '40 to 310'.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a four-figure and a six-figure grid reference.
questions.answer: A four-figure grid reference identifies a 1 km grid square. A six-figure reference divides the square into tenths, giving a point to within 100 m, so it is more precise.
ms: Four-figure locates a grid square (1).
Six-figure gives a precise point within the square, by estimating tenths / to within 100 m (1).
questions.tip: Mention precision: square vs point.

questions.q: A table shows the number of tourists visiting a national park car park on 8 days: 34, 12, 28, 12, 19, 40, 12, 25. Calculate the mean, median and mode.
ms: Median 22 (1).
Mode 12 (1).
questions.tip: With an even number of values, the median is halfway between the two middle values.

questions.q: Global average temperature (relative to the 1951-1980 mean) rose from 0.0°C in 1960 to around 1.0°C in 2020 according to a dataset. Describe what this data shows and suggest one limitation of using it as evidence of climate change.
questions.answer: Temperature has risen by about 1.0°C over 60 years, roughly 0.17°C per decade, showing a warming trend. Limitation: it is an average and hides regional variation; early measurements were less reliable and covered fewer places; short-term variation (e.g. El Niño years) can affect individual years.
ms: Overall trend: increase in temperature (1).
Use of data: about 1.0°C rise over 60 years / about 0.17°C per decade (1).
Limitation identified (1), e.g. global average hides regional differences / early data less reliable / fewer weather stations in the past / a single year may be affected by natural events.
Limitation explained (1).
questions.tip: Always 'use the data' with figures when asked to describe a dataset.

questions.q: A student collected beach sediment sizes at two sites on a spit. Site A mean pebble length 6.2 cm, Site B mean pebble length 2.4 cm. Suggest reasons for the difference and how the reliability of the results could be improved.
questions.answer: Site A may be nearer the source of the sediment where pebbles have had less attrition; Site B further along the spit where longshore drift has carried and rounded material, making it smaller. To improve reliability: take more samples at each site, use random or systematic sampling, repeat on different days, and use the same measuring method (calipers).
ms: Reason: further along the drift direction pebbles are smaller due to attrition over distance (1).
Reason developed or alternative: energy decreases so only smaller material reaches the spit end / sorting by size (1).
Reliability: larger sample size / more sites (1).
Reliability: consistent method, e.g. same equipment, systematic/random sampling, repeat on different days (1).
questions.tip: Reliability is about repeating and sample size; accuracy is about correct measurement. Don't confuse them.

questions.q: Describe how you would show the number of deaths from five different earthquakes on a map.
questions.answer: Use proportional symbols, such as circles, placed on each earthquake location, with the size of each circle proportional to the number of deaths, plus a key.
ms: Proportional symbols e.g. circles/bars located on each epicentre (1).
Size proportional to the number of deaths, with a key/scale (1). Allow: located bar charts.
questions.tip: Name the technique: proportional symbols.

questions.q: A village population changed from 1,500 in 2001 to 2,400 in 2021. A nearby village fell from 410 to 275. Calculate the percentage change for each village to 1 decimal place.
ms: Correct method: (new − old) ÷ old × 100 (1).
questions.tip: Show the sign or say 'increase'/'decrease'.

questions.q: State two things you would use to find the height of land on an OS map.
questions.answer: Contour lines and spot heights. Also triangulation pillars.
ms: Contour lines (1).
Spot heights or triangulation pillars (1).
questions.tip: Only these three show height on OS maps; colour layers are on atlas maps.

questions.q: Using the grid square 4217, a church is located 3 tenths east of easting 42 and 6 tenths north of northing 17. Give its six-figure grid reference and explain how you worked it out.
questions.answer: 423176. Take easting 42 and add 3 tenths (423), then northing 17 and add 6 tenths (176).
ms: 423176 (2). Allow 1 mark for 176423 (reversed) or one value wrong.
Explanation: eastings first with tenths estimated, then northings (1).
questions.tip: Estimate tenths carefully and keep eastings first.

questions.q: Give two reasons why a student might use a pie chart rather than a line graph.
questions.answer: Pie charts show parts of a whole as proportions, e.g. percentage land use. Line graphs show continuous change over time, which pie charts cannot.
ms: Shows proportions/percentages of a total (1).
Data is not continuous / not change over time (1).
questions.tip: Choose graphs based on the type of data.

questions.q: What is urbanisation?
options: An increase in the total area covered by a city
People moving from cities to rural areas
The redevelopment of old inner city areas
An increase in the percentage of people living in towns and cities
ms: Urbanisation is about the proportion (percentage) of people living in urban areas rising, not just the city getting bigger.
questions.tip: Do not confuse urbanisation (a percentage) with urban growth or urban sprawl (area).

questions.q: What is the minimum population of a megacity?
ms: A megacity has a population of over 10 million people.
questions.tip: Learn the threshold exactly: 10 million.

questions.q: Which of these is a PULL factor encouraging rural-urban migration in an LIC or NEE?
options: Better access to healthcare and schools in the city
ms: Pull factors attract people to the city; the other three are push factors from rural areas.
questions.tip: Check which place the factor is about: push = origin, pull = destination.

questions.q: Where is the rate of urbanisation currently fastest?
options: LICs and NEEs, especially in Africa and Asia
ms: Most urban growth is in LICs and NEEs, especially sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia; HICs are already mostly urban, so their rate is slow.
questions.tip: Rate (speed) is not the same as the percentage already urban. HICs have a high percentage but a slow rate.

questions.q: Define natural increase and explain how it contributes to urban growth in LICs.
questions.answer: Natural increase is when the birth rate is higher than the death rate. Rural-urban migrants are often young adults, so cities have high birth rates while better healthcare lowers death rates, so city populations grow.
ms: Correct definition: birth rate exceeds death rate (1 mark)
Link to urban growth, e.g. migrants are young adults of child-bearing age so birth rates in cities are high (1 mark)
questions.tip: Give the definition AND the link to cities to get both marks.

questions.q: In 1950 the world's urban population was 751 million. By 2018 it was 4.2 billion. Calculate the percentage increase. Show your working and give your answer to the nearest whole number.
ms: Method: (4200 - 751) ÷ 751 × 100, with units consistent (1 mark)
Answer: 459% (1 mark). Do not accept 559% (dividing new by old).
questions.tip: Convert both figures into the same units (millions) before calculating.

questions.q: Explain why rates of urbanisation differ between HICs and LICs.
questions.answer: HICs urbanised during the Industrial Revolution and are now around 80% urban, so the rate is slow and some people are moving out to rural areas (counter-urbanisation). In LICs most people still live rurally, but push factors like drought, low farm wages and conflict, and pull factors like jobs, schools and hospitals, cause rapid rural-urban migration. Young migrants then add natural increase, so LIC cities grow very quickly.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. HICs: early industrial urbanisation, already highly urban, slow rate, counter-urbanisation. LICs: mostly rural so far, push-pull migration, natural increase, rapid rate.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Make the contrast explicit with words like 'whereas'. One side only caps you at Level 1.

questions.q: Suggest three reasons why the number of megacities has increased since 1950.
questions.answer: Rapid rural-urban migration into cities in NEEs and LICs; high natural increase among young urban populations; economic growth and industrialisation attracting TNCs and creating jobs in cities like Lagos or Mumbai.
ms: Rural-urban migration (1 mark)
Natural increase in cities (1 mark)
Economic development / industrialisation / globalisation creating jobs (1 mark)
questions.tip: Three separate reasons for three marks. Do not just restate one idea three ways.

questions.q: 'Push factors are more important than pull factors in causing rural-urban migration in LICs and NEEs.' Discuss this statement.
questions.answer: Push factors such as drought, desertification, mechanisation, conflict and a lack of services drive many people out of rural areas, for example people leaving the drought-prone north east of Brazil for Rio. However pull factors like perceived jobs in factories and the informal sector, better schools and healthcare are also strong, and often migrants are attracted by the hope of a better life even if it is not realised. Overall push factors often trigger the move, but pull factors determine where people go, so both matter and they interact.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): thorough, well-developed discussion; accurate place-specific detail; clear links and chains of reasoning.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some development and some specific detail; may be unbalanced or partly generic.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little or no development or place detail.

Indicative content: Push: natural hazards, drought, poverty, mechanisation, conflict, lack of services. Pull: jobs, wages, services, bright lights, family networks. Example of NE Brazil to Rio. Judgement about relative importance, e.g. they work together, or push factors dominate in crisis situations.
questions.tip: Discuss means both sides. End with a judgement, even a short one.

questions.q: State the approximate percentage of the world's population living in urban areas in 2018.
questions.answer: About 55%.
ms: About 55% (accept 50-56%) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Know that the world passed 50% urban around 2007.

questions.q: Explain how globalisation has contributed to the growth of cities in NEEs.
questions.answer: Globalisation has brought TNC investment into NEE cities, such as car factories, which creates formal jobs. These jobs attract rural-urban migrants. The multiplier effect then creates more jobs in services and construction, and better infrastructure attracts even more investment, so the city grows in a cycle.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. TNC investment, factories and call centres, jobs attract migrants, multiplier effect, infrastructure, trade through ports.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Use a chain of reasoning: investment, jobs, migration, multiplier.

questions.q: Rio de Janeiro is located on which coast of Brazil?
ms: Rio lies on the south-east (Atlantic) coast of Brazil on Guanabara Bay.
questions.tip: Learn location for 1-mark 'describe the location' questions: SE coast, Guanabara Bay, Atlantic Ocean.

questions.q: What is the name given to informal settlements in Rio?
ms: In Brazil, informal squatter settlements are called favelas.
questions.tip: Use the local term in your case study answers to show place knowledge.

questions.q: Which is the largest favela in Rio de Janeiro?
ms: Rocinha is Rio's largest favela. Copacabana, Ipanema and Barra da Tijuca are wealthy areas.
questions.tip: Mixing up favelas and rich districts is a common error.

questions.q: The cable car built in Complexo do Alemão was mainly intended to:
options: Improve access between the hillside favela and the city's transport network
ms: The cable car connected hillside favela residents to the rail network, cutting journey times to jobs.
questions.tip: Link a solution to the problem it solves (accessibility, access to work).

questions.q: Which of these was a key feature of the Favela Bairro project?
options: Upgrading existing favelas with paved roads, sanitation and services rather than demolishing them
Building luxury apartments on favela land
Relocating all favela residents to new towns outside the city
ms: Favela Bairro was a site and service upgrading scheme in existing favelas.
questions.tip: Do not describe it as clearance; it was improvement in place.

questions.q: Describe the location of Rio de Janeiro.
questions.answer: Rio is on the south-east coast of Brazil, on the Atlantic Ocean, on the western side of Guanabara Bay, surrounded by mountains such as Sugarloaf Mountain.
ms: South-east coast of Brazil / South America (1 mark)
Further detail: Atlantic Ocean, Guanabara Bay, mountains, in Rio de Janeiro state (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use compass directions and named features, not 'near the sea'.

questions.q: In the 2010 census, about 1.39 million of Rio's 6.32 million people lived in favelas. Calculate the percentage living in favelas. Give your answer to one decimal place.
ms: Answer: 22.0% (1 mark; allow 22%)
questions.tip: Divide the part by the whole, not the other way round.

questions.q: Explain why Rio de Janeiro is important regionally, nationally and internationally.
questions.answer: Regionally, Rio is the capital of Rio de Janeiro state and a hub for jobs and services. Nationally it was Brazil's capital until 1960 and has the HQ of Petrobras and major port activity, so it is a key economic centre. Internationally it is a major tourist destination, with Christ the Redeemer and Copacabana, and hosted the 2014 World Cup final and the 2016 Olympics, raising its global profile.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Port, Petrobras / oil, former capital, tourism, Christ the Redeemer, 2014 World Cup, 2016 Olympics, services and finance, cultural importance (Carnival).
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Cover different scales, and back each with a fact.

questions.q: Explain how urban growth has created social opportunities in Rio.
questions.answer: Growth has improved access to services: the Favela Bairro project brought schools, health clinics and day-care into upgraded favelas, and people in the city have better access to healthcare and education than in rural areas. Water supply has been improved with new pipes and treatment, and electricity has been extended to more homes, which raises quality of life.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Access to healthcare and education, water supply, energy, Favela Bairro services, Bolsa Familia linked to school attendance.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: The question is about social opportunities, so do not drift into economic ones.

questions.q: Explain the environmental challenges caused by rapid urban growth in Rio.
questions.answer: Raw sewage and industrial waste from homes and factories flow into Guanabara Bay, polluting the water and harming marine life and fishing. Rapid growth has increased car use and congestion, causing air pollution and smog. Waste disposal is a problem because many favelas are on steep hillsides that are hard to reach, so rubbish is dumped, blocking drains and increasing flood and landslide risk.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Water pollution in Guanabara Bay, sewage, air pollution and congestion, waste disposal, landslides on hillsides, Jardim Gramacho landfill.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Develop each point: what the problem is AND its impact.

questions.q: Using Rio de Janeiro, discuss the challenges of squatter settlements.
questions.answer: Favelas such as Rocinha are often on steep hillsides, so heavy rain causes landslides. Many homes historically lacked proper sanitation, so sewage runs in open drains, spreading disease. Unemployment and low incomes mean many work in the informal economy with no protection. Crime and drug gangs have been a problem, and the UPP police pacification from 2008 had mixed success. However favelas also have strong communities and residents have improved their own homes over time.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): thorough, well-developed discussion; accurate place-specific detail; clear links and chains of reasoning.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some development and some specific detail; may be unbalanced or partly generic.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little or no development or place detail.

Indicative content: Construction on steep slopes and landslide risk; poor water and sanitation; disease; unemployment and informal economy; crime and drug gangs; UPP; overcrowding; balance: strong communities, self-help.
questions.tip: Be specific to Rio: name Rocinha or Complexo do Alemão.

questions.q: Evaluate the success of urban planning schemes in improving the lives of the urban poor in Rio de Janeiro. [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: The Favela Bairro project upgraded dozens of favelas with paved roads, sanitation, clinics and schools, improving health and living conditions, and the Complexo do Alemão cable car cut journey times to work. However costs were high, maintenance was poor in some places, the cable car stopped running in 2016 and was still out of service years later, and rising property values can push poorer residents out. Some residents felt they were not consulted. Overall the schemes improved quality of life for many but were not sustained everywhere, so they were partly successful.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): detailed, place-specific evidence used accurately; balanced consideration of both sides; well-substantiated final judgement that directly answers the question (grade 8 standard).
Level 2 (4-6 marks): clear points with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): basic, generic points; little evidence; no clear judgement.

Indicative content: Favela Bairro: paved roads, water pipes, sewers, clinics, schools, legal land rights, day-care, training. Cable car in Complexo do Alemão (opened 2011, stopped running in 2016). Morar Carioca. UPP policing. Successes vs limits: cost, maintenance, crime returning, rents rising, closure of cable car, scale relative to hundreds of favelas. Substantiated judgement.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate, grammar controls meaning, wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy, good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy, limited specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant geographical content or errors hinder meaning.
questions.tip: A Level 3 answer weighs successes against failures and ends with a clear 'overall' judgement backed by evidence.

questions.q: Name one event hosted by Rio that increased its international importance.
questions.answer: The 2016 Summer Olympic Games (or the 2014 World Cup final).
ms: 2016 Olympics or 2014 FIFA World Cup (final at the Maracanã) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Be precise with dates.

questions.q: Explain how migration has affected the growth of Rio.
questions.answer: Many migrants came from poorer rural areas, especially the north east of Brazil, looking for jobs and services. This increased the population rapidly and, as housing could not keep up, many settled in favelas, which grew on hillsides and the edges of the city.
ms: Migrants from rural areas / NE Brazil / Amazon (1 mark)
Reason for migrating, e.g. jobs, services, drought (1 mark)
Effect: rapid population growth, growth of favelas (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name where migrants came from to show case study knowledge.

questions.q: Explain the economic opportunities that urban growth has created in Rio.
questions.answer: Rio has a large and growing economy based on services such as banking, retail and tourism, plus manufacturing and offshore oil linked to Petrobras. Growth provides a large workforce, which attracts investment, and the multiplier effect creates jobs in construction and services. Even the informal economy gives people a way to earn money, and some move into formal jobs over time.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Port, oil and Petrobras, manufacturing, tourism, services, finance, informal economy, investment for Olympics, multiplier effect.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Show how the opportunity arises from growth, not just list industries.

questions.q: Approximately what was London's population in the 2021 census?
ms: The 2021 census recorded about 8.8 million people in Greater London.
questions.tip: Know your case study population.

questions.q: The Elizabeth line (Crossrail) is an example of:
ms: The Elizabeth line is a major rail link improving east-west transport across London; it opened in 2022.
questions.tip: Match each London example to the right heading: transport, regeneration, greening.

questions.q: Which policy charges the most polluting vehicles to drive anywhere in Greater London?
ms: ULEZ charges vehicles that do not meet emission standards; it was expanded London-wide in August 2023.
questions.tip: The Congestion Charge (2003) targets traffic in the centre; ULEZ targets pollution.

questions.q: Which statement about the London 2012 Olympic regeneration in Stratford is correct?
options: It regenerated former industrial land in the Lower Lea Valley
It was located in west London
It was built entirely on green belt land
ms: The Olympic Park was built on contaminated, derelict industrial (brownfield) land in the Lower Lea Valley, and the athletes' village became East Village housing.
questions.tip: Stratford is a brownfield regeneration example, not greenfield.

questions.q: What is the green belt around London?
options: A zone of protected open land around the city where building is restricted
An area where only eco-houses can be built
A ring of parks in the city centre
ms: Green belts restrict urban sprawl by limiting development on open land around the city.
questions.tip: Green belt is a planning control, not a type of park.

questions.q: Describe London's location in the UK.
questions.answer: London is in south-east England, on the River Thames, near the coast with easy links to mainland Europe, including the Channel Tunnel.
ms: South-east England (1 mark)
Further detail: River Thames, close to Europe, Channel Tunnel, major airports, Thames Estuary (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mention the River Thames for the second mark.

questions.q: Explain how national and international migration have affected the character of London.
questions.answer: International migration has made London very diverse: around 40% of residents were born outside the UK in 2021, and hundreds of languages are spoken. This has created vibrant areas such as Brick Lane and events like Notting Hill Carnival. National migration brings young graduates from across the UK for jobs in finance and media, which gives inner London a young age structure, while some older people move out of the city.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Proportion born abroad, languages, cultural areas, food, festivals, religious buildings, young age structure, inner-outer contrasts.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Character means culture and age structure as well as numbers.

questions.q: Explain the social opportunities created by urban change in London.
questions.answer: London has a huge range of cultural and entertainment opportunities, such as West End theatres, museums and music venues, many of them free. Its diverse population creates opportunities in food, religion and festivals. Green spaces such as the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park and Royal Parks give recreation, and the city's transport system, including the Elizabeth line and cycle hire, makes these more accessible.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Cultural mix, recreation and entertainment, museums and theatres, green spaces, integrated transport.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Give named London examples, not generic city features.

questions.q: Explain the challenges of urban deprivation in London.
questions.answer: Some boroughs such as Tower Hamlets and Newham have high levels of deprivation, with high unemployment, low incomes and overcrowded housing. High house prices and rents make housing unaffordable, pushing some people into temporary accommodation. Deprivation is linked to lower life expectancy and poorer education outcomes, showing big inequalities across the city.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Inequality in housing, education, health, employment; named boroughs; affordability; life expectancy gaps.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Use the language of inequality: compare two areas.

questions.q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of building new housing on brownfield sites in London.
questions.answer: Advantage: it reuses derelict land, protecting the green belt and reducing urban sprawl, and services are already nearby. Disadvantage: land may be contaminated from industry, so it is expensive to clean up before building.
ms: Advantage identified (1 mark)
Advantage developed, e.g. infrastructure already in place / protects countryside (1 mark)
Disadvantage, e.g. decontamination cost, high land price, cramped sites (1 mark)
questions.tip: Make sure you give one of each.

questions.q: Discuss the environmental challenges London faces as a result of urban change.
questions.answer: Pressure for housing creates a debate over building on brownfield or greenfield land and the green belt, causing urban sprawl at the edges. Waste disposal is a challenge: London produces millions of tonnes of waste, much historically sent to landfill, though recycling is rising. Air pollution from traffic is a serious health issue, which ULEZ is trying to tackle. Dereliction in some former industrial areas has also been an issue, although places like Stratford have been regenerated.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): thorough, well-developed discussion; accurate place-specific detail; clear links and chains of reasoning.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some development and some specific detail; may be unbalanced or partly generic.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little or no development or place detail.
Indicative content: Dereliction, building on brownfield/greenfield, green belt, urban sprawl, waste disposal and recycling, air pollution and ULEZ, Congestion Charge.
questions.tip: Use the spec headings: dereliction, building on brownfield and greenfield sites, waste disposal.

questions.q: 'Urban regeneration in Stratford has benefited local people.' To what extent do you agree? [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: Regeneration for the 2012 Olympics turned derelict, contaminated industrial land into the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, with new green space, sports venues and Westfield Stratford City, creating jobs. The athletes' village became East Village housing, and transport improved with Stratford International and later the Elizabeth line. However house prices and rents rose, so many original residents could not afford new homes, which is gentrification. Some jobs went to people from outside the area. Overall it improved the environment and services, but benefits for the poorest existing residents were more limited, so I partly agree.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): detailed, place-specific evidence used accurately; balanced consideration of both sides; well-substantiated final judgement that directly answers the question (grade 8 standard).
Level 2 (4-6 marks): clear points with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): basic, generic points; little evidence; no clear judgement.

Indicative content: Reasons: derelict brownfield land in Lower Lea Valley, 2012 Olympics. Benefits: Olympic Park, green space, Westfield (opened 2011), jobs, East Village homes, transport links, new schools, UCL East and cultural venues. Drawbacks: rising house prices, gentrification, displacement, affordable housing share criticised, jobs not all local, cost. Judgement weighing who benefited.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate, grammar controls meaning, wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy, good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy, limited specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant geographical content or errors hinder meaning.
questions.tip: Define 'local people' in your judgement: existing residents versus newcomers is a strong evaluative angle.

questions.q: Name one urban regeneration project in London.
questions.answer: Stratford / Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park (accept Canary Wharf / London Docklands, King's Cross, Tottenham Hale).
ms: Named London regeneration project (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name it precisely.

questions.q: Explain how urban change in London has created economic opportunities.
questions.answer: London is a global city and a world financial centre, with the City of London and Canary Wharf employing many people in banking, insurance and law. This attracts TNC headquarters and creates multiplier effects in retail, hospitality and transport. Regeneration projects like Stratford created thousands of construction and retail jobs, and tourism brings in large spending.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Financial services, City and Canary Wharf, TNCs, creative and tech industries, tourism, regeneration jobs, multiplier effect.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Link opportunity to a named place in London.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of sustainable urban living?
options: Building more car parks in the city centre
ms: Rainwater harvesting conserves water, a feature of sustainable living.
questions.tip: Sustainable = meets present needs without harming future generations.

questions.q: BedZED in Sutton, south London, is an example of:
ms: BedZED (Beddington Zero Energy Development) is a sustainable housing scheme using solar power, insulation and water recycling.
questions.tip: Learn one named sustainable housing example.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a 'park and ride' scheme?
options: To create parks in the suburbs
To reduce traffic congestion in city centres by having people park outside and take public transport in
To encourage more parking in city centres
To charge drivers entering a city
ms: Park and ride reduces the number of cars entering city centres.
questions.tip: Charging drivers is a congestion charge, a different strategy.

questions.q: Which is the best explanation of why green space makes cities more sustainable?
options: It removes the need for recycling
It absorbs rainfall reducing flood risk, cools the city and improves wellbeing
It provides space for more roads
ms: Green space reduces surface runoff, reduces the urban heat island effect and improves health.
questions.tip: Give environmental AND social benefits for top marks.

questions.q: Give two features of a sustainable city.
questions.answer: Efficient public transport; recycling and waste reduction; green spaces; renewable energy; water conservation.
ms: Any two valid features, e.g. renewable energy, water conservation, recycling, green space, integrated public transport (1 mark each)
questions.tip: Keep features specific: 'recycling' not 'being green'.

questions.q: Explain how traffic management strategies can reduce traffic congestion in cities.
questions.answer: Congestion charging, such as London's since 2003, makes driving into the centre expensive so people use public transport. Integrated transport like London's Oyster and contactless system makes switching between bus, Tube and rail easy. Cycle hire and cycle superhighways encourage cycling, and bus lanes speed up buses so they become more attractive than cars.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Congestion Charge, ULEZ, integrated transport, cycle hire, bus lanes, park and ride, car sharing, ring roads.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Explain HOW each strategy reduces traffic, not just name it.

questions.q: Explain how water and energy conservation help make urban living more sustainable.
questions.answer: Water conservation, such as rainwater harvesting, water meters and low-flush toilets, reduces demand on reservoirs and the energy used to treat water. Energy conservation, like better insulation and solar panels, reduces fossil fuel use and greenhouse gas emissions, cutting costs for residents and helping tackle climate change for future generations.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Water: harvesting, grey water recycling, meters, efficient appliances. Energy: insulation, solar, district heating, smart meters. Links to future generations.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Link back to 'sustainable' meaning future generations.

questions.q: Discuss how effective traffic management strategies have been in London.
questions.answer: The Congestion Charge reduced traffic in central London soon after it began in 2003, and ULEZ has reduced harmful emissions. The integrated transport system and Elizabeth line have increased public transport use, and Santander Cycles encourage cycling. However congestion is still a problem on many roads, partly because of delivery vans and taxis, and some argue ULEZ unfairly costs poorer drivers in outer London who have fewer alternatives.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): thorough, well-developed discussion; accurate place-specific detail; clear links and chains of reasoning.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some development and some specific detail; may be unbalanced or partly generic.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little or no development or place detail.

Indicative content: Congestion Charge, ULEZ expansion 2023, Oyster/contactless, Elizabeth line, cycle hire and superhighways, bus lanes; limits: congestion persists, delivery traffic, cost to low-income drivers, outer London public transport gaps.
questions.tip: Effectiveness needs evidence of success AND limits.

questions.q: What is meant by sustainable urban living?
questions.answer: Living in a city in a way that meets the needs of people today without harming the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
ms: Meets present needs without compromising future generations (1 mark)
questions.tip: Learn the definition word for word.

questions.q: Explain one way a city can reduce the amount of waste sent to landfill.
questions.answer: Kerbside recycling collections make it easy for households to separate glass, paper and plastic, so these materials are reused instead of buried, which reduces landfill and saves resources.
ms: Strategy identified, e.g. recycling, composting, energy from waste (1 mark)
How it works (1 mark)
Effect on landfill or resources (1 mark)
questions.tip: Three marks = identify, develop, develop again.

questions.q: 'Urban sustainability can only be achieved by changing the behaviour of individuals.' Evaluate this statement. [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: Individuals matter: choosing to recycle, use public transport, cycle and save water directly reduces waste and emissions. However big changes need governments and planners, for example London's ULEZ, the Elizabeth line, green belt protection and eco-developments like BedZED. Without infrastructure, people cannot easily change behaviour, and policies like charging also force behaviour change. Overall individual action is important but it depends on government strategy, so the statement is too strong.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): detailed, place-specific evidence used accurately; balanced consideration of both sides; well-substantiated final judgement that directly answers the question (grade 8 standard).
Level 2 (4-6 marks): clear points with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): basic, generic points; little evidence; no clear judgement.

Indicative content: Individual actions: recycling, water and energy saving, travel choices. Government and planners: transport infrastructure, charging, green space, eco-housing, building regulations, waste collection. Interdependence. Judgement with London examples.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate, grammar controls meaning, wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy, good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy, limited specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant geographical content or errors hinder meaning.
questions.tip: Bring in named examples (ULEZ, BedZED, Olympic Park) even in a general sustainability question.

questions.q: Explain how the creation of green space can improve the sustainability of an urban area.
questions.answer: Parks and trees absorb rainwater, reducing surface runoff and flood risk. Vegetation cools cities, reducing the urban heat island and energy used for air conditioning, and absorbs some air pollution. Green spaces also improve physical and mental health, and increase biodiversity, for example the wetlands in the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Flood reduction, cooling, air quality, health and wellbeing, biodiversity, London as a National Park City.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Combine environmental and social reasons.

questions.q: Which three measures are combined to calculate the Human Development Index (HDI)?
options: Literacy, access to water and GNI
Birth rate, death rate and literacy
Life expectancy, education and income (GNI per capita)
GDP, infant mortality and doctors per person
ms: HDI combines health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and standard of living (GNI per capita).
questions.tip: HDI is a composite measure from 0 to 1.

questions.q: What is infant mortality rate?
options: The number of babies who die before their first birthday per 1,000 live births
The number of deaths per 1,000 people per year
The number of births per 1,000 people per year
The number of children under 5 who die per 100 births
ms: IMR is deaths under 1 year old per 1,000 live births.
questions.tip: Learn exact definitions including 'per 1,000'.

questions.q: In which stage of the Demographic Transition Model is the population growing most rapidly?
ms: In Stage 2 death rates fall quickly while birth rates stay high, so natural increase is highest.
questions.tip: Stage 3 is still growing but more slowly as birth rates fall.

questions.q: A country has a birth rate of 32 per 1,000 and a death rate of 9 per 1,000. What is its natural increase as a percentage?
questions.tip: Per 1,000 to percentage: divide by 10.

questions.q: Why is GNI per capita on its own a limited measure of development?
options: It is an average that hides inequality and ignores quality of life
It is only used in HICs
It cannot be measured in US dollars
ms: Averages hide differences between rich and poor; it also ignores health, education and the informal economy.
questions.tip: Typical 2-mark follow up: give the limitation AND why it matters.

questions.q: A country with a wide-based population pyramid that narrows sharply with age is most likely in:
ms: A wide base (high birth rate) and steep narrowing (high death rate in older ages, falling child deaths) fits Stage 2.
questions.tip: Stage 4/5 pyramids are more rectangular or narrow at the base.

questions.q: Define gross national income (GNI) per head.
questions.answer: The total value of goods and services produced by a country plus money earned from abroad in a year, divided by the population.
ms: Total income / goods and services of a country including overseas earnings, in a year (1 mark)
Divided by the population (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Per head' means divided by the population. Many miss this mark.

questions.q: State two social measures of development.
questions.answer: Literacy rate; life expectancy; infant mortality; access to safe water; people per doctor.
ms: Any two social measures (1 mark each). Do not accept GNI or GDP (economic).
questions.tip: Know which measures are social and which are economic.

questions.q: Explain why birth rates fall as countries develop.
questions.answer: As countries develop, women get better education and careers, so they marry and have children later. Access to contraception and family planning increases. Infant mortality falls because of better healthcare, so families do not need as many children. In urban HIC societies children cost more to raise and are not needed as farm workers.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Education and employment of women, contraception, lower IMR, urbanisation, cost of children, pensions.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Each reason needs the 'so' that links it to fewer births.

questions.q: Explain how the Demographic Transition Model shows the link between a country's development and its population.
questions.answer: In Stage 1 birth and death rates are both high, typical of a pre-industrial society. In Stage 2 death rates fall rapidly due to better food, water and healthcare as the country starts developing, so population grows fast (many LICs). In Stage 3 birth rates fall with education and contraception (NEEs such as India; Brazil has now moved into Stage 4). In Stages 4 and 5 both rates are low and the population is stable or declining, typical of HICs like the UK and Japan.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Stages 1 to 5 linked to development, example countries, causes of changes in birth and death rates.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Name an example country for each stage you mention.

questions.q: Explain the limitations of using a single measure such as GNI per head to compare development.
questions.answer: GNI is an average, so it hides inequality: a few very rich people can raise the figure while many remain poor. It ignores informal and subsistence activity common in LICs. It does not show quality of life, such as health or freedom. Exchange rates can distort it, although PPP helps. Composite measures like HDI give a fuller picture.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Average hides inequality, informal economy, no social data, exchange rate issues, corruption in data, composite measures better.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Top answers suggest a better alternative.

questions.q: Describe the shape of a population pyramid for a country in Stage 4 of the DTM.
questions.answer: It is fairly straight-sided or rectangular, with a narrow base because of low birth rates, and wider at the top because many people live to old age due to high life expectancy.
ms: Narrow base / low birth rate (1 mark)
Straight sides / even distribution through working ages (1 mark)
Wider top / ageing population / high life expectancy (1 mark)
questions.tip: Describe the shape and link it to the rates.

questions.q: Which is a PHYSICAL cause of uneven development?
options: Being prone to frequent natural hazards
ms: Natural hazards are physical; colonialism is historical and debt and trade are economic.
questions.tip: Sort causes into physical, economic and historical.

questions.q: What is 'fair trade'?
options: A loan given by the World Bank
A system where producers in LICs receive a fair, guaranteed price for their goods
ms: Fair trade guarantees a minimum price and a social premium to producers.
questions.tip: Fair trade is not the same as free trade.

questions.q: What is intermediate technology?
options: Simple, affordable technology that local people can use and maintain
ms: Intermediate technology is sustainable, low cost and suited to local skills, e.g. sand dams or water pumps.
questions.tip: Key words: appropriate to local needs, skills and money.

questions.q: Which of these best explains why relying on exports of primary products can keep countries poor?
options: Primary products cannot be grown in LICs
Primary products are never traded internationally
Prices for raw materials are low and fluctuate, and the profit from processing is made elsewhere
Primary products are taxed by the UN
ms: Raw materials have low value and volatile prices; value is added by processing in HICs.
questions.tip: Use the phrase 'value added' to show understanding.

questions.q: Which is a consequence of uneven development?
options: Higher life expectancy in all countries
International migration from poorer to richer countries
ms: Uneven development leads to disparities in wealth and health and drives international migration.
questions.tip: The spec lists consequences as wealth, health and international migration.

questions.q: Give two historical or economic causes of uneven development.
questions.answer: Colonialism exploited resources and left countries dependent; trade in low-value primary products; high national debt.
ms: Any two valid causes from colonialism, trade in primary products, debt, conflict/corruption (1 mark each)
questions.tip: 'Poverty' on its own is not a cause.

questions.q: Explain how tourism can help to reduce the development gap in an LIC or NEE.
questions.answer: In Jamaica tourism brings foreign currency and creates jobs in hotels, restaurants and tour companies around resorts like Montego Bay. Taxes on tourism fund infrastructure such as roads and airports, which also benefit locals. The multiplier effect means farmers and craft sellers gain from extra spending. However leakage to foreign hotel chains and all-inclusive resorts reduces the benefits.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Jobs, foreign exchange, taxes, infrastructure, multiplier effect, named example (e.g. Jamaica); evaluation of leakage.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Use a named example: Jamaica is the common AQA choice.

questions.q: Explain how debt relief and aid can help reduce the development gap.
questions.answer: Debt relief cancels some of a poor country's debt, so money previously spent on repayments can be spent on schools and healthcare instead. Aid, such as NGO water projects, provides direct help for basic needs, improving health so people can work. However aid can create dependency or be misused through corruption.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Debt relief, reinvesting in services, conditional on reforms; types of aid (bilateral, multilateral, NGO, short and long term); limitations.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Explain how the money is used, not just that it is given.

questions.q: Discuss the consequences of uneven development.
questions.answer: Uneven development creates big disparities in wealth, with HICs having much higher GNI per head. It also leads to disparities in health: life expectancy and infant mortality are much worse in LICs because of poor healthcare, diet and water. This drives international migration, as people move from poorer to richer countries for jobs and safety, which can cause a brain drain in source countries but bring remittances home.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): thorough, well-developed discussion; accurate place-specific detail; clear links and chains of reasoning.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some development and some specific detail; may be unbalanced or partly generic.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little or no development or place detail.
Indicative content: Wealth disparities, health disparities, international migration (economic migrants, refugees), brain drain, remittances, benefits and costs for host countries.
questions.tip: Cover all three spec consequences: wealth, health, migration.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of different strategies used to reduce the global development gap. [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: Investment by TNCs creates jobs and infrastructure, as in Brazil, but profits may go abroad. Tourism, as in Jamaica, brings foreign exchange but suffers leakage and is vulnerable to hazards and recessions. Aid and debt relief free money for services but can create dependency. Intermediate technology and microfinance are cheap and sustainable, empowering local people but only at a small scale. Fair trade gives farmers better prices but only covers a small share of trade. Overall, a combination works best; bottom-up strategies are most sustainable but top-down investment has the larger national impact.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): detailed, place-specific evidence used accurately; balanced consideration of both sides; well-substantiated final judgement that directly answers the question (grade 8 standard).
Level 2 (4-6 marks): clear points with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): basic, generic points; little evidence; no clear judgement.

Indicative content: Investment, industrial development, tourism (Jamaica), aid, intermediate technology, fair trade, debt relief, microfinance loans. Strengths and limits of each. Comparison of scale and sustainability. Clear judgement on which are most effective and why.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate, grammar controls meaning, wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy, good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy, limited specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant geographical content or errors hinder meaning.
questions.tip: Don't just list strategies; compare them and decide which is most effective.

questions.q: Explain how microfinance loans can help reduce poverty.
questions.answer: Microfinance gives small loans to poor people, often women, who cannot get loans from normal banks. They use the money to start small businesses such as selling crafts, earning income to repay the loan and support their families, which can reduce poverty over time.
ms: Small loans to poor people without access to banks (1 mark)
Used to start a business / buy equipment (1 mark)
Income generated, families supported, reinvested (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name an example (e.g. Grameen Bank) to strengthen answers.

questions.q: Explain the disadvantages of tourism as a strategy for development in an LIC or NEE.
questions.answer: Much tourist spending leaks out of the economy to foreign-owned hotels, airlines and imported food, especially in all-inclusive resorts. Jobs are often seasonal and low-paid. Tourism can damage environments such as coral reefs, and the economy becomes vulnerable to changes in demand such as recessions, pandemics or hurricanes.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Leakage, low-paid seasonal jobs, environmental damage, cultural impacts, dependence, vulnerability to shocks.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Each disadvantage must be explained, not just listed.

questions.q: Brazil is classified as which type of country?
ms: Brazil is an NEE, and a member of the BRICS group.
questions.tip: Learn the full term: newly emerging economy.

questions.q: Which of these is a Brazilian transnational corporation?
ms: Vale is a Brazilian mining TNC. Nestlé (Swiss), Ford (US) and Fiat (Italian origin) are foreign TNCs operating in Brazil.
questions.tip: Know which TNCs are Brazilian and which invest from abroad.

questions.q: Which country became Brazil's largest trading partner in the 2000s?
ms: China has been Brazil's largest trading partner since 2009, buying soybeans, iron ore and oil.
questions.tip: Link trade partners to the exports they buy.

questions.q: What was Bolsa Família?
options: A deforestation law in the Amazon
A loan from the IMF to build dams
A government programme giving cash to poor families on condition children attend school and get vaccinated
ms: Bolsa Família (2003) gave conditional cash transfers, reducing poverty and improving school attendance.
questions.tip: It is a quality of life strategy, not an economic investment.

questions.q: The 2015 Mariana dam collapse in Brazil is an example of:
options: An environmental impact of economic development (mining)
ms: The Mariana tailings dam collapse released toxic mining waste into the Doce River.
questions.tip: Use specific disasters as evidence of environmental costs.

questions.q: Describe the location of Brazil.
questions.answer: Brazil is in South America, on the east (Atlantic) coast. It borders most other South American countries, including Argentina and Colombia, and the equator runs through the north.
ms: South America (1 mark)
Further detail: Atlantic coast, crossed by the equator, borders named countries, largest country in South America (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use compass points and named features.

questions.q: Explain how the economic structure of Brazil has changed as it has developed.
questions.answer: Brazil's economy used to be dominated by the primary sector, such as coffee and sugar farming. Industrialisation brought growth in manufacturing, such as cars, steel and aircraft (Embraer). Today the tertiary sector employs most people, in retail, finance and tourism, though primary exports like soybeans and iron ore are still very important.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Shift from primary to secondary to tertiary; examples of each; reasons: industrialisation, TNCs, urbanisation, rising incomes.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Use the sector names: primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary.

questions.q: Explain the advantages of TNCs operating in Brazil.
questions.answer: TNCs such as Fiat at Betim in Minas Gerais create thousands of jobs, giving regular incomes. They bring investment, skills and technology, and their taxes help the government fund services. The multiplier effect supports local suppliers and businesses, and exports increase Brazil's income.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Jobs, wages, training, technology transfer, taxes, infrastructure, exports, multiplier effect; named TNC and location.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Name a TNC and a place.

questions.q: Discuss the environmental impacts of economic development in Brazil.
questions.answer: Deforestation in the Amazon for cattle ranching, soya, logging and mining destroys habitats, reduces biodiversity and releases carbon dioxide. Big dams like Belo Monte on the Xingu River flood forest and displace indigenous people. Mining disasters such as Mariana (2015) polluted the Doce River with toxic waste. Cities suffer air pollution and water pollution, e.g. Guanabara Bay. However, Brazil has also expanded renewable energy, especially hydropower and biofuels, which reduces fossil fuel use.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): thorough, well-developed discussion; accurate place-specific detail; clear links and chains of reasoning.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some development and some specific detail; may be unbalanced or partly generic.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little or no development or place detail.
Indicative content: Amazon deforestation, Belo Monte dam, Mariana dam disaster, air and water pollution, Guanabara Bay; positives: hydropower, biofuels from sugar cane, protected areas.
questions.tip: Specific named examples move you into Level 3.

questions.q: To what extent has economic development improved quality of life for people in Brazil? [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: Economic growth raised incomes and created a larger middle class; Bolsa Família lifted millions out of extreme poverty and improved school attendance, and life expectancy and literacy have risen. However inequality is still very high, many people still live in favelas, and the poorer north and north east lag behind the wealthy south east. Development has also harmed indigenous groups and environments. Overall quality of life has improved substantially on average, but benefits are uneven, so it has only partly improved quality of life for all.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): detailed, place-specific evidence used accurately; balanced consideration of both sides; well-substantiated final judgement that directly answers the question (grade 8 standard).
Level 2 (4-6 marks): clear points with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): basic, generic points; little evidence; no clear judgement.

Indicative content: Rising GNI and HDI, middle class growth, Bolsa Família, healthcare and education access, life expectancy rise. Limits: inequality, regional disparities (SE vs NE), favelas, indigenous rights, pollution, recessions and unemployment. Clear judgement.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate, grammar controls meaning, wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy, good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy, limited specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant geographical content or errors hinder meaning.
questions.tip: 'To what extent' needs a judgement like 'to a large extent' or 'partly', backed by evidence.

questions.q: Explain the disadvantages of TNCs for Brazil.
questions.answer: Profits often go back to the TNC's home country rather than staying in Brazil. Jobs can be low-paid and TNCs may close plants and leave if costs rise elsewhere. They can also cause environmental damage, for example mining TNCs.
ms: Profits leave the country (1 mark)
Low wages / poor conditions / footloose, may relocate (1 mark)
Environmental damage or local firms outcompeted (1 mark)
questions.tip: Each mark needs a different disadvantage.

questions.q: Explain how changing relationships with the wider world have helped Brazil's economy develop.
questions.answer: Brazil has increased trade, especially with China, exporting soybeans, iron ore and oil, which earns foreign currency. Membership of BRICS and Mercosur gives political influence and easier trade with neighbours. Hosting the 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympics raised its global profile and attracted investment and tourists.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Trade with China, USA, Mercosur, BRICS, globalisation, TNC investment, global events.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: 'Relationships with the wider world' covers trade, political links and global events.

questions.q: What is deindustrialisation?
options: The decline of manufacturing industry in a country or region
