The move from cities to rural areas
ms: Deindustrialisation is the decline in secondary/manufacturing industry.
questions.tip: Link it to causes: globalisation, cheaper labour abroad, mechanisation.

questions.q: A science park is:
options: A group of scientific and technical businesses on one site, often linked to a university
ms: Science parks such as Cambridge Science Park cluster research firms near universities.
questions.tip: Know the difference between a science park and a business park.

questions.q: Which describes the UK's post-industrial economy?
options: Dominated by tertiary and quaternary sectors such as finance, IT and research
ms: The UK now has most jobs in services and knowledge-based industries.
questions.tip: Quaternary = research and development / knowledge.

questions.q: Which rural area has experienced population DECLINE, used as a UK example?
ms: The Outer Hebrides has seen population decline as young people move away; South Cambridgeshire has grown.
questions.tip: Know one growth and one decline rural example.

questions.q: What is the 'north-south divide' in the UK?
options: A boundary between England and Scotland
Differences in wealth, health and jobs between the north and the south east
ms: It describes economic and social disparities, with the south east generally richer.
questions.tip: Refer to measures like wages, house prices, life expectancy.

questions.q: Give two causes of economic change in the UK.
questions.answer: Deindustrialisation and the decline of traditional industries; globalisation; government policies.
ms: Any two from deindustrialisation, globalisation, government policy (e.g. privatisation, investment) (1 mark each)
questions.tip: These three are the spec causes.

questions.q: Explain how globalisation has changed the UK economy.
questions.answer: Globalisation meant manufacturing moved to countries with cheaper labour, such as China, so UK factories closed and many jobs were lost in the North and Midlands. At the same time the UK attracted foreign investment and became a global financial centre, so jobs grew in finance, IT and services, especially in London. Faster communications helped knowledge-based industries.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Offshoring of manufacturing, imports, deindustrialisation, TNC investment in UK, growth of finance and services, ICT.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Show both negatives and positives of globalisation.

questions.q: Suggest why science parks are often located near universities.
questions.answer: Universities provide a highly skilled, educated workforce and graduates. Firms can share research facilities and work with academics. They also usually have good transport links and a pleasant environment.
ms: Skilled graduates (1 mark)
Research links / sharing ideas and facilities (1 mark)
Other: transport, attractive environment, room to expand (1 mark)
questions.tip: Think about what the firm needs: skills, research, access.

questions.q: Explain how modern industrial developments can be more environmentally sustainable.
questions.answer: At Torr Quarry in Somerset, the site is being landscaped and the plan is to restore it as lakes and habitat for wildlife and recreation once extraction ends. Rail is used to transport the stone, reducing lorry traffic and emissions. Modern business parks may use renewable energy, recycling and sustainable building materials.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Example such as Torr Quarry: landscaping, screening, rail transport, restoration for nature; renewable energy and efficiency in new developments.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Use a named example of an industrial development.

questions.q: Discuss the impacts of population change in rural areas of the UK.
questions.answer: In South Cambridgeshire population growth from commuters and new housing increases house prices and congestion, but brings more customers for local services. In the Outer Hebrides population decline means schools and shops close, the population ages and young people leave, though new jobs in tourism and renewable energy may help. So rural areas face very different social and economic impacts depending on whether they gain or lose people.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): thorough, well-developed discussion; accurate place-specific detail; clear links and chains of reasoning.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some development and some specific detail; may be unbalanced or partly generic.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little or no development or place detail.
Indicative content: Growth area: commuters, rising house prices, pressure on services, traffic, new jobs. Decline area: ageing, service closure, fewer jobs, isolation. Named examples.
questions.tip: You need both a growth and a decline example for full marks.

questions.q: Evaluate the importance of improvements to transport infrastructure for the UK economy. [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: Improvements such as the Elizabeth line, smart motorways, port developments like London Gateway, and airport expansion reduce journey times, attract investment and help trade. HS2 aims to improve capacity between London and Birmingham. However projects are extremely expensive, cause environmental damage and disruption, and HS2's northern leg was cancelled, raising questions about benefits for the north. Some argue digital connections matter more today. Overall transport improvements are important for growth and reducing the north-south divide, but only if investment is spread across regions.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): detailed, place-specific evidence used accurately; balanced consideration of both sides; well-substantiated final judgement that directly answers the question (grade 8 standard).
Level 2 (4-6 marks): clear points with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): basic, generic points; little evidence; no clear judgement.

Indicative content: Road (smart motorways, though new schemes were cancelled in 2023 over safety concerns), rail (HS2, Elizabeth line, Northern Powerhouse Rail), ports (London Gateway), airports (Heathrow expansion debate). Benefits: trade, investment, jobs, reduced congestion. Costs: money, environment, uneven benefit. Judgement.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate, grammar controls meaning, wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy, good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy, limited specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant geographical content or errors hinder meaning.
questions.tip: Mention at least two transport types (road, rail, port, airport) with named examples.

questions.q: Explain the strategies used to reduce the north-south divide in the UK.
questions.answer: Enterprise Zones offer tax breaks and simpler planning to attract businesses to areas such as the north. The Northern Powerhouse aimed to boost investment in northern cities through better transport links and devolution. Relocating organisations, such as parts of the BBC to Salford, brings jobs. However the gap is still large.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Enterprise Zones, Northern Powerhouse, devolution, transport investment, relocation of public bodies (BBC to MediaCityUK, Salford).
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Name the strategy and explain how it creates jobs.

questions.q: Explain one way the UK is linked to the wider world.
questions.answer: Trade: the UK imports and exports goods and services with many countries, such as financial services and cars, which creates jobs and wealth. Since leaving the EU in 2020 it has made new trade agreements.
ms: Link identified, e.g. trade, culture, transport, electronic communications, EU, Commonwealth (1 mark)
Developed explanation (1 mark)
Example or further development (1 mark)
questions.tip: Pick one link and develop it fully.

questions.q: What are 'food miles'?
options: The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten
The number of farms in an area
The amount of food produced per hectare
ms: Food miles measure transport distance, linked to carbon footprint.
questions.tip: Link food miles to carbon footprint for higher marks.

questions.q: Why does the UK have a water deficit in the south east?
options: High population and demand but relatively low rainfall
Water is exported to other countries
ms: The SE has the most people but less rain than the north and west.
questions.tip: Deficit = demand exceeds supply.

questions.q: Which energy source has declined most sharply in UK electricity generation since 1990?
ms: Coal has declined from the main source to zero; the last coal power station, Ratcliffe-on-Soar, closed in 2024.
questions.tip: Know the direction of change for each source.

questions.q: What is an agribusiness?
options: Large-scale, intensive commercial farming run like a business
ms: Agribusiness applies industrial methods to farming to maximise output and profit.
questions.tip: Link agribusiness to its environmental impacts.

questions.q: What is a water transfer scheme?
options: Moving water from an area of surplus to an area of deficit
ms: Water transfer moves water, e.g. from Wales (Elan Valley) to Birmingham.
questions.tip: Use a named example.

questions.q: Give two reasons why demand for high-value foods out of season has increased in the UK.
questions.answer: Rising incomes allow people to buy more exotic foods; a more diverse population demands foods from different cultures; supermarkets import all year.
ms: Any two: rising incomes, multicultural population, supermarket supply chains, travel abroad, health trends (1 mark each)
questions.tip: Think about who is demanding the food and why.

questions.q: Explain the changes in the UK's energy mix.
questions.answer: The UK relied mainly on coal, oil and gas. Coal has declined because of climate targets and pollution, with the last coal power station closing in 2024, and North Sea oil and gas production has fallen, so more gas is imported. Renewables, especially offshore wind, have grown rapidly with government support. Nuclear still provides some electricity and Hinkley Point C is being built.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Decline of coal, falling North Sea reserves, rise of renewables (offshore wind, solar), nuclear (Hinkley Point C), imports, climate targets.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Explain WHY each change happened.

questions.q: Explain one issue linked to the water quality in the UK.
questions.answer: Agricultural runoff with fertilisers enters rivers, causing eutrophication, which reduces oxygen and kills fish. Water companies must treat water more, increasing costs.
ms: Source of pollution, e.g. farming chemicals, sewage, industry (1 mark)
Impact on water / ecosystems (1 mark)
Management or further consequence (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name the pollution source precisely.

questions.q: Discuss the economic and environmental issues of the UK exploiting energy sources.
questions.answer: Nuclear power is low carbon but expensive (Hinkley Point C) and produces radioactive waste. Fracking for shale gas could increase energy security but caused small earthquakes, leading to a moratorium in 2019. Wind farms create jobs and are renewable, but some people object to visual impact and output varies with weather. North Sea oil and gas brings revenue and jobs but adds carbon emissions and resources are running out.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): thorough, well-developed discussion; accurate place-specific detail; clear links and chains of reasoning.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some development and some specific detail; may be unbalanced or partly generic.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little or no development or place detail.

Indicative content: Fossil fuels: jobs, tax, carbon emissions. Nuclear: cost, waste, safety. Fracking: earthquakes, groundwater concerns, moratorium. Renewables: cost falling, intermittency, visual impact, jobs.
questions.tip: Balance economic AND environmental, with named UK examples.

questions.q: Explain why the UK imports a large amount of its food.
questions.answer: The UK climate means some foods, such as bananas and coffee, cannot be grown here. Consumers want seasonal foods all year round, such as strawberries in winter. Imported food can be cheaper because of lower labour costs abroad, and the UK's diverse population demands foods from around the world.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Climate limits, demand for out-of-season produce, cheaper imports, diverse population, supermarket supply chains.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Give a reason AND an example food for each.

questions.q: Explain the role of the organic and local food movements in the UK.
questions.answer: Demand for organic food has grown because people worry about chemicals and animal welfare; it reduces fertiliser and pesticide use. Buying local food from farmers' markets reduces food miles and the carbon footprint and supports local farmers. However these foods are often more expensive and cannot meet all demand.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Organic: fewer chemicals, health and environment concerns. Local: food miles, carbon footprint, support local economy, seasonal eating. Limitations: price, scale.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Link to the trend of reducing carbon footprint.

questions.q: What is food security?
options: When food is stored in warehouses
When farmers grow only one crop
When a country exports more food than it imports
When all people at all times have access to enough safe, nutritious food
ms: Food security means reliable access to sufficient, safe, nutritious food for an active, healthy life.
questions.tip: Food insecurity is the opposite: lack of reliable access.

questions.q: Thanet Earth in Kent mainly uses which technique?
ms: Thanet Earth grows salad crops such as tomatoes, peppers and cucumbers hydroponically in greenhouses.
questions.tip: Hydroponics = growing plants in nutrient solution without soil.

questions.q: Which of these is a factor that REDUCES food supply?
ms: Water stress limits crop growth; the others increase supply.
questions.tip: Learn the spec list: climate, technology, pests and disease, water stress, conflict, poverty.

questions.q: What was the 'Green Revolution'?
options: A plan to grow food in cities
A move to organic farming in HICs
The introduction of high-yielding crop varieties, fertilisers and irrigation from the 1960s to boost food production
ms: The Green Revolution greatly increased yields, especially in Asia, but needed costly inputs.
questions.tip: The 'new green revolution' focuses on more sustainable methods and biotechnology.

questions.q: Which region of the world has the lowest average daily calorie intake?
ms: Many countries in sub-Saharan Africa have the lowest calorie intake.
questions.tip: Describe global patterns with named continents.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a sustainable, small-scale food scheme in an LIC/NEE?
options: Floating gardens in flood-prone areas of Bangladesh
Industrial cattle ranching in the Amazon
ms: Floating gardens made from water hyacinth let farmers grow crops during floods, using cheap local materials.
questions.tip: Local schemes = bottom-up, appropriate technology.

questions.q: Define food insecurity.
questions.answer: When people do not have reliable access to enough affordable, nutritious food.
ms: Lack of access / not enough food (1 mark)
Reference to affordable, safe or nutritious, or reliably / all the time (1 mark)
questions.tip: Include 'nutritious' or 'reliable' for the second mark.

questions.q: Explain why global food consumption is increasing.
questions.answer: The world population is growing, so more food is needed. Economic development in NEEs such as China and Brazil raises incomes, so people eat more food and more meat and dairy, which need more crops to feed animals. Year-round demand for imported foods in HICs also increases consumption.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Population growth, rising incomes, dietary change towards meat, urbanisation, globalised food supply.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Link economic development to diet change for Level 2.

questions.q: Explain the impacts of food insecurity.
questions.answer: Food shortages can cause famine and undernutrition, leading to illness, stunted growth and death. Desperate farmers may overgraze or overcultivate land, causing soil erosion. Food shortages push up prices, so poor people cannot afford food, which can lead to social unrest and conflict.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Famine, undernutrition, soil erosion, rising prices, social unrest; chains of consequence.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: The spec lists these four impacts: learn them.

questions.q: Explain how technology can be used to increase food supply.
questions.answer: Irrigation lets farmers grow crops in dry areas or seasons. Hydroponics and aeroponics grow plants without soil in controlled conditions, using less water. Biotechnology such as GM crops can increase yields and resistance to pests and drought. Appropriate technology like drip irrigation helps small farmers.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Irrigation, aeroponics, hydroponics, new green revolution, biotechnology/GM, appropriate technology.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Explain how each one increases supply, e.g. 'so more crops survive'.

questions.q: Using an example, discuss the advantages and disadvantages of a large-scale agricultural development.
questions.answer: Thanet Earth in Kent is one of the UK's largest greenhouse complexes. It grows tomatoes, peppers and cucumbers hydroponically all year, reducing food miles and imports. It has its own combined heat and power plant, uses captured CO2 to boost growth, harvests rainwater, uses bees for pollination and biological pest control, and creates local jobs. However it was built on farmland, the greenhouses cause light pollution, it relies on gas so is energy-intensive, and many jobs are low-paid and seasonal.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): thorough, well-developed discussion; accurate place-specific detail; clear links and chains of reasoning.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some development and some specific detail; may be unbalanced or partly generic.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little or no development or place detail.

Indicative content: Thanet Earth: hydroponics, rainwater, CHP power plant, CO2 reuse, sells electricity, year-round supply, jobs, fewer imports. Drawbacks: farmland use, light pollution, gas-powered energy, low-paid jobs, landscape. Allow irrigation scheme examples.
questions.tip: Balance is essential for Level 3: both pros and cons with specific detail.

questions.q: 'Large-scale schemes are more effective than small-scale schemes in increasing food supply sustainably.' Do you agree? [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: Large-scale schemes such as Thanet Earth produce large volumes of salad crops year-round, cut food miles and use efficient hydroponics and rainwater. But they are capital and energy-intensive and only possible in rich countries. Small-scale schemes such as Bangladesh floating gardens use cheap local materials, help the poorest people directly and can be maintained locally, making them more sustainable, though they produce less food overall. Overall I disagree: small-scale schemes are more sustainable for food-insecure areas, while large schemes increase supply but often at higher environmental cost.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): detailed, place-specific evidence used accurately; balanced consideration of both sides; well-substantiated final judgement that directly answers the question (grade 8 standard).
Level 2 (4-6 marks): clear points with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): basic, generic points; little evidence; no clear judgement.

Indicative content: Large: Thanet Earth or irrigation scheme; output, technology, jobs; costs, energy, environment. Small: floating gardens, permaculture, urban farming, organic, sand dams; low cost, appropriate tech, community; limited output. Define sustainable. Clear judgement.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate, grammar controls meaning, wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy, good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy, limited specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant geographical content or errors hinder meaning.
questions.tip: Define 'sustainable' early and judge both schemes against that definition.

questions.q: Describe how the Bangladesh floating garden scheme helps local people.
questions.answer: Farmers build rafts of water hyacinth and bamboo that float on flood water, so crops can still be grown during the monsoon floods. They use cheap local materials, the rotting rafts become compost, and families can eat or sell vegetables, improving food security and income.
ms: Floating rafts allow crops during floods (1 mark)
Cheap, local, sustainable materials (1 mark)
Benefit: food security, income, nutrition (1 mark)
questions.tip: Show it is appropriate technology for the local environment.

questions.q: Explain how sustainable food supplies can be achieved.
questions.answer: Organic farming avoids artificial chemicals, protecting soils and water. Permaculture works with natural systems to produce food without depleting resources. Urban farming grows food close to consumers, reducing food miles. Eating seasonal food and reducing waste lowers demand, and buying fish and meat from sustainable sources prevents overfishing.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Organic farming, permaculture, urban farming, sustainable fish and meat, seasonal food consumption, reducing waste.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Every point needs a 'so' showing why it is sustainable.

questions.q: How long before the Paper 3 exam is the pre-release resource booklet made available?
options: It is not released before the exam
ms: AQA releases the pre-release booklet 12 weeks before the exam.
questions.tip: Use this time to learn the resources, not to guess questions.

questions.q: In an issue evaluation question asking you to choose an option, what is the best approach?
options: Choose an option, justify it with evidence from the resources, and explain why it is better than the alternatives
Pick the cheapest option without explaining
Describe every option equally without choosing
ms: Top marks need a clear decision, justified with resource evidence and comparison with other options.
questions.tip: There is no 'right' option. Marks come from justification.

questions.q: What does 'sustainable' mean when judging options in an issue evaluation?
options: Meeting present needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs, considering social, economic and environmental factors
The option with the most jobs
ms: Sustainability balances social, economic and environmental aspects over the long term.
questions.tip: Use SEE: social, economic, environmental.

questions.q: Which statement is the best example of a 'substantiated' judgement?
options: Option 2 is best because it creates 300 jobs (Figure 3) while protecting the wetland, whereas Option 1 would destroy the habitat
All options have advantages and disadvantages
Option 2 is best because it is better
ms: A substantiated judgement uses specific evidence and compares options.
questions.tip: Quote figures from the resources and say which figure they come from.

questions.q: State two types of stakeholders whose views might be considered in an issue evaluation.
questions.answer: Local residents; businesses; the local council or government; environmental groups.
ms: Any two relevant stakeholders (1 mark each)
questions.tip: Think about who wins and who loses.

questions.q: In an area, unemployment fell from 1,240 people to 868 after a regeneration scheme, calculate the percentage change and explain what it suggests about the scheme.
questions.answer: (868 - 1240) ÷ 1240 × 100 = -30%, a 30% fall. It suggests the scheme created jobs and was economically successful, though the data does not show the quality of the jobs or whether local people got them.
ms: Answer: -30% / 30% decrease (1 mark)
Interpretation: suggests economic success / jobs created (1 mark)
Limitation: e.g. jobs may not be for local people, other causes, no data on wages (1 mark)
questions.tip: Questioning the data's reliability shows higher-level skill.

questions.q: Explain why there may be conflict between different groups over a proposed development.
questions.answer: Different groups have different priorities. Businesses may support a development because it brings profit and jobs, while environmental groups oppose it because it damages habitats. Local residents may be split: some want jobs and new services, others worry about noise, traffic and rising house prices.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Different stakeholders, differing priorities (economic vs environmental vs social), winners and losers, short term vs long term.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Name the groups and say what each wants.

questions.q: A council plans to build a new flood defence. Option 1 is a concrete sea wall; Option 2 is managed retreat with saltmarsh creation. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each option for the local community.
questions.answer: The sea wall protects homes and businesses immediately and lets the community stay, but it is expensive, needs maintenance and can increase erosion elsewhere. Managed retreat is cheaper in the long term and creates saltmarsh habitats that absorb wave energy, but some farmland or homes would be lost and owners may need compensation. The best choice depends on the value of the land being protected.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): thorough, well-developed discussion; accurate place-specific detail; clear links and chains of reasoning.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some development and some specific detail; may be unbalanced or partly generic.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little or no development or place detail.

Indicative content: Sea wall: protection, confidence, cost, maintenance, visual impact, erosion downdrift. Managed retreat: cost, habitats, natural defence, loss of land, compensation, opposition. Consider different stakeholders and timescales.
questions.tip: Consider different groups within 'the community'.

questions.q: Using the resources, a planning committee must choose between: Option A, a large retail and housing development on a brownfield riverside site; Option B, a mixed scheme of affordable housing and a public park; Option C, leaving the site as a nature reserve. Which option do you think is the most sustainable? Justify your decision. [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: Option B is the most sustainable. Socially it provides affordable homes, tackling the housing crisis for local people, and a park that improves wellbeing. Economically it brings some construction jobs and local spending. Environmentally the park absorbs rainwater, reducing flood risk on the riverside, and gives habitat. Option A would create more jobs and profit, but expensive housing could cause gentrification and more traffic and pollution. Option C protects wildlife but provides no homes or jobs for a growing population. So Option B best balances social, economic and environmental needs.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): detailed, place-specific evidence used accurately; balanced consideration of both sides; well-substantiated final judgement that directly answers the question (grade 8 standard).
Level 2 (4-6 marks): clear points with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): basic, generic points; little evidence; no clear judgement.

Indicative content: Clear choice; social, economic and environmental justification; use of resource evidence; reasons for rejecting other options; consideration of stakeholders and long-term impacts. Any option can reach Level 3 if well justified.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate, grammar controls meaning, wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy, good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy, limited specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant geographical content or errors hinder meaning.
questions.tip: Spend the last third of your answer explaining why you rejected the other options.

questions.q: Suggest how the pre-release resources should be prepared for before the exam.
questions.answer: Read all resources carefully, annotate key facts and figures, learn the key terms, research the background of the issue and the place, and practise judging options using social, economic and environmental criteria.
ms: Annotate / understand the resources and data (1 mark)
Learn key terms and background to the issue (1 mark)
Practise evaluating options or considering stakeholders (1 mark)
questions.tip: You get a clean copy in the exam; you cannot bring your annotated one in.

questions.q: Explain why it is important to consider long-term impacts when evaluating a development option.
questions.answer: A development might bring short-term benefits like construction jobs, but long-term impacts such as pollution, habitat loss or rising house prices may outweigh them. Considering the long term shows whether an option is sustainable for future generations and whether costs like maintenance will become a burden.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Short-term vs long-term, sustainability, maintenance costs, environmental degradation, intergenerational fairness.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Use the words 'short term' and 'long term' explicitly.

questions.q: What type of data is collected using a questionnaire with yes/no and opinion questions?
options: Primary data, which can be both qualitative and quantitative
ms: You collect it yourself, so it is primary. Opinion answers are qualitative, while yes/no answers can be counted (quantitative).
questions.tip: Primary = collected by you; secondary = collected by others.

questions.q: Which sampling method chooses sites at regular intervals, e.g. every 50 m along a transect?
ms: Systematic sampling uses regular intervals.
questions.tip: Stratified = proportional to subgroups; random = every site has an equal chance.

questions.q: Which instrument measures wind speed in a microclimate investigation?
ms: An anemometer measures wind speed; a hygrometer measures humidity.
questions.tip: Match each instrument to what it measures.

questions.q: Pedestrian counts at 9 sites were: 12, 18, 25, 31, 40, 44, 52, 60, 75. What is the median?
ms: With 9 ordered values, the median is the 5th: 40.
questions.tip: The median is the middle value of the ordered data, not the mean.

questions.q: Using the same data (12, 18, 25, 31, 40, 44, 52, 60, 75), what is the interquartile range?
ms: Lower quartile = median of 12, 18, 25, 31 = 21.5; upper quartile = median of 44, 52, 60, 75 = 56; IQR = 56 - 21.5 = 34.5.
questions.tip: IQR = UQ - LQ. The range (63) is a different measure.

questions.q: Why might a researcher use stratified sampling for a questionnaire in Stratford?
options: To make sure different groups, e.g. age groups, are represented in proportion to the population
To save time by asking only friends
ms: Stratified sampling reflects the proportions of subgroups, reducing bias.
questions.tip: Explain the 'why' of each sampling method, not just the definition.

questions.q: Give two ways to make fieldwork data collection more reliable.
questions.answer: Take repeat readings and use the average; increase the sample size; collect at the same time of day; calibrate equipment.
ms: Any two valid methods (1 mark each)
questions.tip: Reliability = consistency if repeated.

questions.q: In an infiltration investigation in Regent's Park, times (seconds) for 500 ml of water to infiltrate were: grass 95, 110, 88, 120, 102; path 410, 385, 460, 520, 395. Calculate the mean time for each surface.
questions.answer: Grass mean = 515 ÷ 5 = 103 s; path mean = 2170 ÷ 5 = 434 s.
ms: Grass: 103 seconds (1 mark)
Path: 434 seconds (1 mark)
questions.tip: Add all values then divide by the number of values.

questions.q: Using the data in the previous question, describe the difference in infiltration between grass and path surfaces and suggest a reason.
questions.answer: Water took about four times longer to infiltrate on the path (mean 434 s) than on the grass (mean 103 s). This is because path soil is compacted by trampling, so there are fewer pore spaces for water to pass through.
ms: Comparison using data, e.g. path about 4 times slower / 331 s longer (1 mark)
Reason: compaction from footfall (1 mark)
Development: fewer pore spaces / less vegetation and roots (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always use figures when describing data.

questions.q: Explain why a pilot survey might be useful before carrying out a questionnaire in Stratford.
questions.answer: A pilot survey tests the questions on a few people first, so confusing or biased questions can be identified and reworded. It shows how long the survey takes and whether the sites and timings are suitable, improving the accuracy and reliability of the final data.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Testing questions, removing ambiguity and bias, checking timing, practising method, improving reliability and validity.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Use the terms accuracy, reliability or validity.

questions.q: For your human geography enquiry, explain why the location you chose was suitable.
questions.answer: My enquiry investigated whether regeneration in Stratford had improved quality of life. Stratford was suitable because it has been heavily regenerated since the 2012 Olympics, so there were clear contrasts between new areas like the Olympic Park and older areas. It was safe, accessible by public transport, and secondary data such as census and council reports were available.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Link location to the enquiry question, evidence of the issue, accessibility, safety, data availability, contrasts within the area.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Link the site directly to the enquiry question, not just 'it was near school'.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of one data presentation method you used in your physical geography enquiry.
questions.answer: In my Regent's Park microclimate study I used line graphs to show temperature at sites along a transect. They clearly showed trends, such as cooler temperatures near the lake, and made it easy to compare sites. However they implied a continuous change between sites, which may not be true, and they could not show several variables at once, so a map with proportional symbols would have shown the spatial pattern better.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): thorough, well-developed discussion; accurate place-specific detail; clear links and chains of reasoning.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some development and some specific detail; may be unbalanced or partly generic.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little or no development or place detail.
Indicative content: Named method; strengths (clarity, comparisons, trends); weaknesses (data types suitability, misleading lines, missing spatial dimension); suggested improvements; link to enquiry.
questions.tip: Evaluate means strengths, weaknesses and an improvement.

questions.q: Assess the reliability of the conclusions from your human geography enquiry.
questions.answer: My conclusion that regeneration improved quality of life in Stratford was partly reliable. I used 50 questionnaires and environmental quality surveys at 10 sites, giving evidence. However data were collected on one weekday so may not represent weekends, the sample may have been biased towards shoppers in Westfield, and environmental quality scores are subjective. Repeating data collection at different times and with more people would make conclusions more reliable.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): thorough, well-developed discussion; accurate place-specific detail; clear links and chains of reasoning.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some development and some specific detail; may be unbalanced or partly generic.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little or no development or place detail.
Indicative content: Sample size, timing, sampling method, subjectivity, accuracy of equipment, secondary data, how far conclusions are supported, improvements.
questions.tip: Give a clear verdict ('partly reliable') and justify it.

questions.q: 'Primary data is more useful than secondary data in a geographical enquiry.' Using your own fieldwork, evaluate this statement. [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: In my Stratford enquiry, primary data such as questionnaires and environmental quality surveys were useful because they answered my specific question about local people's views. However they were limited by small samples and subjectivity. Secondary data, such as census data and indices of deprivation, gave reliable, large-scale information and showed change over time since before the Olympics, which I could not measure myself. Overall primary data was more relevant, but secondary data was needed to make conclusions reliable, so they were most useful together.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): detailed, place-specific evidence used accurately; balanced consideration of both sides; well-substantiated final judgement that directly answers the question (grade 8 standard).
Level 2 (4-6 marks): clear points with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): basic, generic points; little evidence; no clear judgement.

Indicative content: Named enquiry; primary methods and their strengths and limits; secondary sources (census, IMD, maps, photos, council reports) and their strengths and limits; how they complemented each other; judgement.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate, grammar controls meaning, wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy, good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy, limited specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant geographical content or errors hinder meaning.
questions.tip: Refer explicitly to YOUR enquiry and named methods to reach Level 3.

questions.q: Explain the risks you identified in one fieldwork enquiry and how you reduced them.
questions.answer: In Stratford, traffic was a risk when counting pedestrians near busy roads, so we stayed on pavements and worked in groups. Getting lost was reduced by having maps and teachers' phone numbers. In Regent's Park, slips near the lake were a risk, so we stayed away from the edges and wore suitable footwear.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Named risks (traffic, getting lost, weather, water, strangers), management (groups, high-vis, briefing, staying on paths).
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Pair each risk with a specific way of reducing it.

questions.q: Temperatures at five sites were 18.2, 19.1, 21.4, 22.0 and 17.5 °C. Calculate the range and the mean.
ms: Range: 4.5 °C (1 mark)
Mean: 19.64 °C (allow 19.6) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Include units.

questions.q: Explain how you would improve the accuracy of microclimate measurements in Regent's Park.
questions.answer: Use digital thermometers that are calibrated before use. Take readings at the same height above the ground at each site and wait for the instrument to settle. Take readings at all sites at the same time using several groups, so changing weather does not affect results, and repeat readings to find a mean.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear explanation, developed points linking cause and effect, accurate use of terms. Calibration, same height, settling time, simultaneous readings, repeat readings, shade instruments from sun.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little development or explanation.
questions.tip: Accuracy = closeness to the true value. Repeat readings improve reliability as well.

questions.q: Why are volcanoes at destructive plate margins usually more explosive than those at constructive margins?
options: The magma is hotter and runnier
There is more water in the oceans at destructive margins
The plates move faster at destructive margins
The magma is thicker (more viscous) and traps more gas
ms: At destructive margins melting crust produces viscous, gas-rich magma. Gas cannot escape easily, so pressure builds and eruptions are explosive. Constructive margins have runny basalt lava and gentler eruptions.
questions.tip: Link margin type to magma type to eruption style: that chain is what earns explanation marks.

questions.q: Which of these is a LONG-TERM response to an earthquake?
options: Handing out bottled water and tents
Search and rescue teams digging survivors out of rubble
ms: Long-term responses happen months or years later and aim to restore the area and reduce future risk, e.g. rebuilding to better standards. The other options are immediate responses.
questions.tip: Immediate = hours/days, saving lives. Long-term = months/years, rebuilding and reducing future risk.

questions.q: Figure 1 shows two earthquakes. Earthquake X: magnitude 7.0, focus depth 10 km, in a densely populated LIC city, struck at 5 pm. Earthquake Y: magnitude 7.6, focus depth 300 km, in a sparsely populated HIC region, struck at 3 am. Which statement best explains why X is likely to cause more deaths?
options: Y happened at night when people were asleep, so more would survive
Deep earthquakes always cause tsunamis, so Y would be worse
X was shallow, under a dense population with poorer-quality buildings
ms: A shallow focus means stronger shaking at the surface, and a dense LIC population with weaker buildings means more people are exposed and vulnerable. Y has the larger magnitude but its deep focus and low population reduce its impact.
questions.tip: In data questions, use every column given (magnitude, depth, population, wealth) rather than just magnitude.

questions.q: Give one example of a secondary effect of a volcanic eruption.
questions.answer: E.g. lahars (mudflows) when ash mixes with rain or meltwater.
ms: 1 mark for any valid secondary effect, e.g. lahars/mudflows (1); flooding from melted snow or ice (1); fires (1); loss of tourism income (1); food shortages from crops buried by ash (1); disease or respiratory problems after the eruption (1). Do not accept primary effects such as lava flows or ash fall themselves.
questions.tip: Secondary effects are caused BY the primary effects. Lava flows and ash fall are primary.

questions.q:
Figure 1 shows data for four earthquakes.
Country | Magnitude | Focus depth (km) | GDP per head (US$) | Deaths
P | 7.4 | 15 | 45,000 | 12
Q | 6.9 | 10 | 1,200 | 3,400
R | 7.9 | 35 | 15,000 | 520
S | 6.2 | 8 | 800 | 1,100

Using Figure 1, identify the country with the highest number of deaths and calculate the difference between its death toll and that of country R.
questions.answer: Country Q. 3,400 − 520 = 2,880 deaths.
ms: Country Q identified (1).
Difference of 2,880 deaths (1).
questions.tip: Read the right column. Show the subtraction so you can still pick up marks if you misread one value.

questions.q:
Figure 1 shows data for four earthquakes.
Country | Magnitude | Focus depth (km) | GDP per head (US$) | Deaths
P | 7.4 | 15 | 45,000 | 12
Q | 6.9 | 10 | 1,200 | 3,400
R | 7.9 | 35 | 15,000 | 520
S | 6.2 | 8 | 800 | 1,100

Calculate the mean number of deaths for the four earthquakes in Figure 1. Show your working.
ms: Method: total of 5,032 divided by 4 (1).
Answer: 1,258 deaths (1).
questions.tip: Mean = total ÷ number of values. Here the mean is pulled up by one large value, which is worth commenting on if asked.

questions.q:
Figure 1 shows data for four earthquakes.
Country | Magnitude | Focus depth (km) | GDP per head (US$) | Deaths
P | 7.4 | 15 | 45,000 | 12
Q | 6.9 | 10 | 1,200 | 3,400
R | 7.9 | 35 | 15,000 | 520
S | 6.2 | 8 | 800 | 1,100

Using Figure 1 and your own understanding, suggest why the effects of earthquakes vary between places.
questions.answer: Magnitude alone does not explain deaths: S (M6.2) killed 1,100 but P (M7.4) killed only 12. GDP per head matters most here: P and R are richer, can afford earthquake-resistant buildings, building codes, trained emergency services and drills. Q and S are poor (US$1,200 and US$800) with weak buildings and slower rescue. Depth also matters: Q and S were very shallow (10 km and 8 km), so shaking at the surface was stronger. Other factors not shown: population density, time of day, secondary hazards such as landslides or tsunamis.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Use of Figure 1 data, e.g. S (M6.2) had 1,100 deaths, about 90 times more than P (M7.4) with 12. Wealth: higher GDP means building codes, reinforced buildings, emergency planning, faster rescue and medical care; lower GDP means poorly built homes, less preparation, reliance on aid. Depth: shallow focus (Q 10 km, S 8 km) gives stronger surface shaking. Other factors from own understanding: population density, time of day, quality of infrastructure, secondary hazards (landslides, tsunami, fires), governance. Level 3 requires data from the figure used to support linked explanations.
questions.tip: 'Using Figure 1 and your own understanding' means BOTH: quote data from the table and add factors that are not in it.

questions.q: Explain why volcanic eruptions occur at constructive plate margins.
questions.answer: At constructive margins two plates move apart, driven by convection currents in the mantle (or ridge push). As they separate, pressure on the mantle below falls, so rock partly melts to form magma. The magma rises through the gap and erupts at the surface, forming new crust and shield-type volcanoes, e.g. Iceland on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. The basalt magma is runny so eruptions are usually gentle.
ms: Plates move apart (1).
Caused by convection currents/ridge push/slab pull in the mantle (1).
Magma rises to fill the gap (1), allow decrease in pressure causing melting.
Magma erupts at the surface forming new crust/volcanoes (1). Allow named example such as Iceland or the Mid-Atlantic Ridge as development.
questions.tip: Many students describe destructive margins by mistake. Check which margin the question names.

questions.q: Iceland is a high income country (HIC) with many active volcanoes. Suggest why volcanic eruptions in Iceland rarely cause many deaths.
questions.answer: Iceland's volcanoes are on a constructive margin, so eruptions are mostly effusive with runny lava that moves slowly, giving people time to move. Iceland is wealthy, so it can afford monitoring (seismometers, GPS, gas sensors) and has evacuation plans, so people get warnings. Its population is small and many volcanoes are in remote areas away from settlements.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear, developed points showing understanding, linked accurately to the question focus (and to the figure where one is given).
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple, undeveloped points. Limited link to the question focus.

Indicative content: Physical: constructive margin, basaltic/effusive eruptions, slow-moving lava, many volcanoes under ice or in remote areas. Human: wealth pays for monitoring and prediction, emergency planning and evacuation, good communications, strong infrastructure; low population density. Level 2 needs points developed and linked to Iceland's situation, not just a list of general strategies.
questions.tip: 'Suggest' means apply what you know to a place you may not have studied. Use the clues in the question: HIC and many volcanoes.

questions.q: Explain how earthquake-resistant buildings can reduce the effects of earthquakes.
questions.answer: Features such as cross-bracing, steel frames, rubber shock absorbers in the foundations and counterweights on the roof let buildings sway or absorb shaking instead of collapsing. Fewer buildings collapse, so fewer people are crushed or trapped and fewer are made homeless.
ms: Named feature, e.g. cross-bracing/steel frame/rubber foundations/counterweight/shatterproof glass (1).
How it works: absorbs or reduces shaking, allows the building to flex (1).
Effect: fewer buildings collapse so fewer deaths, injuries or homelessness (1).
questions.tip: Earthquakes rarely kill people directly. Collapsing buildings do. Make that link.

questions.q: Assess the extent to which the level of development is the main factor that determines the effects of a tectonic hazard.
questions.answer: Development is very important: Chile (HIC, M8.8, 2010) had about 500 deaths, whereas Nepal (LIC, M7.8, 2015) had almost 9,000 deaths, even though Chile's earthquake released far more energy. Chile had building codes, trained emergency services and quick restoration of power and water. However, physical factors also matter: Nepal's mountains caused landslides that blocked roads and slowed rescue; Chile's tsunami caused many of its deaths. Depth, magnitude, population density and time of day also affect impacts. Judgement: development is the main factor because it controls how vulnerable people are, but physical factors decide the scale of the hazard.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Evidence for development: Chile 2010 vs Nepal 2015 comparison (magnitude, deaths), building codes, emergency planning, money for rescue and rebuilding, reliance on international aid in Nepal, roughly 3 million homeless in Nepal. Other factors: magnitude, focus depth, distance from epicentre, population density, time of day, relief/terrain (landslides, Everest avalanche), secondary hazards (Chile tsunami). Level 3 requires a supported judgement on 'extent'.
questions.tip: 'Assess the extent' needs a judgement. Say how far you agree and why, not just list factors.

questions.q: Describe the global distribution of earthquakes.
questions.answer: Most earthquakes occur in narrow belts along plate margins, e.g. around the edge of the Pacific Ocean (the Ring of Fire), along the Himalayas and down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. Few occur in the middle of plates.
ms: Mostly along plate margins/in belts or lines (1).
Named area as development, e.g. Pacific Ring of Fire, west coast of South America, Japan, Himalayas, Mid-Atlantic Ridge (1). Allow: few in the centre of continents/plates.
questions.tip: Describe the pattern with named places. 'They are all over the world' gets no marks.

questions.q: Explain why scientists can predict volcanic eruptions more accurately than earthquakes.
questions.answer: Before an eruption, magma rises and gives warning signs: small earthquakes, ground bulging measured by tiltmeters and GPS, and increased sulphur dioxide emissions. These can be monitored so a warning can be issued days or weeks ahead. Earthquakes happen when stress along a fault is suddenly released, and there are no reliable warning signs, so scientists can only estimate where they are likely, not when.
ms: Volcanoes have measurable warning signs (1).
Named signs/instruments, e.g. tremors on seismometers, bulging on tiltmeters, gas emissions (1).
Earthquakes are a sudden release of built-up stress with no reliable warning signs (1).
So only probability/location of earthquakes can be estimated, not exact timing (1).
questions.tip: This is a two-sided explanation. Explain both why volcanoes CAN be predicted and why earthquakes CANNOT.

questions.q: Explain one reason why many people in rural areas were badly affected by the 2015 Nepal earthquake.
questions.answer: Landslides triggered by the earthquake blocked mountain roads, so rescue teams and aid took days to reach remote villages.
ms: Reason identified, e.g. landslides blocked roads/remote mountain terrain/weak stone and mud-brick buildings/few local emergency services (1).
Developed, e.g. so aid and rescue could not reach villages quickly/so homes collapsed easily (1).
questions.tip: For 2 mark 'explain one' questions: one point plus one development. A second separate point earns nothing.

questions.q: 'The immediate responses to a tectonic hazard are more important than the long-term responses.' Using a named example, to what extent do you agree with this statement?
questions.answer: Immediate responses save lives: in Nepal 2015 search and rescue, helicopters, field hospitals and tents from international aid and NGOs reduced deaths and suffering. In Chile 2010 emergency services acted quickly and power and water were restored to most people within days. But long-term responses (rebuilding with earthquake-resistant designs, Chile's housing reconstruction plan, restoring Nepal's heritage sites and tourism economy) reduce vulnerability to the next hazard. Judgement: immediate responses matter most for saving lives now, but long-term responses matter most for reducing future risk, so both are essential; in LICs long-term recovery is often the weak link.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Immediate: rescue, medical care, shelter, food and water, restoring power/water/communications; Chile examples (fast emergency response, most power and water restored within around 10 days); Nepal (international aid from the UK, India, China, Red Cross tents, helicopters). Long-term: rebuilding homes and infrastructure, building codes, economic recovery, Chile's housing reconstruction plan, Nepal's slow rebuilding and repair of heritage sites, rebuilding tourism. Evaluation: depends on wealth (HICs can fund both); immediate responses limit deaths, long-term responses limit future deaths; slow long-term recovery in Nepal left people in temporary shelters. Level 3 needs named, accurate detail and a clear judgement.
questions.tip: There is no SPaG on this one but you still need a clear judgement at the end. Use your case study, not general points.

questions.q: Using a named example, describe the immediate responses to an earthquake in a higher income country (HIC).
questions.answer: Chile, 27 February 2010 (M8.8): emergency services acted quickly; damaged roads were repaired so aid could get through; most of the population had power and water restored within about 10 days; temporary shelter was provided; international help was accepted, and a national appeal raised money.
ms: 1 mark per accurate response, with development credit for detail. E.g. fast response by well-trained emergency services (1); power and water restored to most people within around 10 days (1); key roads repaired and reopened quickly to allow aid (1); national appeal/telethon raised money (1); temporary shelters/emergency supplies (1).
Max 2 if no named example or if responses are generic. Do not credit long-term responses such as the housing reconstruction plan as immediate.
questions.tip: Immediate means the first hours and days. Keep the housing plan for long-term questions.

questions.q: Describe what happens at a conservative plate margin.
questions.answer: Two plates move past each other, either in different directions or in the same direction at different speeds. Friction makes them stick; pressure builds up and is released suddenly as an earthquake. No crust is created or destroyed, so there are no volcanoes. Example: the San Andreas Fault in California.
ms: Plates slide past each other (1).
Friction/pressure builds and is released as earthquakes; no volcanoes (1). Allow named example.
questions.tip: No volcanoes at conservative margins: say so.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, which way do tropical storms spin, and why?
options: Anticlockwise, because warm air sinks in the eye
Anticlockwise, because of the Coriolis effect
Clockwise, because of high pressure at the centre
Clockwise, because of the trade winds
ms: Earth's rotation (the Coriolis effect) deflects air so that it spirals into the low pressure centre anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere (clockwise in the Southern).
questions.tip: Low pressure systems spin anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere. The Coriolis effect is the reason.

questions.q: A weather station recorded air pressure every 3 hours as a tropical storm passed: 1008, 1002, 990, 965, 940, 955, 985, 1004 (hPa). What is the range of the readings?
ms: Range = highest − lowest = 1008 − 940 = 68 hPa. 64 is 1004 − 940 (using the last value instead of the highest).
questions.tip: Use the highest and lowest values, not the first and last.

questions.q: Why does the UK mostly receive winds from the south-west?
options: Air always moves from the sea to the land
It lies under the Hadley cell, where trade winds blow towards the equator
It lies under the polar cell, where cold air flows from the North Pole
It lies under the Ferrel cell, where surface air moves from about 30° towards 60° and is deflected by the Coriolis effect
ms: The UK (about 50-60°N) lies under the Ferrel cell. Surface air flows from the subtropical high (30°) towards the low at 60°, and the Coriolis effect turns it to blow from the south-west (the westerlies).
questions.tip: Know which cell the UK is in and the surface wind that goes with it.

questions.q:
Figure 2 shows sea surface temperatures in August. Caribbean Sea: 29°C. Gulf of Mexico: 28°C. Atlantic off Portugal: 22°C. Atlantic off Ireland: 16°C.

Using Figure 2, suggest why tropical storms form near the Caribbean but not off Portugal.
questions.answer: Tropical storms need sea temperatures of at least about 26-27°C. The Caribbean (29°C) is warm enough to provide heat and moisture, but the sea off Portugal (22°C) is too cool.
ms: Storms need sea temperatures of about 26-27°C or more (1).
Use of data: Caribbean 29°C is above this but Portugal 22°C is below (1). Allow reference to latitude (Caribbean within 5-30°).
questions.tip: Quote figures from the data to earn the second mark.

questions.q: Explain how the eye of a tropical storm forms.
questions.answer: Air spirals rapidly upwards around the centre of the storm. Some of this air sinks down in the very centre, where it warms and dries, so clouds cannot form. This creates a calm, clear area of low pressure in the middle: the eye.
ms: Air rises rapidly around the centre/in the eyewall (1).
Air sinks in the centre (1).
Sinking air warms/dries, so no cloud forms, giving calm, clear conditions (1).
questions.tip: The eye has SINKING air. Saying air rises in the eye is the most common mistake.

questions.q: Explain how climate change may affect the distribution, frequency and intensity of tropical storms.
questions.answer: Warmer seas mean more areas reach the 26-27°C needed, so storms could form further from the equator (distribution). Warmer water gives more energy and moisture, so storms are likely to be more intense, with stronger winds and heavier rain. Scientists are less certain about frequency; the total number may not rise but more storms may reach the strongest categories.
ms: Distribution: more ocean above 26-27°C so storms form over a wider area/further from the tropics (1).
Intensity: warmer seas give more energy so storms are stronger/more rainfall (1).
Frequency: uncertain/may stay similar overall but more high-category storms (1).
Development: e.g. higher sea levels make storm surges more damaging (1).
questions.tip: Cover all three words in the question. Frequency is the least certain, and saying so shows real understanding.

questions.q: Using a named example, explain why the effects of a tropical storm were so severe.
questions.answer: Typhoon Haiyan, Philippines, November 2013. Physical: winds over 300 km/h and a storm surge of up to about 5 m swept into low-lying coastal areas such as Tacloban on Leyte, where around 90% of the city was destroyed. Human: many people lived in poorly built homes on the coast; the Philippines is a lower-middle income country with limited money for defences; many people did not understand what a 'storm surge' meant, so did not evacuate; the airport and roads were damaged, slowing aid. About 6,300 people died and about 4 million were displaced.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Haiyan, 8 November 2013. Physical factors: very strong winds (over 300 km/h), storm surge up to about 5 m, heavy rain causing flooding and landslides, low-lying coastal settlements, Tacloban badly hit. Human factors: poverty and weak housing, dense coastal population, limited warnings understood, damaged airport/roads slowed aid, reliance on fishing and farming (rice, coconuts). Effects for context: about 6,300 deaths, about 4 million displaced, over 1 million houses damaged or destroyed. Level 3 needs both physical and human explanations linked to the scale of the effects.
questions.tip: This asks WHY the effects were severe, not just WHAT they were. Every effect you mention needs a cause attached.

questions.q: Explain how the global atmospheric circulation leads to dry conditions at about 30° north and south of the equator.
questions.answer: At the equator the sun's heating makes air rise, forming low pressure. The air cools, loses moisture as rain and moves towards the poles at high altitude. At about 30° the cool, dry air sinks, forming the subtropical high pressure belt. Sinking air warms and cannot form clouds, so there is very little rain. This is why hot deserts such as the Sahara are found here.
ms: Air rises at the equator/low pressure (1).
Air moves polewards at high altitude and has already lost moisture (1).
Air sinks at about 30° forming high pressure (1).
Sinking air warms, so no clouds/rain form, giving deserts (1).
questions.tip: Name the pressure belt and say what the air is doing (rising or sinking) at each latitude.

questions.q:
Bangladesh is a low-lying, densely populated lower income country at the head of the Bay of Bengal, where tropical cyclones often make landfall.

Suggest how monitoring, prediction, protection and planning could reduce the effects of tropical cyclones in Bangladesh.
questions.answer: Monitoring by satellites and weather stations tracks cyclones over the Bay of Bengal. Prediction of the track and landfall gives several days' warning. Warnings can be spread by radio, mobile phones and volunteers so people move to safety. Protection: raised concrete cyclone shelters, embankments, and planting mangroves to absorb storm surge energy. Planning: evacuation drills, stockpiles of food and water, building away from the coast. Because Bangladesh has limited money, cheap methods such as warnings and shelters are most suitable.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Monitoring: satellites, aircraft, ocean buoys, weather radar. Prediction: computer models forecast path and strength, allowing early warning. Protection: cyclone shelters on stilts or raised ground, sea walls/embankments, mangrove planting, stronger houses. Planning: evacuation routes, community warning volunteers, drills, emergency supplies, land-use planning. Application: low-lying land vulnerable to storm surge, dense population, limited funds so low-cost strategies are effective. Level 3 requires all four strategies explained and linked to Bangladesh's situation.
questions.tip: Use the clues in the question (low-lying, dense, lower income) in your answer. That is what 'suggest' rewards.

questions.q: What is meant by a 'storm surge'?
questions.answer: A large rise in sea level caused by low pressure and strong winds pushing water onto the coast.
ms: Rise in sea level caused by low pressure and/or strong winds driving water towards the coast (1). Do not accept 'a big wave' alone.
questions.tip: A storm surge is not the same as a tsunami or a single big wave.

questions.q:
The Saffir-Simpson scale classifies tropical storms by sustained wind speed: Category 1: 119-153 km/h. Category 2: 154-177 km/h. Category 3: 178-208 km/h. Category 4: 209-251 km/h. Category 5: 252 km/h or more.

A hurricane has sustained winds of 230 km/h. Which category is it?
questions.answer: Category 4.
ms: Category 4 (1).
questions.tip: Read the boundaries carefully: 230 lies between 209 and 251.

questions.q: Explain why tropical storms lose strength when they move over land.
questions.answer: Over land there is no warm ocean to supply heat and moisture, so the storm loses its energy source. Less moist air rises, so less condensation releases heat. Friction with the land surface also slows the winds.
ms: Loss of supply of warm, moist air/heat from the ocean (1).
Less condensation/latent heat released, so the storm's energy falls (1).
Friction with the land surface slows winds (1).
questions.tip: Explain the energy source: warm sea = moisture = condensation = energy.

questions.q: Using a named example, evaluate the effectiveness of the responses to a tropical storm.
questions.answer: Haiyan 2013: about 800,000 people were evacuated before landfall, which saved lives, but warnings did not make clear the danger of the storm surge, so many people stayed in coastal areas. International aid (the UK sent HMS Daring and aircraft, the US military reopened Tacloban airport) brought food, water and shelter, but damage to roads and the airport slowed aid in the first days and there was looting. Long-term: cash-for-work schemes gave income, new storm shelters were built, mangroves replanted and no-build zones set along the coast, although some resettlement was slow and unpopular. Judgement: largely effective after the first few days, but warnings and early access were the weakest parts.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Immediate: pre-storm evacuation of about 800,000 people; emergency food, water, shelter; international aid including UK (HMS Daring, aircraft) and US military reopening the airport; field hospitals. Problems: storm surge warnings misunderstood, aid delayed by blocked roads, looting, shortages. Long-term: cash-for-work clearing debris, rebuilding with stronger designs, more cyclone shelters, mangrove replanting, coastal no-build zones. Evaluation: compare effectiveness of different responses, use criteria (lives saved, speed, sustainability, who benefited). Level 3 needs a clear judgement backed by accurate case study detail.
questions.tip: 'Evaluate' means weigh up strengths AND weaknesses, then decide how effective overall.

questions.q: Explain why the effects of tropical storms are often greater in lower income countries than in higher income countries.
questions.answer: In LICs many homes are self-built from wood or corrugated iron, so they are destroyed by high winds and storm surges. Warning systems may be limited or people may lack radios and phones, and there may be few cyclone shelters, so people cannot evacuate. Dense populations live on low-lying coasts and floodplains because land is cheaper. Governments have less money for sea walls, emergency services and rapid aid, so rescue is slower and secondary effects such as disease and food shortages last longer. Many people rely on farming and fishing, so losing crops and boats destroys their income. For example, Typhoon Haiyan (2013) killed about 6,300 people in the Philippines.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Housing quality, warning and communication systems, shelters, evacuation capacity, coastal and floodplain settlement, money for defences and emergency response, healthcare, reliance on aid, dependence on primary jobs, poor infrastructure slowing aid, corruption or weak governance. Comparison with HICs (better forecasting, insurance, building codes). Level 3 needs linked chains of reasoning and use of an example.
questions.tip: Each factor should lead to a consequence: weak buildings, so more collapse, so more deaths.

questions.q: Using an example, explain how a tropical storm can cause economic effects that last for years.
questions.answer: Typhoon Haiyan (2013) destroyed large areas of rice and coconut crops and many fishing boats, so farming and fishing families lost their income. Coconut trees take years to regrow and produce again, so income losses lasted long after the storm. Damage to homes, roads and businesses in Tacloban meant expensive rebuilding, slowing economic recovery for the region.
ms: Named example (1).
Loss of crops/boats/businesses (1).
Developed: long recovery time, e.g. coconut trees take years to grow/boats costly to replace (1).
Cost of rebuilding infrastructure/loss of jobs slows recovery (1).
questions.tip: 'Last for years' is the focus. Choose effects with a long recovery time.

questions.q: Which type of weather system brought repeated heavy rain to the Somerset Levels in winter 2013-14?
options: A series of Atlantic depressions (low pressure systems)
ms: A run of low pressure systems from the Atlantic, steered by the jet stream, brought storm after storm of heavy rain across southern England.
questions.tip: Depressions = low pressure = wet and windy. Anticyclones = high pressure = settled, dry.

questions.q: Which weather system is most likely to cause a summer heatwave in the UK?
options: A depression moving in from the Atlantic
ms: Anticyclones bring sinking air, clear skies and light winds. In summer, long hours of sunshine under a blocking high cause heatwaves; in winter the same clear skies cause frost and fog.
questions.tip: Learn both the summer and winter weather that an anticyclone brings.

questions.q: Which of these was a long-term management response to the 2014 Somerset Levels floods?
options: Residents of Muchelney being taken to the shops by boat
A 20-year Flood Action Plan including dredging and raising roads
ms: The 20-year Flood Action Plan (about £100 million) is long-term. The others are short-term emergency responses.
questions.tip: Sort responses by time: during the flood vs years afterwards.

questions.q: Describe two effects of extreme cold weather in the UK.
questions.answer: Roads and railways close because of snow and ice, disrupting travel and work. Elderly people are at greater risk of hypothermia and deaths rise.
ms: One mark per effect, e.g. transport disruption/roads and rail closed (1); schools close (1); increased deaths/hypothermia among elderly (1); burst water pipes (1); higher energy bills (1); crop or livestock losses (1).
questions.tip: Two different effects. Don't give 'roads close' and 'trains stop' as two points, they are both transport.

questions.q: Explain how the physical geography of the Somerset Levels made the 2014 floods worse.
questions.answer: The Levels are very flat and low-lying, much of it close to sea level, so water drains away slowly. Several rivers, including the Parrett and Tone, flow through the area. High tides in the Bristol Channel stopped river water draining out to sea. After weeks of heavy rain the ground was saturated, so more rain ran straight off into the rivers, which burst their banks.
ms: Flat, low-lying land at or near sea level (1), so drains slowly/water collects (1).
Rivers Parrett and Tone flow through it (1).
High tides prevented rivers emptying/tidal locking (1).
Saturated ground increased surface runoff (1).
Max 4.
questions.tip: The question says PHYSICAL. Lack of dredging is a human factor and gets no credit here.

questions.q: Explain how the 2014 Somerset Levels floods affected farmers.
questions.answer: About 6,900 hectares of farmland was under water for weeks, so grass and crops were ruined. Over 1,000 livestock had to be evacuated, which was costly, and farmers had to buy in fodder. Fields stayed waterlogged and contaminated by silt, so they could not be used for some time and incomes fell.
ms: 1 mark per developed point or 2 for a well developed point. E.g. around 6,900 ha of farmland flooded (1) so crops/grass destroyed (1); over 1,000 livestock evacuated (1) at high cost/stress to animals (1); fodder had to be bought in (1); land waterlogged or contaminated for months so income lost (1).
questions.tip: Use the case study figures. They are what lift an answer to full marks.

questions.q: Using a named example, explain how the social and economic effects of a UK weather hazard were linked.
questions.answer: Somerset Levels 2014: economic damage caused social problems. The A361 and other roads and the Bridgwater-Taunton railway was disrupted, so people could not get to work and businesses lost trade. Around 600 homes were affected by flooding, so families had to move out, causing stress, and insurance costs rose. Farmers lost income as about 6,900 ha of farmland flooded and over 1,000 livestock were evacuated, putting pressure on rural families. Villages such as Muchelney were cut off, so residents relied on boats for supplies, and local schools and services were disrupted.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Somerset Levels 2013-14. Social: around 600 homes affected by flooding, evacuations, Muchelney cut off (boats needed), stress, damaged possessions, school and community disruption. Economic: around 6,900 ha farmland flooded, over 1,000 livestock evacuated, roads (including the A361) closed and the Bridgwater-Taunton railway disrupted, businesses lost trade, insurance claims, cost of clean-up. Links: transport closure affects jobs and access to services; farm losses affect rural livelihoods. Level 3 requires clear links between the two types of effect.
questions.tip: This question rewards LINKS. Use phrases like 'this meant that...' to join economic and social effects.

questions.q: Suggest one reason why dredging rivers may reduce flood risk on the Somerset Levels.
questions.answer: Dredging removes silt from the river bed, so the channel is deeper and can carry more water before it overflows.
ms: Removes silt/sediment from the channel (1).
Increases channel capacity so more water can be carried before the river floods (1).
questions.tip: Dredging increases capacity. Say what happens to the water.

questions.q: 'UK weather is becoming more extreme because of climate change.' Assess this statement.
questions.answer: Evidence for: a record 40.3°C at Coningsby in July 2022; winter 2013-14 was one of the wettest on record; most of the UK's warmest years have been since 2000; frequent named storms bring flooding. Warmer air holds more moisture so heavy rain events are likely to be more intense.
