Evidence against: the UK has always had extreme events (e.g. the 1953 North Sea flood); records only go back around 150 years; one event cannot be blamed on climate change on its own; natural variation in the jet stream also causes extremes. Judgement: the trend in records and the physics of a warmer atmosphere strongly support the statement, although single events are hard to attribute.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: For: record temperatures (40.3°C, 2022), Somerset 2014 wet winter, increase in warm years since 2000, heavier rain events, more named storms in the news. Reasons: warmer atmosphere holds more water vapour, changes to the jet stream. Against: natural variability, limited length of reliable records, past extremes such as the 1953 floods, improved reporting and naming of storms making them seem more frequent. Level 3 requires a supported judgement.
questions.tip: Avoid saying 'every year is hotter'. Talk about trends and the frequency of record events.

questions.q: Give one way the Environment Agency warns people about flooding.
questions.answer: Flood warnings sent by text, phone or email (Floodline), and published online.
ms: Any valid method: flood warning texts/calls/emails (1); online flood warning maps (1); news/radio broadcasts (1); sirens/local wardens (1).
questions.tip: Keep one-mark answers short and specific.

questions.q: Evaluate whether dredging was the best response to the 2014 Somerset Levels floods.
questions.answer: Dredging around 8 km of the Parrett and Tone increased channel capacity and was what local people wanted, so it reduced flood risk in the short term. However, rivers silt up again, so dredging has to be repeated and is expensive. Other parts of the Flood Action Plan, such as raising roads, raising riverbanks and the planned tidal barrier at Bridgwater, plus catchment measures like planting trees upstream, deal with the problem more widely. Dredging was a useful part of the plan but not the best response on its own.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear, developed points showing understanding, linked accurately to the question focus (and to the figure where one is given).
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple, undeveloped points. Limited link to the question focus.

Indicative content: For dredging: increases capacity, quick to show results, strongly supported by residents and farmers who blamed lack of dredging. Against: silt returns, ongoing cost, does not stop water arriving from upstream or tidal locking, may move problem downstream. Alternatives: raising roads and banks, pumping stations, tidal barrier at Bridgwater, upstream land management. A judgement is needed for Level 2.
questions.tip: 'Evaluate whether X was the best' means compare it with other responses before deciding.

questions.q: In winter 2013-14 Muchelney, a village on the Somerset Levels, was cut off by floodwater for several weeks. Suggest why some people argue that the money spent on protecting the Somerset Levels would be better spent elsewhere.
questions.answer: The Levels are mainly farmland with a low population, so the value of property protected per pound spent is lower than in cities. The land is naturally a flood plain and wetland, so it will flood again; dredging must be repeated and costs keep rising. Money could protect more people in towns, or be spent upstream on tree planting and land management that reduces runoff over a wider area. Some argue the Levels should be allowed to flood naturally in winter as wetland habitat, with farmers compensated. On the other hand, residents, farmers and transport links such as the A361 and the railway suffer heavily when flooding happens.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Cost-benefit: low population density, farmland value vs urban areas; repeated cost of dredging (silt returns); naturally low-lying wetland/floodplain; climate change may make protection harder; alternatives such as upstream catchment management, managed flooding with compensation, habitat value of wetlands. Counter-view: homes, livelihoods, transport links (A361, Bridgwater-Taunton railway), mental health and community. Level 3 requires reasoned argument linked to the Somerset context, ideally acknowledging the other side.
questions.tip: 'Suggest why some people argue...' still rewards a balanced answer. Show you understand the counter-argument.

questions.q: Describe two effects of a drought in the UK.
questions.answer: Hosepipe bans and water shortages for homes. Crops fail or yields fall, so food prices may rise. Also: wildfires on moorland, rivers falling and fish dying.
ms: One mark per effect, e.g. hosepipe bans/water restrictions (1); lower crop yields (1); wildfires (1); low river levels harming wildlife (1); subsidence of buildings on clay (1).
questions.tip: Two different effects, not two examples of the same one.

questions.q: Atmospheric CO₂ was about 280 parts per million (ppm) before the Industrial Revolution and is now about 420 ppm. What is the percentage increase?
ms: (420 − 280) ÷ 280 × 100 = 140 ÷ 280 × 100 = 50%. 33% comes from dividing by the new value (420); 140 is the actual increase in ppm, not a percentage.
questions.tip: Percentage change: always divide by the ORIGINAL value.

questions.q: Which of the following is evidence for climate change over the Quaternary period (the last 2.6 million years), rather than just the last 150 years?
options: Satellite images of shrinking Arctic sea ice
Records of the Thames frost fairs
Air bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice cores
ms: Ice cores go back around 800,000 years, covering many glacial and interglacial periods. Thermometer and satellite records are recent, and frost fair records cover only a few centuries.
questions.tip: Match each piece of evidence to its time span.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of mitigation?
options: Replacing coal power stations with wind farms
Building higher flood defences in coastal towns
Changing the types of crops farmers grow
ms: Mitigation reduces the causes of climate change by cutting greenhouse gas emissions. Wind farms replace fossil fuel burning. The others are adaptation to the effects.
questions.tip: Mitigation tackles causes. Adaptation copes with effects.

questions.q: Describe how the orbit of the Earth (Milankovitch cycles) can cause climate change.
questions.answer: The shape of Earth's orbit changes from circular to more elliptical over about 100,000 years (eccentricity), and the tilt of the axis changes over about 41,000 years. These change how much solar energy reaches Earth and when, causing glacial and interglacial periods.
ms: Named cycle, e.g. eccentricity/orbit shape (about 100,000 years), axial tilt (about 41,000 years), precession/wobble (about 26,000 years) (1).
Changes the amount or distribution of solar radiation reaching Earth, causing glacial/interglacial periods (1).
questions.tip: Link the cycle to the amount of energy received. Naming it alone is only 1 mark.

questions.q:
Figure 3 shows global average temperature compared with the 1951-1980 average (°C).
Year | 1900 | 1920 | 1940 | 1960 | 1980 | 2000 | 2020
Anomaly | −0.2 | −0.3 | 0.1 | 0.0 | 0.3 | 0.4 | 1.0

Describe the trend shown in Figure 3. Use data in your answer.
questions.answer: Overall temperatures rose, from −0.2°C in 1900 to 1.0°C in 2020, an increase of 1.2°C. The rise was not steady: there was a small fall to −0.3°C in 1920 and little change between 1940 (0.1°C) and 1960 (0.0°C). The fastest rise was between 2000 and 2020 (0.6°C).
ms: Overall trend: temperature has increased (1).
Use of data, e.g. from −0.2°C in 1900 to 1.0°C in 2020/increase of 1.2°C (1).
Anomaly or change in rate identified, e.g. dip in 1920, levelling off 1940-1960, faster rise since 2000 (1).
questions.tip: Overall trend + data + anomaly is the formula for 3 mark 'describe the trend' questions.

questions.q: Explain how evidence from ice cores and tree rings helps scientists understand past climate.
questions.answer: Ice cores: as snow builds up and turns to ice, it traps tiny bubbles of air. Scientists measure CO₂ in these bubbles, and the chemistry of the ice shows past temperatures. Antarctic cores go back about 800,000 years and show that CO₂ and temperature rose and fell together. Tree rings: a tree grows one ring each year; wide rings show warm, wet years and narrow rings show cold or dry years, giving yearly climate records for thousands of years.
ms: Ice: air bubbles trapped in layers of ice (1); CO₂ levels/isotopes give past temperatures (1); records back about 800,000 years (1).
Tree rings: one ring per year (1); ring width shows how good growing conditions were (warm/wet = wide) (1).
Max 4. Max 3 if only one type of evidence covered.
questions.tip: Explain HOW each one records climate, not just that it does.

questions.q: Explain how climate change could affect people living in low-lying coastal areas such as Bangladesh.
questions.answer: Sea levels are rising through thermal expansion of warmer water and melting land ice. In Bangladesh much of the land is a low delta, so rising seas cause more frequent flooding and coastal erosion. Salt water gets into soils and drinking water, which reduces rice yields and harms health. Warmer seas may make cyclones more intense, so storm surges are more damaging. These effects could force millions to migrate to cities like Dhaka, adding pressure on jobs and housing.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Causes: thermal expansion, melting glaciers and ice sheets, more intense tropical storms. Effects: more frequent and severe flooding, erosion, loss of farmland, saltwater intrusion into soil and water, lower crop yields, food insecurity, health problems (water-borne disease), loss of homes, migration to cities or abroad, economic losses, cost of defences that an LIC may not afford. Level 3 requires linked chains from cause to effect on people.
questions.tip: Use the place in the question. Bangladesh's flat delta, dense population and rice farming are all worth using.

questions.q: Explain how planting trees and carbon capture can help to mitigate climate change.
questions.answer: Trees absorb CO₂ from the atmosphere through photosynthesis and store carbon in their wood, so planting forests reduces greenhouse gases. Carbon capture and storage (CCS) collects CO₂ from power stations or factories before it is released, then pipes it underground into old oil and gas fields. Both lower the amount of CO₂ in the atmosphere, reducing the enhanced greenhouse effect.
ms: Trees absorb CO₂ through photosynthesis (1) and store carbon (act as a carbon sink) (1).
CCS captures CO₂ from power stations/industry (1) and stores it underground (1).
Allow link to reducing the enhanced greenhouse effect as development.
questions.tip: Two methods, two developed points each. Balance your answer.

questions.q: 'Adapting to climate change is more important than trying to mitigate it.' To what extent do you agree with this statement? (9 marks + 3 SPaG)
questions.answer: Adaptation helps people cope with changes that are already happening: flood defences, drought-resistant crops, water storage and changing farming practices. It is urgent in vulnerable places like Bangladesh and the Sahel, and can be cheap. But adaptation alone cannot cope if warming continues rising; at some point defences fail and crops cannot cope. Mitigation (renewables, CCS, tree planting, the Paris Agreement aim of well below 2°C, ideally 1.5°C) tackles the cause and reduces future damage, but needs global cooperation and results take decades. Judgement: both are needed; mitigation is more important long term, while adaptation is more important for the poorest countries now.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): Thorough knowledge and understanding. Detailed, well-balanced evaluation of both sides. Detailed, accurate, place-specific evidence. Clear, substantiated judgement that answers the question.

Level 2 (4-6 marks): Reasonable knowledge and understanding. Partly balanced evaluation, may favour one side. Some place-specific evidence, but general or patchy. A judgement is given but only partly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Limited knowledge. Simple, unbalanced points with little evaluation. Little or no relevant evidence. No clear judgement.

SPaG (3 marks): High performance 3 = accurate spelling and punctuation, grammar controls meaning, wide range of specialist terms used precisely. Intermediate 2 = considerable accuracy, good range of specialist terms. Threshold 1 = reasonable accuracy, limited range of specialist terms.

Indicative content: Adaptation: flood defences, raised homes, managing water supply, drought-resistant crops, changing agriculture, reducing risk from sea level rise. Mitigation: alternative energy, carbon capture, planting trees, international agreements (Paris 2015). Evaluation: timescale (emissions already locked in), cost and who pays, LICs contribute least but suffer most, global cooperation difficult, mitigation prevents worst outcomes. Level 3 needs a clear, supported judgement and specific examples.
questions.tip: Define both terms early, then argue. Examiners reward a conclusion that says 'it depends on...' only if you explain what it depends on.

questions.q: State one human activity, other than burning fossil fuels, that increases greenhouse gases.
questions.answer: Deforestation (or cattle farming, rice farming, cement production, landfill).
ms: Any one: deforestation (1); cattle/livestock farming (methane) (1); rice paddies (methane) (1); fertiliser use (nitrous oxide) (1); cement production (1); landfill (1).
questions.tip: The question rules out fossil fuels. Read the 'other than'.

questions.q: Explain why the period of reliable thermometer records is not enough on its own to prove that recent warming is caused by humans.
questions.answer: Thermometer records only go back to about 1850, which is a very short time compared with natural climate cycles lasting thousands of years. To show recent warming is unusual, scientists compare it with longer records from ice cores, tree rings and other evidence. They also compare temperature with CO₂ levels and with natural factors like solar output, which has not risen enough to explain the warming.
ms: Records cover only about 150-170 years (1).
Natural cycles happen over much longer timescales so a longer record is needed for comparison (1).
Other evidence, e.g. ice cores/linking to CO₂ rise/ruling out solar or volcanic causes, is needed (1).
questions.tip: This is about the limits of evidence. Show you can judge evidence, not just list it.

questions.q: Assess the relative importance of natural and human causes of recent climate change.
questions.answer: Natural causes (Milankovitch cycles, changes in solar output, volcanic eruptions) explain past changes such as glacial periods and the Little Ice Age. But orbital cycles act over tens of thousands of years, solar output has not increased enough since 1950, and eruptions such as Pinatubo cool the Earth only for a year or two. Human causes (burning fossil fuels, deforestation, farming) have raised CO₂ from about 280 to about 420 ppm, matching the rise of over 1°C since around 1850. So recent warming is mainly human, while natural factors cause short-term variation.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Natural: orbital changes (timescale too long for recent warming), solar output (sunspots, Maunder Minimum linked to Little Ice Age, no significant rise recently), volcanic eruptions (short-term cooling). Human: fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture (methane), industry; CO₂ about 280 ppm to about 420 ppm; warming over 1°C. Judgement that human causes dominate recent change needed for Level 3, with reasons.
questions.tip: 'Relative importance' means compare them and say which matters more, with reasons.

questions.q: Explain how volcanic eruptions and changes in solar output can cause climate change.
questions.answer: Large eruptions throw ash and sulphur dioxide high into the atmosphere. Sulphur dioxide forms tiny droplets that reflect sunlight, cooling the Earth for one or two years; Mount Pinatubo (1991) cooled global temperature by about 0.5°C. Solar output varies with sunspot activity. Fewer sunspots means less energy; the Maunder Minimum (1645-1715) coincided with part of the Little Ice Age.
ms: Volcanic ash/sulphur dioxide reflects/blocks sunlight (1).
Short-term cooling, e.g. Pinatubo cooled about 0.5°C (1).
Solar output varies with sunspots (1).
Low sunspot activity linked to cooler periods, e.g. Maunder Minimum/Little Ice Age (1).
questions.tip: Volcanic effects are short-term. Saying they cause long-term warming is wrong.

questions.q:
Figure 4 describes a food web in a UK freshwater pond.
Algae and pondweed are eaten by water snails and mayfly larvae.
Water snails are eaten by frogs and sticklebacks.
Mayfly larvae are eaten by sticklebacks and water beetles.
Sticklebacks are eaten by herons and pike.
Frogs are eaten by herons.
Water beetles are eaten by frogs.

Using Figure 4, which organism is a producer?
ms: Pondweed (like algae) makes its own food by photosynthesis, so it is a producer. Snails are primary consumers; sticklebacks and herons are higher consumers.
questions.tip: Producers are always plants or algae at the start of a food chain.

questions.q:
Figure 4 describes a food web in a UK freshwater pond.
Algae and pondweed are eaten by water snails and mayfly larvae.
Water snails are eaten by frogs and sticklebacks.
Mayfly larvae are eaten by sticklebacks and water beetles.
Sticklebacks are eaten by herons and pike.
Frogs are eaten by herons.
Water beetles are eaten by frogs.

Using Figure 4, which organism is a primary consumer?
ms: Mayfly larvae eat algae and pondweed (producers), so they are primary consumers. Sticklebacks eat consumers, so they are secondary (or higher) consumers.
questions.tip: Primary consumer = eats producers. Trace the arrow back one step.

questions.q:
Figure 4 describes a food web in a UK freshwater pond.
Algae and pondweed are eaten by water snails and mayfly larvae.
Water snails are eaten by frogs and sticklebacks.
Mayfly larvae are eaten by sticklebacks and water beetles.
Sticklebacks are eaten by herons and pike.
Frogs are eaten by herons.
Water beetles are eaten by frogs.

A disease kills most of the sticklebacks in the pond. Which is the most likely effect?
options: Herons stop visiting because there are no frogs
Mayfly larvae numbers increase because fewer are eaten
Pike numbers increase because there is less competition
Pondweed increases because sticklebacks eat it
ms: Sticklebacks eat mayfly larvae, so fewer predators means more larvae survive. Pike would decrease (they lose a food source), sticklebacks don't eat pondweed, and frogs are unaffected directly.
questions.tip: Follow the arrows in both directions: what the organism eats and what eats it.

questions.q: Which global biome has a cold climate, coniferous trees such as pine and spruce, and is found mainly between about 50° and 65°N across Canada, Scandinavia and Russia?
ms: Boreal forest (taiga) lies south of the tundra across the northern continents. Tundra is further north and treeless.
questions.tip: Learn biomes in order from the equator to the poles: rainforest, savanna, desert, grassland/deciduous, boreal, tundra.

questions.q: Which global biome has hot temperatures all year, a distinct wet and dry season, and grassland with scattered trees such as baobab and acacia?
ms: Savanna lies between the rainforests and hot deserts (roughly 5-15° from the equator) and has a wet and a dry season.
questions.tip: Savanna sits between rainforest and desert both on the map and in its climate.

questions.q: Why does the tundra have very low biodiversity?
options: The soil is too fertile for most plants
The ground is permanently frozen below the surface, the growing season is short and temperatures are low
It is too close to the equator
ms: Permafrost, low temperatures and a short growing season limit plant growth, so there is little energy at the base of food chains to support many species.
questions.tip: Link biodiversity to energy: fewer producers means fewer consumers.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the nutrient cycle of a UK deciduous woodland with that of a tropical rainforest?
options: The biomass store is larger in the UK woodland, because its trees grow faster
Nutrients move between stores faster in the UK woodland, because it has more rainfall
The UK woodland has no soil store, because leaching removes all nutrients
The litter store is larger in the UK woodland, because cooler temperatures and autumn leaf fall mean litter decomposes more slowly
ms: In UK deciduous woodland, leaves fall in autumn and decompose slowly in the cool climate, so the litter store is much larger than in a rainforest, where hot, wet conditions break litter down within weeks. The soil store is also relatively larger in UK woodland. The rainforest has the larger biomass store and faster transfers.
questions.tip: Compare the stores: rainforest = big biomass, small litter and soil; UK woodland = bigger litter and soil stores, slower transfers.

questions.q:
Figure 4 describes a food web in a UK freshwater pond.
Algae and pondweed are eaten by water snails and mayfly larvae.
Water snails are eaten by frogs and sticklebacks.
Mayfly larvae are eaten by sticklebacks and water beetles.
Sticklebacks are eaten by herons and pike.
Frogs are eaten by herons.
Water beetles are eaten by frogs.

Using Figure 4, complete a food chain of four organisms that ends with a heron.
questions.answer: E.g. pondweed → water snail → stickleback → heron (or algae → water snail → frog → heron).
ms: Correct producer at start and organisms in a valid order from Figure 4 (1).
Four organisms ending with heron, arrows pointing towards the consumer (1). E.g. algae/pondweed → water snail → frog/stickleback → heron, or algae/pondweed → mayfly larvae → stickleback → heron.
questions.tip: Arrows point in the direction energy flows: from the thing eaten to the eater.

questions.q:
Figure 4 describes a food web in a UK freshwater pond.
Algae and pondweed are eaten by water snails and mayfly larvae.
Water snails are eaten by frogs and sticklebacks.
Mayfly larvae are eaten by sticklebacks and water beetles.
Sticklebacks are eaten by herons and pike.
Frogs are eaten by herons.
Water beetles are eaten by frogs.

Using Figure 4, explain how a fall in the amount of pondweed could affect other organisms in the pond.
questions.answer: Less pondweed means less food for water snails and mayfly larvae, so their numbers fall. Frogs and sticklebacks then have less food, so they decline. Herons and pike would be affected in turn. Less pondweed also means less oxygen released into the water and less shelter for small animals.
ms: Primary consumers (snails, mayfly larvae) have less food so decrease (1).
Knock-on effect on secondary consumers, e.g. frogs/sticklebacks/water beetles decline (1).
Further effect on top predators (herons/pike) (1).
Other link, e.g. less oxygen from photosynthesis/less habitat or shelter/nutrient change (1).
questions.tip: Name the organisms from the figure. Generic 'animals will die' answers stay at 1-2 marks.

questions.q: Explain the role of decomposers in a woodland ecosystem.
questions.answer: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead leaves, wood and animals in the litter layer. This releases nutrients back into the soil, where they are taken up again by plant roots. Without decomposers nutrients would stay locked in dead material and plants would not grow.
ms: Named decomposer, e.g. fungi/bacteria (1). Allow earthworms as detritivores.
Break down dead organic matter/leaf litter (1).
Release nutrients into the soil to be taken up by plants/recycling nutrients (1).
questions.tip: Use the term 'nutrient cycling' to show you see the bigger picture.

questions.q: Describe the climate and vegetation of the temperate deciduous forest biome.
questions.answer: Climate: mild with four seasons; summers warm (about 15-20°C), winters cool (above or just below 0°C); rainfall of about 500-1,500 mm spread through the year. Vegetation: broadleaved trees such as oak, beech and ash that lose their leaves in autumn to save water and energy in winter; layers of canopy, shrubs (hazel, holly) and ground flora (bluebells) that flower in spring before the canopy closes.
ms: Climate: distinct seasons/mild (1); rainfall throughout the year (1).
Vegetation: deciduous broadleaved trees e.g. oak, beech (1); lose leaves in autumn/layered structure/spring flowers before canopy shade (1).
questions.tip: Split your answer between climate and vegetation, as the question asks for both.

questions.q: Using a named example of a small-scale UK ecosystem, explain how human activity has affected it.
questions.answer: Example, a UK pond or woodland. Fertiliser runoff from nearby farmland adds nitrates to a pond; algae grow rapidly (an algal bloom), block light so pondweed dies, and bacteria decomposing the dead material use up oxygen, so fish die (eutrophication). In woodland, clearing hedgerows or trees removes habitats and food sources; trampling by visitors compacts soil and damages ground flora; but management such as coppicing and conservation can increase biodiversity by letting light reach the floor.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Named small-scale UK ecosystem (pond, hedgerow, woodland, e.g. Epping Forest). Negative impacts: fertiliser runoff and eutrophication, pollution, draining, clearing land for farming or building, trampling, invasive species, overfishing. Positive impacts: coppicing, pollarding, conservation management, replanting, protected status. Chains of reasoning showing how a change to one component affects others (interdependence). Level 3 requires named example, specific detail and linked explanations.
questions.tip: Name your ecosystem and give specific species. The chain of effects is what gets you to Level 3.

questions.q: Describe the global distribution of the tundra and boreal (coniferous) forest biomes.
questions.answer: Tundra is found in the far north, mainly above about 65°N, along the northern coasts of Canada, Alaska, Greenland, Scandinavia and Russia. Boreal forest lies to the south of the tundra, in a broad band roughly between 50° and 65°N across Canada, Scandinavia and Russia (Siberia). Both are almost entirely in the Northern Hemisphere because there is little land at those latitudes in the south.
ms: Tundra: high latitudes/above about 65°N/Arctic (1); named area, e.g. northern Canada, Alaska, Siberia, Greenland coasts (1).
Boreal: band south of tundra/about 50-65°N (1); named area, e.g. Canada, Scandinavia, Russia (1). Allow mostly in Northern Hemisphere.
questions.tip: Distribution answers need latitude AND named places or continents.

questions.q:
Figure 5 shows climate data for a location.
Month | J | F | M | A | M | J | J | A | S | O | N | D
Temp (°C) | 4 | 5 | 7 | 9 | 12 | 15 | 17 | 17 | 14 | 11 | 7 | 5
Rainfall (mm) | 80 | 60 | 55 | 50 | 50 | 50 | 55 | 60 | 60 | 75 | 80 | 85

Using Figure 5, calculate the annual temperature range and the total annual rainfall. Suggest which biome this location is in.
questions.answer: Temperature range = 17 − 4 = 13°C. Total rainfall = 760 mm. Biome: temperate deciduous forest (e.g. the UK).
ms: Range 13°C (1).
Total 760 mm (1).
Temperate deciduous forest (1). Allow temperate/UK-type woodland.
questions.tip: Range is one number with units. Don't write '4 to 17'.

questions.q: Give two ways that humans manage small-scale ecosystems such as woodlands.
questions.answer: Coppicing (cutting trees to the base so they regrow) and planting new trees. Others: pollarding, creating nature reserves, controlling access with footpaths.
ms: One mark per valid method, e.g. coppicing (1); pollarding (1); replanting (1); managing access/footpaths (1); designating protected areas/nature reserves (1); removing invasive species (1).
questions.tip: Use the proper terms like coppicing; they show subject knowledge.

questions.q: Suggest why nutrient cycling in a tropical rainforest is faster than in a UK deciduous woodland.
questions.answer: Rainforests are hot (about 27°C) and wet all year, so decomposers like fungi and bacteria break down leaf litter very quickly, often within weeks. There is no winter, so leaves fall and are recycled all year. In the UK, cooler temperatures and a cold winter slow decomposition, so litter builds up and nutrients are released slowly into the soil.
ms: Rainforest is hot and wet/humid all year (1), so decomposition is rapid (1).
Leaf fall continuous, no season (1).
UK cooler/winter slows decomposers, so litter and soil stores build up (1).
questions.tip: Comparison questions need both places. Use words like 'whereas'.

questions.q: Assess the importance of interdependence in maintaining a healthy small-scale ecosystem.
questions.answer: Interdependence is central: producers such as pondweed provide food and oxygen for consumers; consumers control each other's numbers through predator-prey links; decomposers recycle nutrients from dead material back to the soil or water so producers can keep growing. Abiotic factors also matter: light, water quality and temperature control how well producers grow. If one link is broken, e.g. fertiliser runoff causing eutrophication, algae block light, plants die, oxygen falls and fish die. So the health of the ecosystem depends on the balance of all components. However, ecosystems can recover from small changes, as food webs offer alternative food sources.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Producers, consumers, decomposers and abiotic factors; nutrient cycling; food webs; predator-prey balance; examples of disruption (eutrophication, removal of a species, invasive species, hedgerow removal); resilience from complex food webs. Level 3 needs a judgement on importance supported by examples from a named small-scale UK ecosystem.
questions.tip: 'Assess the importance' needs a conclusion about how important. Include a counterpoint such as resilience.

questions.q: Compare the nutrient cycles of a tropical rainforest and a temperate deciduous forest.
questions.answer: In the rainforest the biomass is the largest store because plants grow rapidly and take up nutrients quickly, whereas in the temperate deciduous forest the soil store is much larger than in the rainforest (similar in size to the biomass store) because decomposition is slower and humus builds up. The litter store is small in the rainforest because fast decomposition in hot, wet conditions recycles it quickly, while in temperate forest litter builds up in autumn. Transfers are faster in the rainforest; rainforests also lose more nutrients through leaching from heavy rain.
ms: Rainforest: biomass largest store (1).
Temperate deciduous: soil store much larger than in the rainforest/soil and biomass both large (1).
Litter: small in rainforest due to fast decomposition, larger in temperate forest especially after autumn leaf fall (1).
Rate of transfer/leaching comparison (1). Comparison words needed for full marks.
questions.tip: Learn the shape of each Gersmehl diagram: which circle is biggest.

questions.q: Explain why the biome found at a location depends on its latitude.
questions.answer: Latitude controls temperature: near the equator the sun's rays are concentrated so it is hot, whereas near the poles they are spread over a larger area and it is cold. Latitude also controls rainfall through atmospheric circulation: rising air at the equator gives heavy rain (rainforest), sinking air at about 30° gives dry conditions (hot desert), and rising air near 60° gives moderate rain (temperate forests). Temperature and rainfall decide which plants can grow, so they decide the biome.
ms: Latitude affects temperature/angle and intensity of sunlight (1).
Atmospheric circulation: low pressure and rain at equator (1).
High pressure and dry at about 30° (1).
Temperature and rainfall determine vegetation and therefore biome (1).
questions.tip: Use the global circulation model here. It links Section A and Section B.

questions.q: Give two reasons why hedgerows are important in UK farmland ecosystems.
questions.answer: They provide habitat and food for birds, insects and small mammals. They act as corridors so wildlife can move between woodlands. Also: windbreaks reducing soil erosion.
ms: One mark per reason, e.g. habitat/food for wildlife (1); wildlife corridors (1); reduce soil erosion as windbreaks (1); shelter for livestock (1).
questions.tip: Hedgerows are a classic small-scale UK ecosystem. Know why removing them matters.

questions.q: What is meant by the term 'biome'?
questions.answer: A large-scale global ecosystem with a distinctive climate, vegetation and animals, e.g. tropical rainforest.
ms: Large-scale/global ecosystem (1). Allow 'a large area with a similar climate and vegetation'.
questions.tip: Biome = global scale. A pond is an ecosystem, not a biome.

questions.q: Describe the characteristics of the hot desert biome's vegetation.
questions.answer: Sparse vegetation with lots of bare ground; drought-resistant plants such as cacti and thorny shrubs with small or waxy leaves, spines and long roots.
ms: Sparse/scattered vegetation, much bare ground (1).
Drought-tolerant plants, e.g. cacti, thorny shrubs, with an adaptation named (1).
questions.tip: Describe what you would see. Explanation isn't needed.

questions.q:
Figure 16 shows light intensity and the number of plant species at five points along a transect from an open meadow into a UK woodland.
Point | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
Light (% of open meadow) | 90 | 60 | 35 | 20 | 10
Number of ground plant species | 14 | 11 | 8 | 5 | 3

Describe the relationship shown and suggest why it exists.
questions.answer: There is a positive relationship: as light falls from 90% to 10%, the number of ground plant species falls from 14 to 3. Deeper in the wood the tree canopy blocks more light, so fewer plants have enough light for photosynthesis. Only shade-tolerant plants such as ferns, ivy or mosses survive, and some like bluebells flower in spring before the leaves come out.
ms: Positive relationship/as light decreases, species decrease (1).
Data used, e.g. 90% and 14 species to 10% and 3 species (1).
Canopy intercepts light deeper in the woodland (1).
Less light for photosynthesis so only shade-tolerant species survive, or spring flowering example (1).
questions.tip: Describe first, then explain. Two different skills, two marks each.

questions.q: Why do many rainforest trees have thin, smooth bark?
options: To attract animals that spread seeds
To store water in dry seasons
Because there is no cold season to protect against, and smooth bark helps water run off and stops other plants climbing
ms: No cold season means no need for thick insulating bark; smooth bark lets heavy rain run off and makes it harder for epiphytes and lianas to attach.
questions.tip: Always link an adaptation to a specific condition of the climate.

questions.q: Which of these is a reason why deforestation can make local rainfall decrease?
options: Cleared land has a lower albedo, so absorbs more heat
Less transpiration from trees means less water vapour returned to the atmosphere
Soils hold more water once trees are cut down
ms: Rainforest trees transpire huge amounts of water, which forms clouds and rain locally. Removing them breaks this part of the water cycle, so the climate can become drier.
questions.tip: Deforestation affects the water cycle as well as the carbon cycle.

questions.q: What is a debt-for-nature swap?
options: Farmers swap land in the forest for land in cities
A country buys rainforest land from another country
Part of a country's foreign debt is cancelled in return for protecting its forest
Logging companies pay a fee for each tree cut
ms: In a debt-for-nature swap, a lender (government or conservation group) cancels or reduces debt in exchange for the country spending money on conservation.
questions.tip: Know at least four sustainable management strategies by name.

questions.q:
Figure 6 shows annual deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon (km² per year, rounded to the nearest 100).
Year | 2004 | 2008 | 2012 | 2016 | 2020
Area | 27,800 | 12,900 | 4,600 | 7,900 | 10,900

Using Figure 6, calculate the percentage decrease in annual deforestation between 2004 and 2012. Give your answer to one decimal place.
questions.tip: Divide by the 2004 (original) figure. Dividing by 4,600 is the most common error.

questions.q:
Figure 6 shows annual deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon (km² per year, rounded to the nearest 100).
Year | 2004 | 2008 | 2012 | 2016 | 2020
Area | 27,800 | 12,900 | 4,600 | 7,900 | 10,900

Describe the trend in annual deforestation shown in Figure 6. Use data in your answer.
questions.answer: Deforestation fell sharply from 27,800 km² in 2004 to a low of 4,600 km² in 2012. After that it rose again, reaching 10,900 km² in 2020, more than double the 2012 figure, but still well below 2004.
ms: Overall fall from 2004 to 2012 (1).
Rise again from 2012 to 2020 (1).
Data used with units, e.g. 27,800 km² to 4,600 km² or 10,900 km² in 2020 (1).
questions.tip: Describe the pattern and quote data with units at the turning points.

questions.q:
Figure 6 shows annual deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon (km² per year, rounded to the nearest 100).
Year | 2004 | 2008 | 2012 | 2016 | 2020
Area | 27,800 | 12,900 | 4,600 | 7,900 | 10,900

Suggest reasons for the changes in deforestation shown in Figure 6.
questions.answer: The fall from 2004 to 2012 could be due to stronger government protection: more protected areas, satellite monitoring and fines for illegal clearing, and pressure from international buyers. The rise after 2012 could be due to weaker enforcement and changes in government policy, rising demand for beef and soya, and more road building opening up new areas.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear, developed points showing understanding, linked accurately to the question focus (and to the figure where one is given).
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple, undeveloped points. Limited link to the question focus.

Indicative content: Fall: more protected reserves and indigenous lands, satellite monitoring, enforcement and fines, international pressure and consumer boycotts, soya moratorium. Rise: weaker enforcement or policy change, cuts to environmental agencies, rising global demand for beef and soya, mining, road building, economic pressures. Both parts of the trend should be addressed for Level 2.
questions.tip: 'Suggest' means plausible reasons; you are not expected to know the exact cause. Cover both the fall and the rise.

questions.q: Explain how animals have adapted to life in the tropical rainforest.
questions.answer: Spider monkeys have long limbs and strong grasping tails to move through the canopy and reach fruit. Sloths move slowly and sleep for long periods to save energy from their low-nutrient leaf diet; algae on their fur give camouflage. Many animals, such as tree frogs and toucans, are brightly coloured to warn predators or attract mates. Some species are nocturnal to avoid the heat and predators.
ms: 1 mark for each adaptation with a further mark for explaining how it helps survival (2 x 2). E.g. spider monkey long tail (1) to grip branches in the canopy (1); sloth slow movement (1) saves energy from low-nutrient diet (1); camouflage (1) avoids predators (1); flying/gliding (1) moves between trees (1).
questions.tip: Name the animal and the condition. 'Animals have camouflage' alone is 1 mark at most.

questions.q: Using a named example, explain how the impacts of deforestation affect local people and the wider world.
questions.answer: Malaysia: local people benefit from jobs in logging and palm oil plantations, and Malaysia earns export income (it is one of the world's largest palm oil producers). Roads improve access. But indigenous people such as the Penan in Sarawak lose their land and way of life, and the Bakun Dam displaced thousands. Soil erosion and river silting harm fishing. Globally, burning and clearing forest releases CO₂, adding to climate change, and loss of biodiversity reduces sources of new medicines and food.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Named example (Malaysia or Amazon). Local economic: jobs, income, roads, HEP power (Bakun Dam). Local social/environmental: loss of indigenous land and culture, displacement, soil erosion, flooding, river silting, loss of resources. Global: CO₂ emissions and climate change, biodiversity loss, loss of potential medicines, disruption to the water cycle. Level 3 needs both scales with specific detail.
questions.tip: Use two scales: local and global. Questions that name two scales want both covered.

questions.q: State two reasons why the soils of the tropical rainforest are not fertile.
questions.answer: Heavy rainfall leaches nutrients out of the soil. Plants take up nutrients so quickly that few remain in the soil.
ms: Leaching by heavy rainfall (1).
Nutrients rapidly taken up by plants/stored in biomass (1). Allow: thin topsoil/humus layer.
questions.tip: Use the word 'leaching'.

questions.q: 'Sustainable management of tropical rainforests can only succeed with international help.' Using examples, to what extent do you agree with this statement? (9 marks + 3 SPaG)
questions.answer: International help matters: debt-for-nature swaps relieve debt in exchange for protection; international agreements and funding (such as REDD+ payments for keeping forests standing); consumers buying FSC-certified timber and certified palm oil put pressure on companies. But national and local action is just as important: governments create protected areas and national parks, enforce laws against illegal logging, and use satellite monitoring; local communities run ecotourism and practise agroforestry and selective logging. Judgement: international help provides money and markets, but without national laws and local benefits it fails, so success needs both.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): Thorough knowledge and understanding. Detailed, well-balanced evaluation of both sides. Detailed, accurate, place-specific evidence. Clear, substantiated judgement that answers the question.

Level 2 (4-6 marks): Reasonable knowledge and understanding. Partly balanced evaluation, may favour one side. Some place-specific evidence, but general or patchy. A judgement is given but only partly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Limited knowledge. Simple, unbalanced points with little evaluation. Little or no relevant evidence. No clear judgement.

SPaG (3 marks): High performance 3 = accurate spelling and punctuation, grammar controls meaning, wide range of specialist terms used precisely. Intermediate 2 = considerable accuracy, good range of specialist terms. Threshold 1 = reasonable accuracy, limited range of specialist terms.

Indicative content: International: debt-for-nature swaps, international conventions and agreements, aid funding conservation, global consumer demand for certified products (FSC), boycotts. National: protected areas, laws against illegal logging, monitoring and enforcement, replanting targets. Local: ecotourism, agroforestry, selective logging, indigenous land rights. Use of named examples (Malaysia, Amazon). Evaluation of strengths and limits of each. Level 3 needs a clear, supported judgement.
questions.tip: Pick a side and defend it. Use 'to a large extent' or 'only partly' in your conclusion.

questions.q: Explain how the climate of the tropical rainforest leads to high rates of plant growth.
questions.answer: High temperatures (about 27°C all year) and heavy rainfall (over 2,000 mm) give ideal conditions for photosynthesis. There are no seasons, so plants can grow all year round. Strong sunlight near the equator provides plenty of energy.
ms: Hot all year/about 27°C (1).
Wet all year/over 2,000 mm rain (1).
No seasons so continuous growing season/high sunlight for photosynthesis (1).
questions.tip: Link climate to growth through photosynthesis.

questions.q: Give one example of a product from tropical rainforests that people in the UK use.
questions.answer: Palm oil (or timber, rubber, cocoa, coffee, Brazil nuts, medicines).
ms: Any valid product, e.g. palm oil, hardwood timber (mahogany), rubber, cocoa, coffee, bananas, nuts, medicines (1).
questions.tip: One-mark questions need one clear answer. Don't list five.

questions.q: Explain how ecotourism can help to protect tropical rainforests.
questions.answer: Ecotourism brings in income from visitors who come to see the forest and its wildlife, so the standing forest has more economic value than if it were cleared. Local people are employed as guides, cooks and in lodges, so they have an alternative to logging or farming. Small group sizes and limited infrastructure reduce damage. Some of the money can fund conservation and protected areas.
ms: Gives value to standing forest/income from forest without cutting it (1).
Local jobs as guides etc. (1), so less need for logging/farming (1).
Low-impact, small-scale/money funds conservation (1).
questions.tip: The key idea is an incentive: why does ecotourism make people want to keep the forest?

questions.q: Why does the Thar Desert have high rates of evaporation from the Indira Gandhi Canal?
options: Very high temperatures and clear skies mean intense heating of open water
Heavy monsoon rain fills the canal
ms: Daytime temperatures often above 40°C with clear skies make open canals lose large amounts of water to evaporation, which also contributes to salinisation of irrigated soils.
questions.tip: Evaporation links to salinisation: water evaporates, leaving salts behind.

questions.q: In the Thar Desert, irrigation can lead to salinisation. What is salinisation?
options: The use of salt water from the sea for irrigation
The build-up of salt in soils as water evaporates and draws salts to the surface
ms: When irrigation water evaporates in hot conditions, dissolved salts are left behind and build up in the soil, eventually making it too salty for crops.
questions.tip: Salinisation is caused by evaporation, not by the sea.

questions.q:
Figure 7 shows climate data for Jaisalmer, a town in the Thar Desert (illustrative values).
Month | J | F | M | A | M | J | J | A | S | O | N | D
Max temp (°C) | 23 | 26 | 30 | 35 | 39 | 40 | 38 | 37 | 36 | 32 | 27 | 24
Min temp (°C) | 8 | 11 | 16 | 21 | 25 | 27 | 27 | 26 | 24 | 19 | 13 | 9
Rainfall (mm) | 2 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 5 | 15 | 40 | 38 | 12 | 2 | 1 | 1

Using Figure 7, calculate the total annual rainfall. Is this location a hot desert? Give a reason.
questions.answer: Total = 122 mm. Yes, it is a hot desert because it receives less than 250 mm of rain per year.
ms: Total 122 mm (1).
Yes, because below 250 mm per year (1).
questions.tip: Add the bars carefully. One misread value loses the first mark.

questions.q:
Figure 7 shows climate data for Jaisalmer, a town in the Thar Desert (illustrative values).
Month | J | F | M | A | M | J | J | A | S | O | N | D
Max temp (°C) | 23 | 26 | 30 | 35 | 39 | 40 | 38 | 37 | 36 | 32 | 27 | 24
Min temp (°C) | 8 | 11 | 16 | 21 | 25 | 27 | 27 | 26 | 24 | 19 | 13 | 9
Rainfall (mm) | 2 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 5 | 15 | 40 | 38 | 12 | 2 | 1 | 1

Using Figure 7, calculate the difference between the maximum and minimum temperature in January and in July. Suggest why the January difference is larger.
questions.answer: January: 23 − 8 = 15°C. July: 38 − 27 = 11°C. In July there is more cloud and humidity from the monsoon rain, which traps heat at night, whereas clear skies in January let heat escape quickly at night.
ms: Both calculations correct: 15°C and 11°C (1).
Reason: clearer skies in January/more cloud and humidity in July during the monsoon reducing night-time heat loss (1).
questions.tip: Spot clues in the data: July is the wettest month, so think about cloud cover.

questions.q:
Figure 7 shows climate data for Jaisalmer, a town in the Thar Desert (illustrative values).
Month | J | F | M | A | M | J | J | A | S | O | N | D
Max temp (°C) | 23 | 26 | 30 | 35 | 39 | 40 | 38 | 37 | 36 | 32 | 27 | 24
Min temp (°C) | 8 | 11 | 16 | 21 | 25 | 27 | 27 | 26 | 24 | 19 | 13 | 9
Rainfall (mm) | 2 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 5 | 15 | 40 | 38 | 12 | 2 | 1 | 1

Using Figure 7, describe the pattern of rainfall and suggest one challenge it creates for farmers.
questions.answer: Almost all rain falls in June to September, with peaks in July (40 mm) and August (38 mm); the rest of the year is almost dry, with 1-5 mm a month. Total is only 122 mm. The challenge is that there is no reliable water for most of the year, so crops can only be grown in the short wet season unless irrigation is used, and the rain may fail in some years.
ms: Pattern: rain concentrated in June to September/summer monsoon (1).
Data: July 40 mm and August 38 mm/most months under 5 mm (1).
Challenge identified, e.g. water shortage for most of the year/short growing season/unreliable rainfall (1).
Developed: so need irrigation or crops fail, or livestock lack fodder (1).
questions.tip: Two-part question: make sure you answer both parts and use data in the first.

questions.q:
Figure 7 shows climate data for Jaisalmer, a town in the Thar Desert (illustrative values).
Month | J | F | M | A | M | J | J | A | S | O | N | D
Max temp (°C) | 23 | 26 | 30 | 35 | 39 | 40 | 38 | 37 | 36 | 32 | 27 | 24
Min temp (°C) | 8 | 11 | 16 | 21 | 25 | 27 | 27 | 26 | 24 | 19 | 13 | 9
Rainfall (mm) | 2 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 5 | 15 | 40 | 38 | 12 | 2 | 1 | 1

Using Figure 7, what percentage of the annual rainfall falls in July and August combined? Give your answer to one decimal place.
questions.tip: Total the whole year first, then work out the share.

questions.q: Explain the interdependence between climate, soil, plants and animals in a hot desert.
questions.answer: Low rainfall and high temperatures mean few plants can grow. Few plants means little leaf litter, so soils are thin, sandy and low in organic matter. Thin, dry soils hold little water, which limits plants further. Animals depend on plants for food, water and shade, so animal numbers are low and many are nocturnal. If plants are removed, soils are eroded by wind, making it even harder for plants to re-establish.
ms: Climate limits plant growth (1).
Few plants means little organic matter, so thin, infertile soils (1).
Animals depend on plants for food, moisture and shelter (1).
Chain of change, e.g. removing plants leads to soil erosion and less vegetation (1).
questions.tip: Interdependence = links in both directions. Use 'so' and 'which means'.

questions.q: Using a named example, explain how the challenges of developing a hot desert area are being managed.
questions.answer: Thar Desert: water shortage is the main challenge. The Indira Gandhi Canal brings water from Punjab rivers for irrigation, allowing wheat and cotton to be grown, though evaporation and salinisation are problems. Extreme temperatures limit outdoor work, so activities like tourism are concentrated in the cooler months. Poor accessibility is being improved with new roads, which allow minerals like gypsum and limestone and oil from Barmer to be transported. Wind farms such as Jaisalmer Wind Park and solar power use the climate as an opportunity.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Thar challenges: extreme heat, water supply (scarce, high evaporation, canal leakage), salinisation, poor accessibility (shifting sand, few roads), remote population. Management: Indira Gandhi Canal irrigation, drip irrigation, new roads and rail, mining and oil (Barmer) infrastructure, renewable energy (Jaisalmer Wind Park, solar), tourism in the cooler season, camel safaris. Level 3 needs challenges clearly linked to the strategies used and the limits of those strategies.
questions.tip: Match each challenge with how it is managed, then say how well it works.

questions.q: Suggest how increasing population can lead to desertification in semi-arid areas such as the Sahel.
questions.answer: More people need more food, so more land is farmed and fields are not left fallow, which exhausts the soil. More livestock leads to overgrazing, removing the vegetation that holds soil together. More fuelwood is collected for cooking, removing trees and shrubs. With less vegetation, wind and rain erode the soil, and the land becomes desert-like.
ms: 1 mark per valid point, up to 4, or 2 for a developed point. E.g. more food needed so over-cultivation (1) leading to exhausted soil (1); more animals so overgrazing (1) removes vegetation (1); more fuelwood removal (1); bare soil eroded by wind/rain (1).
questions.tip: Link each human activity to loss of vegetation and then to soil erosion.

questions.q: 'The opportunities for development in hot deserts are greater than the challenges.' Using a named example, to what extent do you agree with this statement?
questions.answer: Thar: opportunities include minerals (gypsum, feldspar, kaolin, limestone, phosphorite), oil from Barmer, energy (Jaisalmer Wind Park, high solar potential), tourism around Jaisalmer (camel safaris, festivals), and irrigated farming via the Indira Gandhi Canal. Challenges: extreme temperatures, scarce and unreliable water, high evaporation and salinisation, poor accessibility over sand and shifting dunes. Judgement: technology like irrigation and renewable energy has turned many challenges into opportunities, but water remains the limiting factor, so opportunities only outweigh challenges where water can be supplied sustainably.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Opportunities: mineral extraction, oil, energy (wind and solar), tourism, irrigated farming. Challenges: extreme heat, water supply, salinisation, accessibility, transport costs, poverty. Evaluation: who benefits (companies vs locals), sustainability of canal use, costs of technology, links between opportunities and challenges. Level 3 requires accurate Thar detail and a supported judgement.
questions.tip: No SPaG here, but the judgement still matters most. Say who the opportunities benefit.

questions.q: Describe two ways that people can use appropriate technology to reduce desertification.
questions.answer: Building stone lines (magic stones) along contours to slow rainwater runoff so it soaks into the soil. Digging zai pits filled with compost to collect water around crops.
ms: One mark per method with a brief description, e.g. stone lines/magic stones slow runoff and trap soil (1); zai pits collect water and compost (1); solar cookers reduce fuelwood use (1); tree planting/shelter belts reduce wind erosion (1); drip irrigation saves water (1).
questions.tip: Appropriate technology is cheap, simple and uses local materials. Describe what it does.

questions.q: Explain why the Thar Desert is attractive for renewable energy development.
questions.answer: It has very high levels of sunshine and clear skies for most of the year, which is ideal for solar power. There are strong winds in parts of the desert, used by wind farms such as Jaisalmer Wind Park. Large areas of land are cheap and thinly populated, so large solar and wind farms can be built with few conflicts.
ms: High sunshine/clear skies for solar (1).
Strong winds for wind farms, e.g. Jaisalmer Wind Park (1).
Large areas of cheap, sparsely populated land (1).
questions.tip: Link each physical feature of the desert to the type of energy it supports.

questions.q: State one way the fennec fox is adapted to life in hot deserts.
questions.answer: Large ears radiate heat to keep it cool (also: nocturnal, thick fur on its feet protects against hot sand).
ms: Any valid adaptation: large ears lose heat (1); nocturnal (1); furry soles protect feet from hot sand (1); light-coloured fur for camouflage/reflecting heat (1); gets water from food (1).
questions.tip: One clear adaptation, ideally with what it does.

questions.q: Which type of weathering happens when rainwater, which is slightly acidic, reacts with rocks such as chalk and limestone on a cliff face?
ms: Carbonation is chemical weathering: carbonic acid in rain reacts with calcium carbonate in chalk and limestone, dissolving it. Abrasion is erosion, not weathering.
questions.tip: Weathering breaks rock in place. Erosion is removal by the sea.

questions.q: What is a slump on a coastal cliff?
options: Rock falling freely from a steep cliff
Sand blown inland by the wind
Saturated soft rock moving downwards along a curved surface
ms: Slumping happens in soft rocks like the boulder clay of Holderness: rain saturates the clay, it becomes heavy, and it slides down along a curved slip plane.
questions.tip: Slumping = soft, saturated rock and a curved surface. Rockfall = hard rock and steep cliff.

questions.q: On the Holderness coast the dominant waves approach from the north-east, across the longest fetch of the North Sea. In which direction does longshore drift mainly move sediment?
ms: Dominant waves from the north-east move sediment south along the coast, which is why Spurn Head grows at the southern end and why the Mappleton groynes starved Cowden to the south.
questions.tip: Longshore drift moves sediment in the direction the dominant waves are travelling towards. On Holderness that is north to south.

questions.q: Which statement best explains how a bar differs from a spit?
options: A bar extends across a bay to join two headlands, trapping a lagoon behind it
A spit forms only in estuaries
A bar is formed by erosion
A bar is made of rock, a spit of sand
ms: Both form by longshore drift and deposition, but a bar grows right across a bay, sealing it off and creating a lagoon (e.g. Slapton Sands).
questions.tip: A bar is a spit that has 'finished the job' of crossing the bay.

questions.q:
Figure 8 describes part of a 1:25,000 OS map of a coastline.
The coast runs north to south along easting 40.
Grid square 4012 contains a headland of chalk with cliffs, with a stack marked at 405123.
Grid square 4011 contains a sandy beach with five groynes.
Grid square 4010 contains a village with a caravan park, a car park (P) at 402104 and a sea wall along the beach.

In which grid square is the stack?
ms: The six-figure reference 405123 starts 40 (easting) and 12 (northing), so it is in square 4012. 1240 has the northing and easting reversed.
questions.tip: Along the corridor, then up the stairs: easting first.

questions.q:
Figure 8 describes part of a 1:25,000 OS map of a coastline.
The coast runs north to south along easting 40.
Grid square 4012 contains a headland of chalk with cliffs, with a stack marked at 405123.
Grid square 4011 contains a sandy beach with five groynes.
Grid square 4010 contains a village with a caravan park, a car park (P) at 402104 and a sea wall along the beach.

Using Figure 8, give two pieces of map evidence that the coast in grid square 4010 is used for tourism.
questions.answer: A caravan park and a car park at 402104.
ms: One mark per piece of map evidence, e.g. caravan park (1); car park at 402104 (1); allow beach/sea wall promenade if linked to tourist use (1).
questions.tip: Map evidence means features you can see on the map, ideally with a grid reference.

questions.q:
Figure 8 describes part of a 1:25,000 OS map of a coastline.
The coast runs north to south along easting 40.
Grid square 4012 contains a headland of chalk with cliffs, with a stack marked at 405123.
Grid square 4011 contains a sandy beach with five groynes.
Grid square 4010 contains a village with a caravan park, a car park (P) at 402104 and a sea wall along the beach.

Using Figure 8, suggest why the coast in grid squares 4011 and 4010 has been protected with hard engineering.
questions.answer: Grid square 4010 contains a village and caravan park with valuable property, homes and tourism businesses, so the cost of protection is justified. The groynes in 4011 trap sediment from longshore drift to build a wide beach, which absorbs wave energy and is attractive to tourists. The sea wall protects the village directly from erosion and flooding.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear, developed points showing understanding, linked accurately to the question focus (and to the figure where one is given).
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple, undeveloped points. Limited link to the question focus.

Indicative content: Map evidence: village, caravan park, car park in 4010; groynes in 4011; sea wall. Reasons: high land value, homes, tourism income, infrastructure; groynes trap sediment and widen beach; sea wall reflects wave energy; cost-benefit justified. Level 2 needs map evidence linked to reasons.
questions.tip: Quote grid squares and features. Answers with no map evidence are capped at Level 1.

questions.q: Explain how longshore drift transports sediment along a coastline.
questions.answer: Waves approach the beach at an angle, driven by the prevailing wind. The swash carries sediment up the beach at the same angle. The backwash then pulls the sediment straight back down the beach at right angles to the coast, because of gravity. This is repeated, so sediment moves along the beach in a zig-zag pattern in the direction of the prevailing wind.
ms: Waves approach at an angle/direction of prevailing wind (1).
Swash carries sediment up the beach at an angle (1).
Backwash carries it straight down the beach due to gravity (1).
Repeated zig-zag movement along the coast (1).
questions.tip: Use the terms 'swash', 'backwash' and 'prevailing wind'. A labelled diagram description can help.

questions.q: Explain how a headland and bay are formed on a discordant coastline.
questions.answer: On a discordant coastline bands of hard and soft rock run at right angles to the coast. Waves erode the softer rock (such as clay) more quickly by hydraulic power and abrasion, forming bays. The harder rock (such as chalk or limestone) is more resistant, so it is left sticking out as headlands. Once bays form, waves refract around headlands, concentrating erosion on them, while bays become sheltered and beaches build up.
ms: Alternating bands of hard and soft rock at right angles to the coast (1).
Soft rock eroded faster forming bays (1), named erosion process as development (1).
Hard rock more resistant, left as headlands (1).
Allow: example such as Swanage (Swanage Bay in clays and sands, Handfast Point in chalk).
questions.tip: Discordant = rock bands at right angles to the coast. Concordant = parallel.

questions.q: Using a named example, explain how the landforms of coastal deposition have been formed.
questions.answer: Spurn Head (Holderness): longshore drift moves sediment eroded from the boulder clay cliffs south along the coast. At the Humber Estuary the coastline changes direction, so the sediment is deposited in the more sheltered water, building a long ridge of sand and shingle into the estuary. Changing wind directions curve the end into a hook. Behind it, in calmer water, mud is deposited to form salt marsh. Beaches form in sheltered bays where constructive waves deposit sand.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Named example such as Spurn Head (Holderness), Hurst Castle Spit, Studland, Slapton Sands bar. Processes: longshore drift, deposition where energy falls (change in coastline direction, sheltered water, estuary), constructive waves, recurved end from changing wind direction, salt marsh behind spit, sand dunes formed by wind and stabilised by marram grass. Level 3 needs accurate sequence of processes with named location detail.
questions.tip: Name your example and explain WHY deposition happens there: loss of energy is the key idea.

questions.q: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of rock armour as a method of coastal defence.
questions.answer: Advantages: large boulders absorb wave energy and reduce erosion of the cliff behind; it is relatively cheap compared with a sea wall and lasts a long time; it can be used for fishing. Disadvantages: rocks are often brought from elsewhere so don't match local geology; it can look unattractive; it can be dangerous to climb on; it may need topping up if storms move rocks.
ms: Advantages (max 2): absorbs/breaks up wave energy (1); cheaper than a sea wall/easy to construct (1); long lasting (1).
Disadvantages (max 2): unattractive/does not fit local geology (1); dangerous to climb (1); can be moved by big storms (1); may increase erosion further along the coast (1).
questions.tip: Balance both sides. Two marks each way.

questions.q: Assess the impact of coastal management at Mappleton on the Holderness coast.
questions.answer: In 1991 about £2 million was spent on two rock groynes and rock armour at Mappleton. This protected the village and the B1242 coast road, and trapped sediment to build a beach that protects the cliffs. However, the groynes stopped sediment moving south, so erosion increased down-drift; at Cowden, south of Mappleton, the cliffs eroded faster and properties were lost. Judgement: successful for Mappleton but it moved the problem down the coast, so overall impact is mixed.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Scheme details: 1991, around £2 million, two rock groynes, rock armour at the base of the cliff, cliff face regraded. Positive: village and B1242 protected, wider beach. Negative: sediment starved down-drift, faster erosion south of the scheme, for example at Cowden; cost; arguably not sustainable. Level 3 requires a judgement on overall impact weighing local and wider effects.
questions.tip: 'Assess' needs a verdict. Who won and who lost from the scheme?

questions.q: Give two reasons why waves on the Holderness coast are powerful.
questions.answer: There is a long fetch across the North Sea from the north-east. Strong winds create destructive waves.
ms: Long fetch from the north-east across the North Sea (1).
Strong winds/frequent storms producing destructive waves (1). Allow: narrow beaches give little protection.
questions.tip: Fetch is a key term. Use it.

questions.q: 'Coastal management strategies on the Holderness coast have created more problems than they have solved.' To what extent do you agree with this statement? (9 marks + 3 SPaG)
questions.answer: Holderness erodes at an average of about 1.8 m a year, one of the fastest rates in Europe. Defences at places like Mappleton (1991, about £2 million for two rock groynes and rock armour), Hornsea and Withernsea have protected towns, roads and businesses, so they have solved local problems. But groynes trap sediment moving south by longshore drift, starving beaches down-drift, so cliffs at places like Cowden erode faster. Less sediment reaches Spurn Head and the Humber, possibly affecting the spit. Much of the coast is left undefended because it is not cost-effective, so farmers and some residents lose land. Judgement: management has solved problems where it was built but created new ones elsewhere, so the statement is partly true; an integrated shoreline plan is needed.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): Thorough knowledge and understanding. Detailed, well-balanced evaluation of both sides. Detailed, accurate, place-specific evidence. Clear, substantiated judgement that answers the question.

Level 2 (4-6 marks): Reasonable knowledge and understanding. Partly balanced evaluation, may favour one side. Some place-specific evidence, but general or patchy. A judgement is given but only partly supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Limited knowledge. Simple, unbalanced points with little evaluation. Little or no relevant evidence. No clear judgement.

SPaG (3 marks): High performance 3 = accurate spelling and punctuation, grammar controls meaning, wide range of specialist terms used precisely. Intermediate 2 = considerable accuracy, good range of specialist terms. Threshold 1 = reasonable accuracy, limited range of specialist terms.

Indicative content: Rate of erosion (about 1.8 m/year), soft boulder clay, North Sea fetch. Strategies: rock groynes and armour at Mappleton, sea walls and groynes at Hornsea and Withernsea. Solved: settlements, roads (B1242) and tourist beaches protected. Created: down-drift erosion (Cowden), less sediment for Spurn Head, conflict between protected and unprotected communities, cost. Level 3 needs specific place detail and a clear judgement.
questions.tip: Use specific places along Holderness, not just Mappleton.

questions.q:
Figure 9 shows cliff retreat at a site on the Holderness coast measured from a 2000 baseline.
Year | 2000 | 2005 | 2010 | 2015 | 2020
Total retreat (m) | 0 | 9.5 | 19.0 | 27.0 | 37.5

Calculate the mean annual rate of retreat between 2000 and 2020, and identify the five-year period with the fastest retreat.
questions.answer: 37.5 ÷ 20 = 1.875 m per year (about 1.9 m/yr). Fastest period: 2015-2020 (10.5 m, 2.1 m per year).
ms: Answer: 1.875 m per year, allow 1.9 (1).
Fastest period 2015-2020 (10.5 m) (1).
questions.tip: Total retreat ÷ number of years. Then compare the differences between each pair of years for the fastest period.

questions.q: Name the process where waves force air into cracks in a cliff, causing the rock to break apart.
questions.answer: Hydraulic power (or hydraulic action).
ms: Hydraulic power/hydraulic action (1).
questions.tip: Spell it right; 'hydrolic' is a common misspelling.

questions.q: Suggest why managed retreat may be chosen for some stretches of coastline instead of hard engineering.
questions.answer: Where land is low value, such as farmland or marsh, the cost of building sea walls is greater than the value of what is protected. Managed retreat is cheaper and lets the sea flood the land naturally, creating salt marsh that absorbs wave energy and acts as a natural defence. It also creates habitat for birds and wildlife, and it is more sustainable as sea levels rise. For example, at Medmerry in West Sussex, a managed realignment scheme (2013) created new intertidal habitat.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear, developed points showing understanding, linked accurately to the question focus (and to the figure where one is given).
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple, undeveloped points. Limited link to the question focus.

Indicative content: Cost-benefit: low land value, high cost of hard defences; sustainability with rising sea levels; natural defence from salt marsh absorbing wave energy; habitat creation; avoids down-drift problems of groynes. Allow named example such as Medmerry. Level 2 requires developed reasons linked to the decision.
questions.tip: Cost-benefit analysis is the key phrase. Use it.

questions.q: Describe the difference between abrasion and attrition.
questions.answer: Abrasion is when rocks carried by waves are thrown at or scraped against the cliff, wearing it away. Attrition is when rocks carried by waves hit each other and break into smaller, rounder pieces.
ms: Abrasion: material carried by waves wears away the cliff/coastline (1).
Attrition: material collides with other material, becoming smaller and rounder (1).
questions.tip: Abrasion attacks the cliff; attrition attacks the sediment itself.

questions.q: What is the main difference between till and outwash?
options: Till is only found in valleys
Outwash is always larger than till
Till is sorted, outwash is unsorted
Till is deposited directly by ice and is unsorted; outwash is deposited by meltwater and is sorted
ms: Ice drops everything it carries as it melts, so till is a jumble of sizes. Meltwater sorts material by size as it slows down.
questions.tip: Ice cannot sort material. Water can.

questions.q: Which glacial landform is a sharp, pointed mountain peak formed by three or more corries eroding back to back?
ms: A pyramidal peak forms when three or more corries erode back towards each other. In the Lake District, Helvellyn is surrounded by corries; the classic example worldwide is the Matterhorn.
questions.tip: Two corries back to back = arête. Three or more = pyramidal peak.

questions.q: Which of these is the best evidence that a valley was once occupied by a glacier rather than a river?
options: The valley has a flat floor, steep sides, truncated spurs and hanging valleys
The valley has a V-shaped cross-section with interlocking spurs
The valley has a delta at its mouth
ms: A U-shaped glacial trough with truncated spurs and hanging valleys is classic glacial evidence. V-shapes, interlocking spurs and meanders are river features.
questions.tip: Compare river and glacial valleys side by side when you revise.

questions.q: Explain how a drumlin is formed.
questions.answer: Drumlins form under a moving glacier. When the ice is overloaded with sediment, or meets an obstacle, it deposits till. The moving ice then moulds the till into a smooth, egg-shaped mound. The steep, blunt end (stoss) faces the direction the ice came from, and the gentler, tapered end (lee) points in the direction the ice moved. They often occur in groups called swarms, e.g. in the Eden Valley in Cumbria.
ms: Deposition of till beneath the glacier (1).
Due to ice being overloaded or meeting an obstacle/friction (1).
Moulded/streamlined by moving ice into an egg shape (1).
Blunt end faces up-glacier, tapered end down-glacier (1). Allow named example such as the Eden Valley.
questions.tip: Describe the shape AND explain its orientation. That's what gets full marks.

questions.q: Explain the formation of an arête.
questions.answer: An arête forms when two corries develop back to back (or side by side). Plucking and abrasion deepen each corrie, and freeze-thaw weathering attacks the backwalls. As both backwalls retreat, the ridge of land between them becomes narrower and steeper until a knife-edged ridge is left, e.g. Striding Edge on Helvellyn.
ms: Two corries next to each other/back to back (1).
Erosion by plucking and abrasion/rotational slip deepens corries (1).
Freeze-thaw weathering on backwalls makes them retreat (1).
Leaves a narrow, knife-edged ridge (1). Allow named example: Striding Edge.
questions.tip: Use a named Lake District example to reach the top marks.

questions.q: Describe the characteristics of a hanging valley.
questions.answer: A smaller tributary valley that sits high above the floor of the main glacial trough, often with a waterfall where its stream drops down into the main valley.
ms: Tributary valley high above the main trough floor (1).
Often has a waterfall/steep drop into the main valley (1).
questions.tip: Describe = what it looks like. Formation isn't needed here.

questions.q:
Figure 10 describes part of a 1:25,000 OS map of a Lake District valley.
A long, narrow lake runs from 3510 to 3514.
Steep contours close together line both sides of the valley; the valley floor is around 150 m and the ridge tops are around 700 m.
A small lake surrounded on three sides by steep cliffs is at 337135, at a height of about 600 m.
A stream falls steeply from a side valley into the main valley at 346118, marked with the word 'Force' (waterfall).

Identify three glacial landforms shown in Figure 10 and give the evidence for each.
