questions.answer: Ribbon lake: long, narrow lake running from 3510 to 3514 in the valley floor. Corrie with tarn: small lake at 337135 surrounded on three sides by steep cliffs. Hanging valley: side valley with a waterfall dropping into the main valley at 346118. Also glacial trough: steep valley sides with a flat floor at 150 m.
ms: One mark per landform correctly matched to map evidence, max 3. E.g. ribbon lake, long narrow lake 3510-3514 (1); corrie/tarn at 337135 with steep cliffs on three sides (1); hanging valley/waterfall at 346118 (1); glacial trough/U-shaped valley from steep contours and flat floor (1).
questions.tip: Always quote the grid reference given as your evidence.

questions.q:
Figure 10 describes part of a 1:25,000 OS map of a Lake District valley.
A long, narrow lake runs from 3510 to 3514.
Steep contours close together line both sides of the valley; the valley floor is around 150 m and the ridge tops are around 700 m.
A small lake surrounded on three sides by steep cliffs is at 337135, at a height of about 600 m.
A stream falls steeply from a side valley into the main valley at 346118, marked with the word 'Force' (waterfall).

Using Figure 10, calculate the approximate height difference between the valley floor and the ridge tops, and state what this tells you about the shape of the valley.
questions.answer: 700 − 150 = 550 m. The large height difference and steep contours close together show a deep valley with steep sides, typical of a U-shaped glacial trough.
ms: Deep, steep-sided valley/U-shaped glacial trough (1).
questions.tip: Close contours = steep. Use that in shape questions.

questions.q: Using a named example, explain the conflicts between different land uses in a glaciated upland area and how they are managed.
questions.answer: Lake District: tourism vs farming: walkers leave gates open and dogs worry sheep; managed with signs and the Countryside Code. Tourism vs residents: second homes and holiday lets push up house prices, so local young people cannot afford to live there; some new homes are restricted to local people. Water sports vs quiet recreation and wildlife on Windermere: managed by the 10 knot (about 11.5 mph) speed limit, enforced from 2005. Quarrying vs conservation: quarries such as Honister provide jobs but scar the landscape; planning controls limit new quarries. Forestry vs natural landscape: conifer plantations can look unnatural; more mixed planting now.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Lake District National Park (designated 1951, World Heritage Site 2017, about 18 million visitors per year). Conflicts: tourism vs farming, tourism vs local residents (second homes, house prices, traffic), speedboats vs quieter users and wildlife, quarrying vs conservation, forestry vs landscape, water supply reservoirs (Thirlmere, Haweswater). Management: National Park Authority planning rules, Windermere 10 knot speed limit (enforced from 2005), Fix the Fells, park-and-ride, public transport schemes, local-occupancy housing. Level 3 needs conflicts explained with who is involved and specific management responses.
questions.tip: A conflict needs two groups who want different things. Name both.

questions.q: Explain how glaciers transport material.
questions.answer: Glaciers carry material in three ways. On top of the ice (supraglacial) is rock that has fallen from valley sides after freeze-thaw weathering. Within the ice (englacial) is material that has fallen into crevasses or been buried by snow. At the base (subglacial) is material plucked and abraded from the bed. Glaciers also push loose material in front of them as they advance, which is called bulldozing.
ms: Material on the surface from freeze-thaw/rockfall from valley sides (1).
Material within the ice/fallen into crevasses (1).
Material at the base from plucking/abrasion (1).
Bulldozing: pushing debris in front of the snout (1).
questions.tip: Use the terms bulldozing and plucking accurately.

questions.q: 'Quarrying brings more benefits than costs to glaciated upland areas.' Using a named example, to what extent do you agree with this statement?
questions.answer: Lake District: Honister Slate Mine extracts distinctive green slate used for roofing and building, providing local jobs in an area where jobs outside tourism are limited, and it has become a tourist attraction itself. Other quarries supply stone for building and repairing traditional buildings and footpaths. Costs: quarries scar the landscape, create noise, dust and heavy lorry traffic on narrow roads, and harm habitats. They conflict with the National Park's aim of conserving natural beauty. Judgement: benefits outweigh costs only for small, well-managed quarries; large-scale quarrying conflicts with the park's main economic activity, tourism.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Benefits: jobs, local building materials, distinctive slate keeps traditional character, tourist attraction (Honister), economic diversification. Costs: visual scarring, noise, dust, traffic on narrow roads, habitat loss, conflict with tourism and conservation. Management: planning permission from the National Park Authority, restoration after closure, limits on size. Level 3 needs named place detail and a clear judgement.
questions.tip: Use specific Lake District examples. Generic 'quarrying creates jobs' answers stay at Level 1-2.

questions.q: Name the type of moraine found where two glaciers join.
questions.answer: Medial moraine.
ms: Medial moraine (1).
questions.tip: Lateral = sides, medial = middle, terminal = end.

questions.q: Explain how glacial erosion and weathering combine to form a corrie, arête and pyramidal peak.
questions.answer: Snow collects in a north-facing hollow, where less sunlight means it lasts longer, and compacts into ice. Freeze-thaw weathering loosens rock on the backwall. As the ice moves by rotational slip, plucking pulls rock from the backwall, making it steep, while abrasion by rock frozen into the base deepens the floor. Less erosion at the front leaves a rock lip; when the ice melts a tarn may fill the hollow. Where two corries erode back to back, the ridge between them narrows into a knife-edged arête, e.g. Striding Edge. Where three or more corries erode back towards each other, a sharp pyramidal peak is left.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed knowledge and understanding. Thorough, well-developed explanation with clear chains of reasoning. Accurate place-specific detail or data used where relevant.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear knowledge and understanding. Some developed explanation, but chains of reasoning are partial. Some relevant detail or data used.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge. Simple points with little or no development. Little or no relevant detail.

Indicative content: Corrie: snow accumulation, compaction to ice, north/north-east facing, freeze-thaw on backwall, plucking steepens backwall, abrasion deepens floor, rotational slip, rock lip, tarn (e.g. Red Tarn). Arête: two corries back to back, retreating backwalls (Striding Edge). Pyramidal peak: three or more corries. Level 3 needs clear sequence for all three landforms and correct use of processes.
questions.tip: Sequence matters. The corrie must form first before the arête and peak can.

questions.q: What is a glacial erratic?
questions.answer: A large boulder carried by a glacier and deposited in an area of different rock type.
ms: Boulder transported by ice and dropped on a different rock type/far from its source (1).
questions.tip: The key is the different rock type.

questions.q: On a 1:50,000 OS map, two farms are 4.6 cm apart. What is the real distance between them?
ms: On a 1:50,000 map 1 cm = 0.5 km, so 4.6 × 0.5 = 2.3 km. 1.15 km would be the answer on a 1:25,000 map.
questions.tip: Check the scale before converting. 1:50,000: 2 cm = 1 km. 1:25,000: 4 cm = 1 km.

questions.q: A village is at grid reference 456789. Which of these describes where it is?
options: In grid square 7845, 9 tenths east and 6 tenths north
In grid square 4578, 6 tenths east and 9 tenths north
In grid square 5678, 4 tenths east and 9 tenths north
In grid square 4567, 8 tenths east and 9 tenths north
ms: In a six-figure reference the first three digits are the easting (45 and 6 tenths) and the last three the northing (78 and 9 tenths), so it is in square 4578.
questions.tip: Split six figures into 3 + 3, not 2 + 2 + 2.

questions.q: Contour lines on a map form a V shape with the point of the V aiming uphill. What does this show?
ms: Contour Vs pointing uphill (towards higher numbers) show a valley, usually with a stream. Vs pointing downhill show a spur or ridge.
questions.tip: Look at the numbers on the contours to see which way is uphill.

questions.q: On a map, point A is at 180 m and point B is at 420 m. They are 1.2 km apart horizontally. What is the average gradient from A to B?
ms: Height difference = 240 m. Horizontal distance = 1,200 m. 1,200 ÷ 240 = 5, so the gradient is 1 in 5 (or 0.2). Remember to put both values in the same units.
questions.tip: Convert km to metres before dividing.

questions.q: Fifteen ordered values of daily footpath users are: 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18, 21, 24, 26, 30. What is the interquartile range?
ms: Median is the 8th value (14). Lower quartile is the 4th value (8), upper quartile the 12th value (21). IQR = 21 − 8 = 13. 27 is the range.
questions.tip: Find the position of each quartile: (n+1)/4 and 3(n+1)/4.

questions.q: Deaths from seven tropical storms were: 12, 25, 40, 18, 9, 2,400, 30. Which average best represents the typical storm, and why?
options: The median (25), because it is not distorted by the extreme value of 2,400
The mean (362), because it uses all the values
The range, because it shows the spread
The mode, because it is the most common
ms: One extreme value (2,400) pulls the mean up to 362, much higher than six of the seven storms. The median (25) is not affected by outliers. The data has no mode, and the range is not an average.
questions.tip: When data has an outlier, the median is the better average. Say why.

questions.q: Which type of map uses shading, with darker colours for higher values, to show data such as population density by area?
ms: Choropleth maps shade areas according to a value. Isolines join points of equal value, flow lines show movement, and dot maps use one dot per set quantity.
questions.tip: Know one strength and one weakness of each map type.

questions.q: A scatter graph shows that as distance from the sea increases, average pebble size on a beach decreases. Which line of best fit and correlation does this describe?
options: A line sloping upwards, positive correlation
A line sloping downwards, negative correlation
ms: As one variable rises and the other falls, the correlation is negative and the best-fit line slopes down from left to right.
questions.tip: Correlation describes the relationship, not the cause.

questions.q:
Figure 11 describes part of a 1:50,000 OS map.
A river flows from north-west to south-east through grid squares 2134, 2233 and 2332.
In grid square 2233 there is a village with a church with a tower at 226337 and a school at 228333.
A main road (A-road) crosses the river by a bridge at 224335.
Contours on the north-east bank of the river are close together; on the south-west bank they are widely spaced.
A spot height of 312 m is shown at 238348.

Give the six-figure grid reference of the bridge.
questions.tip: Copy carefully. A transposed digit loses the mark.

questions.q:
Figure 11 describes part of a 1:50,000 OS map.
A river flows from north-west to south-east through grid squares 2134, 2233 and 2332.
In grid square 2233 there is a village with a church with a tower at 226337 and a school at 228333.
A main road (A-road) crosses the river by a bridge at 224335.
Contours on the north-east bank of the river are close together; on the south-west bank they are widely spaced.
A spot height of 312 m is shown at 238348.

In which direction is the spot height at 238348 from the church at 226337?
questions.answer: North-east.
ms: North-east (1).
questions.tip: Compare eastings (238 is more than 226, so east) and northings (348 is more than 337, so north).

questions.q:
Figure 11 describes part of a 1:50,000 OS map.
A river flows from north-west to south-east through grid squares 2134, 2233 and 2332.
In grid square 2233 there is a village with a church with a tower at 226337 and a school at 228333.
A main road (A-road) crosses the river by a bridge at 224335.
Contours on the north-east bank of the river are close together; on the south-west bank they are widely spaced.
A spot height of 312 m is shown at 238348.

Compare the relief on the two sides of the river.
questions.answer: The north-east bank is steep because the contours are close together, whereas the south-west bank is gently sloping because the contours are widely spaced.
ms: North-east bank steep/close contours (1).
South-west bank gentle/widely spaced contours, with a comparative word such as 'whereas' (1).
questions.tip: 'Compare' needs a comparison word in one sentence, not two separate descriptions.

questions.q:
Figure 11 describes part of a 1:50,000 OS map.
A river flows from north-west to south-east through grid squares 2134, 2233 and 2332.
In grid square 2233 there is a village with a church with a tower at 226337 and a school at 228333.
A main road (A-road) crosses the river by a bridge at 224335.
Contours on the north-east bank of the river are close together; on the south-west bank they are widely spaced.
A spot height of 312 m is shown at 238348.

Using Figure 11, suggest why the village grew at this location.
questions.answer: The village is on the river, which would have provided water supply and possibly power. There is a bridging point at 224335 where the A-road crosses, so it is a route centre with good access. The south-west bank is gently sloping, giving flat land for building and farming, whereas the steep north-east side would be harder to build on.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): Clear, developed points showing understanding, linked accurately to the question focus (and to the figure where one is given).
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple, undeveloped points. Limited link to the question focus.

Indicative content: Map evidence: river (water supply, transport), bridge at 224335 (bridging point, route centre), A-road (communications), gentle slopes on the south-west bank (flat land for building/farming), steep north-east bank possibly sheltered or defensive. Level 2 requires map evidence (grid references or named features) linked to settlement factors.
questions.tip: Use site factors (water, flat land, bridging point) and back each with map evidence.

questions.q:
A student counted the number of people walking past eight sites in a town centre in 10 minutes: 18, 22, 15, 30, 25, 10, 40, 35.

Calculate the mean, the median and the range.
ms: Median 23.5 (1).
Range 30 (1).
questions.tip: For an even number of values the median is halfway between the two middle values. Put the data in order first.

questions.q: The population of a coastal town rose from 1,500 in 2001 to 2,400 in 2021. Calculate the percentage increase. Show your working.
ms: Answer: 60% (1).
questions.tip: Divide by the original value. 900 ÷ 2,400 gives 37.5%, which is wrong.

questions.q:
Figure 12 shows how visitors travelled to a national park.
Car 72% | Coach 10% | Train 8% | Bicycle 5% | Walk 5%

If Figure 12 was drawn as a pie chart, calculate the angle of the sector for car and for coach.
ms: Coach 36° (1).
questions.tip: 1% = 3.6° on a pie chart.

questions.q:
Figure 12 shows how visitors travelled to a national park.
Car 72% | Coach 10% | Train 8% | Bicycle 5% | Walk 5%

Using Figure 12, suggest two problems caused by the way visitors travel to the national park and one way they could be reduced.
questions.answer: With 72% arriving by car, narrow rural roads become congested at weekends and bank holidays, and parking on verges damages the landscape. Car exhaust adds to air pollution and noise. This could be reduced by park-and-ride schemes or improving bus and train services, for example a shuttle bus from the railway station.
ms: Problem 1, e.g. traffic congestion on narrow roads (1), linked to data (72% by car) (1).
Problem 2, e.g. air/noise pollution or parking damage to verges (1).
Solution, e.g. park-and-ride/improved public transport/cycle hire/higher parking charges (1).
questions.tip: Use the 72% figure to show you have used the data.

questions.q:
Figure 13 shows the results of a river study at five sites downstream.
Site | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
Distance from source (km) | 1 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 9
Channel width (m) | 1.2 | 2.5 | 3.1 | 4.8 | 5.6

Describe the relationship shown in Figure 13 and calculate the mean increase in channel width per km between site 1 and site 5.
questions.answer: There is a positive relationship: channel width increases from 1.2 m at site 1 (1 km) to 5.6 m at site 5 (9 km). The increase is not steady: between sites 3 and 4 it widens by 1.7 m but between sites 2 and 3 by only 0.6 m. Mean increase = (5.6 - 1.2) ÷ (9 - 1) = 4.4 ÷ 8 = 0.55 m per km.
ms: Positive relationship/width increases downstream (1).
Data used, e.g. 1.2 m to 5.6 m (1).
Anomaly or uneven rate, e.g. small increase between sites 2 and 3 (0.6 m) compared with sites 3 and 4 (1.7 m) (1).
questions.tip: Name the relationship (positive), back it with data, point out any uneven change, and show the working for rates.

questions.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using a dot map to show population distribution.
questions.answer: Advantage: shows clearly where people are concentrated or spread out. Disadvantage: dots can merge in crowded areas so it is hard to count, and they take a long time to draw.
ms: Advantage, e.g. shows distribution/clusters clearly, easy to see patterns (1).
Disadvantage, e.g. dots merge in dense areas/time-consuming/hard to count exact values (1).
questions.tip: Evaluating a technique always means strength + weakness.

questions.q:
Figure 14 is a climate graph for a location in the Southern Hemisphere. Temperature is highest (about 25°C) in January and lowest (about 12°C) in July. Rainfall is highest in June (about 140 mm) and lowest in January (about 10 mm).

Describe the climate shown in Figure 14.
questions.answer: Warm summers peaking at about 25°C in January and mild winters of about 12°C in July, a range of about 13°C. Wet winters (about 140 mm in June) and dry summers (about 10 mm in January), so rain falls mainly in winter.
ms: Temperature pattern with data, e.g. highest 25°C in January, lowest 12°C in July (1).
Rainfall pattern with data, e.g. wettest June 140 mm, driest January 10 mm (1).
Overall: hot dry summers, mild wet winters/temperature range about 13°C/recognises the Southern Hemisphere seasons are reversed (1).
questions.tip: In the Southern Hemisphere, January is summer. Spot that.

questions.q: A student wants to investigate whether footpath erosion in a national park increases closer to a car park. Suggest a suitable sampling method and explain how the data could be presented.
questions.answer: Systematic sampling: measure path width and depth every 50 m along the path from the car park. This gives an even spread of data and avoids bias. The results could be shown on a scatter graph of distance from the car park (x-axis) against path width (y-axis), with a line of best fit to show any correlation. A map with proportional bars at each site would show the spatial pattern.
ms: Sampling method named, e.g. systematic (regular intervals) (1).
Justified, e.g. even coverage/reduces bias (1).
Presentation, e.g. scatter graph with distance on x-axis and width on y-axis (1).
Justified, e.g. shows correlation/line of best fit; or proportional symbols on a map show spatial pattern (1).
questions.tip: Explain WHY the method suits the question. Methods with no justification only get half marks.

questions.q: Explain why a line of best fit on a scatter graph does not prove that one variable causes the other.
questions.answer: Correlation only shows that two variables change together. The pattern could be caused by a third factor, or be coincidence, so further evidence is needed to show cause.
ms: Correlation shows a relationship/link only (1).
Could be due to another factor/coincidence, so causation needs other evidence (1).
questions.tip: Correlation is not causation: a favourite examiner line.

questions.q: On a 1:50,000 map, a road between two villages measures 5.5 cm. A bus takes 3 minutes to travel between them. Calculate the real distance and the average speed of the bus in km/h.
ms: Distance 2.75 km (1).
Speed 55 km/h (1).
questions.tip: Convert minutes into hours before dividing: 3 minutes = 0.05 hours.

questions.q:
Figure 15 shows population and area for three wards.
Ward | Population | Area (km²)
A | 12,000 | 4.0
B | 8,400 | 1.2
C | 3,500 | 7.0

Calculate the population density of each ward (people per km²).
ms: Ward A 3,000 people per km² (1).
Ward B 7,000 people per km² (1).
Ward C 500 people per km² (1).
questions.tip: Density = population ÷ area. Ward B has fewer people than A but a much higher density.

questions.q:
Figure 15 shows population and area for three wards.
Ward | Population | Area (km²)
A | 12,000 | 4.0
B | 8,400 | 1.2
C | 3,500 | 7.0

A student wants to show population density for every ward in a city on one map. Suggest the most suitable type of map and evaluate its use.
questions.answer: A choropleth map, shading each ward darker for higher density (e.g. B darkest at 7,000 per km², C lightest at 500 per km²). Strength: the pattern across the city is clear at a glance and easy to compare between wards. Weakness: it suggests density is the same across the whole ward and changes suddenly at boundaries, and the choice of class intervals can change how the pattern looks.
ms: Choropleth map identified (1).
Description of how, e.g. darker shading for higher density, using data from Figure 15 (1).
Strength, e.g. clear visual pattern/easy comparison (1).
Weakness, e.g. assumes uniform density within each area/sharp boundaries/class intervals affect appearance (1).
questions.tip: Evaluate = one strength and one weakness, plus a decision.

questions.q: Describe how to give a six-figure grid reference.
questions.answer: Find the easting of the grid square (the line to the left), then estimate tenths across to the point. Then find the northing (line below) and estimate tenths up. Write the easting first then the northing, e.g. 345678.
ms: Eastings first (along the bottom), estimating tenths across (1).
Then northings (up the side), estimating tenths up (1).
questions.tip: 'Along the corridor and up the stairs.'

questions.q: What does a blue line on an OS map usually represent?
questions.answer: A river or stream.
ms: River/stream/watercourse (1).
questions.tip: Learn the common OS symbols: blue = water, brown = contours, black dots = buildings.

questions.q: A student measured beach width at two places either side of a groyne: 22 m on the north side and 9 m on the south side. Suggest what this shows about longshore drift and how the student could make the results more reliable.
questions.answer: Sediment builds up against the groyne on the side it is coming from, so a wider beach on the north side (22 m vs 9 m) suggests longshore drift moves sediment from north to south. To improve reliability the student could take measurements at several groynes along the beach, repeat them on different days or at the same tide each time, and calculate a mean.
ms: Wider beach on north side means sediment trapped there (1).
Direction of drift north to south (1).
Improvement, e.g. measure at several groynes/more sample points (1).
Improvement, e.g. repeat on different days/same tide/calculate a mean (1).
questions.tip: Reliability = repeating and taking more samples. Accuracy = better equipment.

questions.q: In 1950 only two cities in the world had over 10 million people. Which were they?
ms: New York and Tokyo were the only megacities in 1950; most megacities today are in LICs and NEEs.
questions.tip: Do not assume megacities have always been in poorer countries; the shift happened after 1950.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the global pattern of urban growth since 1950?
options: Urban populations have fallen in LICs
Most urban growth has taken place in HICs
Urban growth has been fastest in LICs and NEEs, especially in Asia and Africa
ms: The fastest urban growth has been in LICs and NEEs in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa; HICs urbanised earlier.
questions.tip: Distinguish rate of urbanisation (fast in LICs) from level of urbanisation (high in HICs).

questions.q: A country is 82% urban and its urban population is growing at 0.3% per year. It is most likely to be:
ms: High level of urbanisation but a slow rate is typical of HICs, which urbanised in the 19th and 20th centuries.
questions.tip: High level plus slow rate = HIC. Low level plus fast rate = LIC.

questions.q: A city of 4 million grows by 3.5% per year, mostly from natural increase. Which explanation of this natural increase is most accurate?
options: Cities have higher death rates than rural areas
Migrants are mostly elderly so death rates rise
Natural increase is caused by people moving in
Migrants are mostly young adults of child-bearing age, so birth rates in the city are high
ms: Rural-urban migrants are mainly young adults, so they raise urban birth rates; better healthcare keeps death rates low.
questions.tip: Migration and natural increase are different processes, but migration feeds natural increase.

questions.q: State the number of megacities in the world in 2018 according to the United Nations.
questions.answer: 33 megacities.
ms: 33 (1 mark). Allow 'about 33' or 'just over 30'.
questions.tip: Learn one key figure for global trends; 2 in 1950, 33 in 2018.

questions.q: Define 'rate of urbanisation' and 'level of urbanisation'.
questions.answer: Rate of urbanisation is how fast the proportion of people living in urban areas is increasing (e.g. % per year). Level of urbanisation is the percentage of a country's population living in urban areas at a given time.
ms: Rate: the speed at which the urban proportion grows over time (1 mark).
Level: the percentage of population living in urban areas at one point in time (1 mark).
questions.tip: Mixing these up is the most common error in 'describe the pattern' questions.

questions.q: Figure 1 shows that Africa's urban population was 14% in 1950 and 43% in 2018. Calculate the increase in percentage points.
questions.answer: 43 - 14 = 29 percentage points.
ms: Correct subtraction 43 - 14 (1 mark).
29 percentage points (1 mark). Do not accept '29%' alone, or a percentage change of 207%, for the answer mark.
questions.tip: A change between two percentages is in percentage points, not per cent.

questions.q: Africa's urban population was 14% of its total population in 1950 and 43% in 2018. Calculate the percentage change in Africa's urban share from 1950 to 2018. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
ms: Answer 207% (1 mark).
questions.tip: Divide by the ORIGINAL value (14), not the new value.

questions.q: Suggest how a lack of formal jobs in a rapidly growing city in an LIC affects the people who live there.
questions.answer: Formal jobs cannot keep up with the number of migrants arriving, so many people work in the informal economy, such as street selling or waste picking. This work is irregular and low paid, so families cannot afford good housing and live in squatter settlements. Informal workers pay no tax and have no sick pay or pensions, so illness quickly pushes families deeper into poverty, and cities collect less tax to pay for services.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: informal economy; low and irregular pay; no contracts, sick pay or pensions; squatter housing; child labour; less tax revenue for services; some positives: entrepreneurship, flexible work, cheap goods for others.
questions.tip: 'Suggest' means apply your knowledge to the situation: you do not need a named example, but chains of reasoning get Level 2.

questions.q: Lagos, Nigeria, is one of the fastest-growing cities in Africa. Using your knowledge of why cities grow, suggest reasons for its rapid growth.
questions.answer: Lagos is Nigeria's main port and business centre, so it attracts migrants from rural areas where farming is low paid and affected by drought or conflict. Migrants are mostly young, so the city has a high birth rate and natural increase adds to growth. Investment from TNCs and oil-related businesses creates jobs, which act as a pull factor, and family networks mean new migrants follow relatives already in the city.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: pull factors: jobs, port, oil and business investment, services; push factors: rural poverty, drought, conflict, mechanisation; natural increase from young migrant population; chain migration. Credit any reasonable application to an unfamiliar place.
questions.tip: For unfamiliar places, use the general causes (migration + natural increase) and apply them to the clues in the question.

questions.q: Explain why urban growth in LICs and NEEs can be both a cause and a consequence of economic development.
questions.answer: Economic development creates factory and service jobs in cities, which pull migrants from rural areas, so growth is a consequence of development. In turn, a large urban workforce and market attracts more investment from TNCs and allows a multiplier effect, so urban growth also drives further development. However if growth is too fast, the city cannot provide enough jobs and services, so squatter settlements and the informal economy grow.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: development creates jobs which pull migrants; concentration of labour and consumers attracts investment (agglomeration); multiplier effect; taxes fund infrastructure; but uncontrolled growth leads to slums, congestion, pollution.
questions.tip: Grade 9 answers show two-way links, not just a list of reasons.

questions.q: 'The growth of megacities brings more problems than opportunities.' Discuss this statement.
questions.answer: Opportunities: megacities concentrate jobs, services and investment, so migrants earn more than in rural areas and get better access to schools and hospitals; they act as engines of national economies. Problems: when growth outpaces planning, many live in squatter settlements without clean water or sanitation, leading to disease; traffic congestion and air pollution are severe; unemployment pushes people into the informal economy. Judgement: problems are often greatest in the short term in fast-growing LIC cities, but with management (e.g. Rio's favela upgrading or BRT schemes) the opportunities can outweigh the problems, so the statement is only partly true.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, well-developed points with accurate place-specific evidence; balanced discussion; clear, supported judgement where the command word asks for one.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points and some specific evidence; may be unbalanced or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little evidence or development; no judgement.

Indicative content: opportunities: jobs, wages, services, economies of scale, culture, innovation; problems: slums, water and sanitation, waste, congestion, pollution, crime, informal economy; examples from Rio or another city; judgement linked to how well growth is managed and the type of country.
questions.tip: Use your Rio knowledge as evidence even when the question does not name it.

questions.q: Until 1960, Rio de Janeiro was:
options: The largest city in South America
ms: Rio was Brazil's capital until 1960, when the capital moved to Brasília.
questions.tip: Former capital status is a key part of Rio's national importance.

questions.q: Which Brazilian company has its headquarters in Rio and is central to the city's role in the oil industry?
ms: Petrobras, the state-controlled oil company, is headquartered in Rio; offshore oil fields lie off the coast.
questions.tip: Embraer is an aircraft maker based in São Paulo state; Fiat and Nestlé are foreign TNCs.

questions.q: The Jardim Gramacho landfill site near Rio closed in 2012. Which problem does this example best illustrate?
options: The challenge of managing waste in a rapidly growing city
ms: Jardim Gramacho was one of the largest landfills in Latin America; its closure shows the scale of Rio's waste challenge.
questions.tip: Match each named example to the correct environmental challenge.

questions.q: Rocinha's official 2010 census population was about 70,000, but many local estimates are far higher. What is the best explanation for the difference?
options: Only adults are counted in a census
Informal housing, dense alleys and distrust of officials make favela populations hard to count
ms: Unregistered homes, density and distrust mean official data often undercount favelas.
questions.tip: Questioning the reliability of data is a high-level evaluation skill.

questions.q: Name the bay on which Rio de Janeiro is located.
questions.answer: Guanabara Bay.
ms: Guanabara Bay (1 mark).
questions.tip: Spell it correctly: it is the most quoted location fact for Rio.

questions.q: Give two reasons why Rio de Janeiro attracts international tourists.
questions.answer: Famous landmarks such as Christ the Redeemer and Sugarloaf Mountain; beaches such as Copacabana and Ipanema; events such as Carnival.
ms: One reason with named detail (1 mark).
Second different reason (1 mark). Accept: landmarks, beaches, Carnival, sporting events, UNESCO World Heritage landscape.
questions.tip: Name a specific landmark or beach to secure each mark.

questions.q: Describe the location of Rocinha within Rio de Janeiro.
questions.answer: Rocinha is in the south zone of Rio, built on steep hillsides between the wealthy districts of Gávea and São Conrado, close to the beaches.
ms: Located in the south zone / near wealthy areas (1 mark).
On steep hillside / slopes, named neighbouring district or close to the coast (1 mark).
questions.tip: Use location words: next to, between, on the slopes of.

questions.q: Explain why the location of favelas on steep hillsides creates challenges for residents.
questions.answer: Heavy summer rain saturates thin soils on steep slopes, so landslides can destroy self-built homes and kill residents. The steep, narrow alleys make it hard for rubbish trucks, ambulances and buses to get in, so waste piles up and blocks drains, which increases flooding and disease. Residents also face long, tiring journeys to formal jobs in the city, which is why schemes such as the Complexo do Alemão cable car were built.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: landslides after heavy rain; poor access for services and emergency vehicles; waste collection difficult, blocked drains; flooding and disease; long journeys to work; cost of laying pipes and electricity; example of cable car.
questions.tip: Link the physical site (slope, rain) to a human impact each time.

questions.q: Explain how the hosting of the 2016 Olympic Games affected transport in Rio.
questions.answer: The city built new Bus Rapid Transit lines with dedicated lanes, which cut journey times between the west zone and the rest of the city. Metro Line 4 was extended to Barra da Tijuca, where many venues were located, so more people could travel by public transport. However much of the investment favoured wealthier areas such as Barra, and some homes were demolished to make way for the routes, so the benefits for the poorest were limited.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: BRT lines; Metro Line 4 to Barra da Tijuca; reduced journey times; improved links to west zone; criticisms: focus on wealthier areas, evictions (e.g. Vila Autódromo), cost, debt.
questions.tip: Balance gets you to the top of Level 2 even on an 'explain' question.

questions.q: Explain why migrants from the north east of Brazil moved to Rio de Janeiro.
questions.answer: The north east suffers from frequent droughts which cause crop failure, so farming families lost their income. Large landowners and mechanised farming reduced jobs, and services such as schools and hospitals were poor. Rio offered pull factors such as jobs in construction, services and industry, higher wages and better access to healthcare and education, and family members already living in favelas made it easier to move.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: push: drought, poverty, lack of land, mechanisation, poor services; pull: jobs, wages, services, family networks; result: growth of favelas.
questions.tip: Separate push and pull clearly, then link both to Rio's growth.

questions.q: Explain how inequality in Rio de Janeiro can be seen in the contrast between different areas of the city.
questions.answer: Wealthy areas such as Copacabana and Ipanema have high-rise apartments, good services and high incomes, while nearby favelas such as Rocinha have self-built housing, poorer sanitation and many informal workers. Because favelas grew without planning, residents have less access to formal jobs and education, so incomes stay low, and this reinforces the divide. The fact that rich and poor live side by side, for example Rocinha next to São Conrado, shows inequality is spatial as well as economic.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: contrasts in housing, income, services, sanitation, life chances; named areas; reasons: unplanned growth, informal economy, lack of education; inequality reinforced over time.
questions.tip: Use paired named places to show you understand spatial inequality.

questions.q: Assess the effectiveness of attempts to reduce pollution in Guanabara Bay.
questions.answer: New sewage treatment plants and pipes were built, and a clean-up was promised as part of the 2016 Olympics, with a target to treat most sewage entering the bay. Some ecoboats collected floating waste. However the target was not met, so large amounts of untreated sewage and industrial waste still flowed into the bay, and sailing events took place in polluted water. Rapid favela growth without sewers continues to add waste. Overall the measures had limited effectiveness because investment did not keep pace with urban growth.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, well-developed points with accurate place-specific evidence; balanced discussion; clear, supported judgement where the command word asks for one.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points and some specific evidence; may be unbalanced or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little evidence or development; no judgement.

Indicative content: sewage treatment plants and pipes; ecoboats and eco-barriers on rivers; Olympic clean-up target missed; industrial pollution from refineries and ships; favela sewage; judgement: limited or partial success with reasons.
questions.tip: 'Assess' needs a judgement on HOW effective, not just a description of the strategies.

questions.q: 'The 2016 Olympic Games did more harm than good for the people of Rio de Janeiro.' Evaluate this statement. [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: Model Level 3 outline: Intro: define who 'the people' are (favela residents vs wealthier groups). Good: BRT lines and Metro Line 4 improved transport; Porto Maravilha regenerated the old port area; global profile raised tourism; construction jobs. Harm: evictions such as Vila Autódromo; Guanabara Bay clean-up failed; cost and debt left the state in financial crisis, with public sector wages delayed; many venues later underused; investment concentrated in Barra da Tijuca rather than poorer north and west zones. Judgement: for most of the urban poor the harm outweighed the benefits, because gains were concentrated in wealthier areas and promised social legacies were not delivered, though transport improvements were a lasting benefit.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): thorough knowledge and understanding; detailed, accurate place-specific evidence (named places, dates, figures) used to support points; both sides weighed; a clear, well-substantiated judgement that answers the question directly.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): reasonable knowledge with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is asserted rather than supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): limited, generic knowledge; little evidence; descriptive with no clear judgement.

Indicative content: transport (BRT, Metro Line 4), Porto Maravilha port regeneration, tourism and image; evictions (Vila Autódromo), costs and debt, state financial crisis, unused venues, Guanabara Bay targets missed, uneven spread of benefits by area and group; substantiated judgement about who benefited.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate; grammar controls meaning; wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy; good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy; limited range of specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant content or errors seriously hinder meaning.
questions.tip: Top-band answers question who the 'people' are: the impact differed between groups and areas.

questions.q: In the 2010 census Rio's population was about 6.3 million and about 22% lived in favelas. Calculate approximately how many people lived in favelas. Give your answer in millions to 1 decimal place.
questions.answer: 0.22 × 6.3 = 1.386, so about 1.4 million.
ms: Method: 22% of 6.3 million, e.g. 0.22 × 6.3 (1 mark).
1.4 million (1 mark).
questions.tip: Convert the percentage to a decimal before multiplying.

questions.q: In which year was ULEZ expanded to cover all London boroughs?
ms: ULEZ launched in central London in 2019 and was expanded London-wide in August 2023. 2003 was the Congestion Charge.
questions.tip: Do not confuse the Congestion Charge (2003) with ULEZ (2019, London-wide 2023).

questions.q: The Thames Tideway Tunnel was built mainly to:
options: Stop sewage overflowing into the River Thames
Carry the Elizabeth line under the river
Supply drinking water to east London
ms: The 'super sewer' captures combined sewer overflows that previously discharged sewage into the Thames.
questions.tip: The Thames Barrier, not Tideway, protects against tidal surges.

questions.q: Which regeneration scheme turned former railway land and warehouses into offices, housing and a university campus, now home to Google's UK headquarters?
ms: King's Cross Central regenerated former railway land; Central Saint Martins and Google are major occupiers.
questions.tip: Canary Wharf is the 1980s Docklands financial district.

questions.q: Inner London boroughs such as Tower Hamlets have high average wages but also some of the highest child poverty rates. Which is the best explanation?
options: House prices are very low in inner London
High-paid jobs in places like Canary Wharf go mainly to commuters and newcomers, while many long-term residents work in low-paid jobs and face high housing costs
Child poverty is measured only in rural areas
Everyone in the borough earns the same
ms: Averages hide inequality: high earners and poor households live side by side, and housing costs push poor households further into poverty.
questions.tip: Averages hide inequality is a key evaluation point in urban and development questions.

questions.q: Name the river on which London is located.
questions.answer: The River Thames.
ms: River Thames (1 mark).
questions.tip: Simple marks: do not lose them through misspelling.

questions.q: Give two reasons why London is important internationally.
questions.answer: It is a global financial centre (the City and Canary Wharf). It has major international transport hubs such as Heathrow Airport.
ms: One reason with detail, e.g. global finance (1 mark).
A second, different reason, e.g. Heathrow hub, tourism, culture, universities, headquarters of TNCs (1 mark).
questions.tip: Two different reasons, not two examples of the same one.

questions.q: State two ways urban sprawl around London has been controlled.
questions.answer: The green belt restricts building on land around London. Building is encouraged on brownfield sites within the city.
ms: Green belt (1 mark).
Brownfield development / densification / new towns beyond the green belt (1 mark).
questions.tip: Know both the restriction (green belt) and the alternative (brownfield).

questions.q: Newham's population rose from about 308,000 in 2011 to about 351,000 in 2021. Calculate the percentage increase to 1 decimal place.
ms: Method: increase ÷ original × 100 (1 mark).
14.0% (1 mark). Allow 14%.
questions.tip: Divide by the original 2011 figure. Dividing by the 2021 figure gives a smaller, wrong answer (12.3%).

questions.q: Explain how inequality in housing affects people in London.
questions.answer: House prices and private rents in London are far higher than average incomes, so many lower-income households cannot buy and spend a large share of income on rent. This leads to overcrowding and long council housing waiting lists, which can harm children's health and education. Rising prices in regenerated areas can push long-term residents out, which is gentrification. Wealthier households in areas such as Kensington live in large homes, showing a clear divide.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: high prices and rents relative to incomes; overcrowding; homelessness and temporary accommodation; long waiting lists; gentrification and displacement; contrast between boroughs; links to health, education outcomes.
questions.tip: Link housing to wider effects on quality of life for Level 2.

questions.q: Explain why many people have moved out of London to surrounding towns.
questions.answer: High house prices in London mean families can get larger homes for the same price in towns outside the green belt. Better transport, such as fast rail links and the Elizabeth line to Reading and Shenfield, means people can commute into London. Others want a quieter environment with less pollution and more green space, which is counter-urbanisation, and remote working since 2020 has made this easier.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: house prices; space and gardens; commuting links; lower crime and pollution; remote and hybrid working; counter-urbanisation; retirement moves.
questions.tip: Name the process: counter-urbanisation.

questions.q: Explain how the Thames Barrier and the Thames Tideway Tunnel help London manage environmental challenges.
questions.answer: The Thames Barrier, in operation since 1982, can be closed when a tidal surge comes up the estuary, protecting low-lying areas from flooding, which matters more as sea levels rise. The Tideway Tunnel captures sewage that overflowed into the Thames during heavy rain, because London's Victorian sewers combine rainwater and sewage, so water quality and river wildlife improve. Together they reduce risks created by a growing population and climate change.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: Barrier: closes against tidal surges, protects low-lying land, closures more frequent with sea-level rise; Tideway: 'super sewer' capturing combined sewer overflows, improving water quality and ecosystems; links to growing population and climate change.
questions.tip: Explain the mechanism (how it works), not just what it is.

questions.q: Using an example of a regeneration project in London, assess how far it has improved quality of life for local residents.
questions.answer: Stratford: the Olympic Park created green space, sports venues and new transport (Stratford is a major rail hub with the Elizabeth line). Westfield brought thousands of retail jobs and East Village provided new homes, some affordable. However house prices and rents rose quickly, making it hard for long-term residents to stay, and many new jobs were low paid or went to people from outside Newham. Overall quality of life has improved for the area, but less for the poorest existing residents.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, well-developed points with accurate place-specific evidence; balanced discussion; clear, supported judgement where the command word asks for one.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points and some specific evidence; may be unbalanced or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little evidence or development; no judgement.

Indicative content: named scheme (Stratford, King's Cross, Canary Wharf, Tottenham); jobs, housing, green space, transport, education (UCL East); gentrification, displacement, affordability, low-paid jobs; judgement on how far and for whom.
questions.tip: Use 'how far' language: 'to a large extent for... but less for...'.

questions.q: 'The challenges of urban change in London are greater than the opportunities.' To what extent do you agree? [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: Model Level 3 outline: Opportunities: global financial hub with high-paid jobs; cultural mix from migration (Notting Hill Carnival); regeneration schemes such as Stratford and King's Cross; Elizabeth line and ULEZ improving transport and air. Challenges: housing affordability and overcrowding; deprivation in boroughs such as Newham and Tower Hamlets; air pollution; urban sprawl pressure on the green belt; waste and sewage (Tideway Tunnel needed). Weigh: many challenges are being managed, but inequality persists and is linked to the very growth that creates opportunity. Judgement: e.g. 'I largely disagree: opportunities are greater overall, but they are unevenly shared, so for deprived groups challenges dominate.'
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): thorough knowledge and understanding; detailed, accurate place-specific evidence (named places, dates, figures) used to support points; both sides weighed; a clear, well-substantiated judgement that answers the question directly.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): reasonable knowledge with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is asserted rather than supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): limited, generic knowledge; little evidence; descriptive with no clear judgement.

Indicative content: social, economic and environmental opportunities and challenges with London-specific detail (Stratford, King's Cross, Elizabeth line 2022, ULEZ 2019/2023, Tideway, green belt, brownfield, deprivation in named boroughs, housing costs, migration); clear judgement; acknowledges different groups and timescales.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate; grammar controls meaning; wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy; good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy; limited range of specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant content or errors seriously hinder meaning.
questions.tip: Weigh by group and timescale to reach Level 3; avoid two lists with a one-line conclusion.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of grey water recycling?
options: Collecting rain from roofs in a butt
Reusing water from showers and sinks to flush toilets
ms: Grey water is used household water (not from toilets) reused for non-drinking purposes.
questions.tip: Rainwater harvesting and grey water recycling are different methods.

questions.q: Which feature of BedZED reduces the need for heating?
options: Homes face north to avoid sunlight
South-facing glass and thick insulation capture and keep solar heat
Each house has a large gas boiler
ms: BedZED uses passive solar design: south-facing sunspaces and heavy insulation.
questions.tip: Know HOW each feature reduces resource use, not just the list.

questions.q: A city's household waste was 120,000 tonnes, of which 30,000 tonnes were recycled. Five years later waste was 110,000 tonnes with 41,800 tonnes recycled. What was the new recycling rate?
questions.tip: Divide by the new total, not the old total.

questions.q: A city's household waste was 120,000 tonnes, of which 30,000 tonnes were recycled. Five years later waste was 110,000 tonnes, with 41,800 tonnes recycled. By what percentage did the amount of waste NOT recycled fall?
questions.tip: Multi-step data questions: work out the new variable first, then the percentage change.

questions.q: Give two ways a city can conserve energy.
questions.answer: Insulating buildings; fitting solar panels on roofs.
ms: One valid method (1 mark).
A second, different method, e.g. LED street lighting, smart meters, district heating, energy-efficient appliances (1 mark).
questions.tip: Two different methods, not two examples of insulation.

questions.q: State two benefits of a city having integrated transport.
questions.answer: Journeys are quicker and easier because people can switch between bus, rail and bike with one ticket. Fewer people drive, so congestion and air pollution fall.
ms: One benefit (1 mark).
Second benefit (1 mark): e.g. less congestion, cleaner air, cheaper travel, better access to jobs.
questions.tip: Integrated means linked: mention ticketing or interchanges.

questions.q: Explain how sustainable urban drainage systems (SuDS) can reduce flood risk in cities.
questions.answer: SuDS use permeable paving, green roofs and swales so rainwater soaks in or is stored instead of running straight into drains. This slows the movement of water and increases lag time, so sewers and rivers are less likely to overflow during heavy rain. Ponds and rain gardens also store water and filter out pollutants, improving water quality and creating habitats.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: permeable surfaces increase infiltration; green roofs intercept and store rain; swales and ponds store water; reduced surface runoff; longer lag time and lower peak discharge; fewer combined sewer overflows; water quality and biodiversity benefits.
questions.tip: Link to the hydrograph terms: lag time and peak discharge.

questions.q: Suggest why sustainable housing schemes such as BedZED have not been built widely across the UK.
questions.answer: They cost more to build than ordinary housing because of the special materials, insulation and renewable systems, so developers make less profit. Some technologies at BedZED, such as the original biomass heating system, did not work as planned, which put off investors. Planning rules and land prices in cities also make large eco-developments difficult, and many people are not willing to pay more for green features.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: higher build costs; developers' profit; technical problems (BedZED's wood-chip combined heat and power plant was switched off); land costs; planning; lack of demand or awareness; retrofitting existing homes is harder.
questions.tip: 'Suggest' rewards realistic, reasoned ideas: costs, technical problems and demand.

questions.q: Explain why traffic congestion is harder to manage in LIC and NEE cities than in HIC cities.
questions.answer: Many LIC and NEE cities grew rapidly without planning, so roads are narrow and public transport networks are limited. Car ownership is rising quickly as incomes grow, and governments have less money to build metro or BRT systems. Large informal settlements on the edge mean long journeys to work, and enforcement of traffic rules can be weak, so congestion and pollution build up quickly.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: rapid unplanned growth; limited public transport; rising car ownership; lack of funds; long commutes from peripheral settlements; weak enforcement; contrasts with HIC schemes like London's congestion charge and Tube.
questions.tip: Comparison questions need comparative words: 'whereas', 'than'.

questions.q: A council wants to make a city more sustainable. Assess whether improving public transport or creating more green space would be more effective.
questions.answer: Public transport: reduces car use, congestion and emissions; improves access to jobs for low-income residents; e.g. London's Elizabeth line. But expensive and slow to build. Green space: reduces flood risk, cools the urban heat island, improves health and biodiversity, cheaper and quicker. But does not tackle transport emissions directly. Judgement: e.g. public transport is more effective because transport is a major source of urban emissions, but green space gives wider social and environmental benefits at lower cost, so both are needed.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, well-developed points with accurate place-specific evidence; balanced discussion; clear, supported judgement where the command word asks for one.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points and some specific evidence; may be unbalanced or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little evidence or development; no judgement.

Indicative content: public transport: emissions, congestion, accessibility, cost; green space: flooding, heat island, wellbeing, biodiversity, air quality; examples (London National Park City, Santander Cycles, Elizabeth line); a supported judgement.
questions.tip: Decide, then justify why the other option is weaker: that is the Level 3 move.

questions.q: 'Making cities sustainable is more important for LICs and NEEs than for HICs.' Evaluate this statement. [9 marks]
questions.answer: Model Level 3 outline: For: LIC/NEE cities are growing fastest, so planning now prevents slums, pollution and congestion becoming locked in; many residents lack clean water and sanitation; air pollution and waste are often severe (e.g. Rio). Against: HIC city dwellers consume far more resources and produce higher emissions per person; HICs have the money and technology to lead (BedZED, ULEZ); global climate change needs HIC cuts. Judgement: both matter, but for different reasons; LICs need sustainability to meet basic needs, HICs to cut consumption, so the statement is only partly true.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): thorough knowledge and understanding; detailed, accurate place-specific evidence (named places, dates, figures) used to support points; both sides weighed; a clear, well-substantiated judgement that answers the question directly.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): reasonable knowledge with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is asserted rather than supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): limited, generic knowledge; little evidence; descriptive with no clear judgement.
Indicative content: rate of growth; basic needs; per capita consumption and emissions; resources and technology; examples from Rio and London; global responsibility; supported judgement.
questions.tip: A 9-mark answer without SPaG still needs a clear, supported conclusion.

questions.q: Which measure of development is an ECONOMIC indicator?
ms: GNI per head measures income; the others are social indicators.
questions.tip: Classify indicators as economic or social: it is often asked.

questions.q: In which DTM stage is the death rate low but the birth rate still falling?
ms: In stage 3 death rates are already low and birth rates fall, so growth slows.
questions.tip: Stage 2: death rate falls. Stage 3: birth rate falls.

questions.q: Country X: birth rate 38 per 1,000, death rate 8 per 1,000, life expectancy 61. Country Y: birth rate 11, death rate 9, life expectancy 81. Which statement is correct?
options: Both have the same natural increase
X has a natural increase of 0.2%, Y of 3.0%
X has a natural increase of 3.0%, Y of 0.2%
questions.tip: Per 1,000 to per cent: divide by 10.

questions.q: Why might the HDI of a country rise even if its GNI per head stays the same?
options: Improvements in life expectancy and years of schooling raise HDI
ms: HDI combines health, education and income, so gains in health or education raise it independently of income.
questions.tip: Know the three HDI components and that each can change separately.

questions.q: Which is the best reason infant mortality rate is a useful single indicator of development?
options: It is the same in every country
It reflects healthcare, clean water, sanitation and the mother's education
ms: Infant mortality is sensitive to many aspects of development, especially healthcare and sanitation.
questions.tip: Explain WHY an indicator is useful, linking to the factors it reflects.

questions.q: Describe how the death rate changes from Stage 1 to Stage 3 of the Demographic Transition Model.
questions.answer: In Stage 1 the death rate is high and fluctuates. In Stage 2 it falls rapidly, and by Stage 3 it continues to fall more slowly and becomes low.
ms: High / fluctuating in Stage 1 (1 mark).
Falls rapidly in Stage 2 and is low by Stage 3 (1 mark).
questions.tip: Describe the change stage by stage, using comparative words.

questions.q: Give the formula for natural increase as a percentage.
questions.answer: (Birth rate - death rate) ÷ 10.
ms: (Birth rate - death rate) ÷ 10, with rates per 1,000 (1 mark).
questions.tip: Remember it ignores migration.

questions.q: Figure 1 shows: Country A GNI per head US$1,200, life expectancy 64; Country B GNI per head US$9,400, life expectancy 76; Country C GNI per head US$45,000, life expectancy 82. Describe the relationship shown and suggest one reason for it.
questions.answer: There is a positive relationship: as GNI per head increases, life expectancy increases (from 64 in A to 82 in C). Richer countries can spend more on healthcare, clean water and sanitation, so people live longer. However the increase in life expectancy is smaller at higher incomes.
ms: Positive relationship identified (1 mark).
Use of data from the figure (1 mark).
Valid reason, e.g. more spending on healthcare, diet, sanitation (1 mark).
questions.tip: Quote figures from the resource in 'describe' questions.

questions.q: Explain how a population pyramid for an LIC differs from one for an HIC.
questions.answer: An LIC pyramid has a wide base because of high birth rates, and it narrows quickly with age because of high death rates and lower life expectancy, giving a triangular shape. An HIC pyramid has a narrower base because of low birth rates and straighter sides with a wider top because people live longer, so there is a large elderly dependent population.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: LIC: wide base, high birth rate, concave sides, few elderly, young dependents; HIC: narrow base, straight sides, wide top, ageing population, elderly dependents; link to DTM stages.
questions.tip: Explain the shape using birth rate, death rate and life expectancy.

questions.q: Explain why a combined measure such as HDI is more useful than GNI per head for comparing development.
questions.answer: GNI per head only measures average income, and it can be high in a country where wealth is held by a small elite. HDI combines life expectancy, education and income, so it shows how far wealth has been turned into better health and schooling. This gives a more rounded picture of quality of life, although it still hides inequality within a country.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: GNI per head: income only, averages hide inequality, ignores informal economy and quality of life; HDI: health, education and income combined, more rounded; limitations of HDI too.
questions.tip: A grade 9 touch is noting that HDI also has limitations.

questions.q: Explain why the DTM may not accurately predict the future population of some LICs.
questions.answer: The DTM was based on the experience of European countries, where industrialisation drove change. Some LICs may not follow it, because cultural or religious factors keep birth rates high even as death rates fall. Diseases such as HIV/AIDS or conflict can push death rates up again, and migration is not included in the model, so it can mislead.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: Eurocentric model; cultural and religious factors; government policy (e.g. China's one-child policy); disease and conflict; migration ignored; time scale may be faster or slower.
questions.tip: Criticising a model is a level 3 skill: give a reason the assumption may not hold.

questions.q: Country P has GNI per head US$15,000, HDI 0.75 and literacy 94%. Country Q has GNI per head US$8,000, HDI 0.80 and literacy 98%. Assess which country is more developed.
questions.answer: P has a higher GNI per head, so on income alone it appears more developed. However Q has a higher HDI and literacy rate, which suggests it has turned its income into better health and education. P's wealth may be concentrated, for example from oil exports, so its average hides inequality. Judgement: Q is more developed in terms of quality of life, because HDI is a composite measure, though more data, such as inequality or infant mortality, would help confirm this.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, well-developed points with accurate place-specific evidence; balanced discussion; clear, supported judgement where the command word asks for one.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points and some specific evidence; may be unbalanced or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little evidence or development; no judgement.
Indicative content: use of all data; GNI vs HDI vs literacy; reasons income may not reflect quality of life; inequality; need for more indicators; supported judgement.
questions.tip: Always use the data given and reach a clear decision.

questions.q: Money sent home by migrants working abroad is called:
ms: Remittances are private transfers from migrants to families in their home country.
questions.tip: Remittances are a consequence of uneven development and can help reduce it.

questions.q: Which is the best example of 'tourism leakage'?
options: Profits from a foreign-owned all-inclusive hotel go to its overseas headquarters
A government taxes tourists at the airport
A tourist buys crafts from a local market
A local guide is paid in cash
ms: Leakage is when tourist spending leaves the host country, e.g. foreign-owned resorts and imported food.
questions.tip: Leakage limits how much tourism reduces the development gap.

questions.q: Why can landlocked countries find it harder to develop?
options: They depend on neighbours' ports and roads, raising the cost of trade
They always have more natural hazards
ms: Landlocked countries pay more to move goods through other countries to reach the sea.
questions.tip: Physical causes must be linked to an economic effect.

questions.q: A country spends 20% of its export income repaying debt. Which outcome of debt relief is most likely?
options: More money could be spent on health and education
The country would become an HIC immediately
ms: Debt relief frees government revenue for services and infrastructure, though conditions may apply.
questions.tip: Explain the opportunity cost of debt repayment.

questions.q: Give two ways that intermediate technology can help people in LICs.
questions.answer: It is cheap and uses local materials, so communities can afford it. Local people can maintain it themselves, so it lasts and does not need outside experts.
ms: One way (1 mark).
Second different way (1 mark), e.g. improves water supply (sand dams), raises crop yields, creates local jobs, sustainable.
questions.tip: Focus on why it suits poorer communities.

questions.q: Define 'bilateral aid'.
questions.answer: Aid given directly from one government to another.
ms: Aid from one country's government to another country (1 mark). Do not accept 'aid from an NGO'.
questions.tip: Multilateral aid goes through organisations such as the World Bank.

questions.q: Explain how uneven development leads to international migration.
questions.answer: Large differences in wages and job opportunities between LICs and HICs act as push and pull factors, so people move to earn more. Conflict and poor services in poorer countries can force people to leave as refugees. Migrants often send remittances home, which can help their families, but the loss of skilled workers is a brain drain that can slow development further.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: wage and job gaps; push and pull factors; economic migrants and refugees; remittances; brain drain; impacts on host and source countries.
questions.tip: Explain the chain: gap leads to migration, which then affects both countries.

questions.q: Figure 2 shows a country's international tourist arrivals rose from 1.8 million in 2005 to 3.7 million in 2019. Calculate the percentage increase and suggest one reason why this growth might not reduce the development gap.
questions.answer: (3.7 - 1.8) ÷ 1.8 × 100 = 105.6%. Much of the money may be lost through leakage to foreign-owned hotels and airlines.
ms: Method (1 mark).
Valid reason: leakage, seasonal or low-paid jobs, vulnerable to hazards or recessions, benefits concentrated in resort areas (1 mark).
questions.tip: Do the maths, then link to a limitation.

questions.q: Explain why trading mainly in primary products can increase the development gap.
questions.answer: Primary products such as coffee or cocoa have low value and their prices change a lot on world markets, so income is unpredictable. HICs process the products and sell them at a much higher price, so most of the profit goes to HIC companies. Trade barriers and tariffs on processed goods can make it hard for poorer countries to add value, so they stay dependent.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: low and volatile prices; value added elsewhere; tariffs and trade barriers; dependence on one export; little investment in manufacturing; contrast with HIC exports.
questions.tip: Use the phrase 'adding value' and explain why it matters.

questions.q: Explain why aid can sometimes fail to reduce the development gap.
questions.answer: Some aid is tied, so the receiving country must spend it on goods from the donor, which benefits the donor's economy. Corruption can mean money does not reach the poorest people. Large top-down projects may not suit local needs or may not be maintained, and long-term dependence on aid can reduce the incentive to develop local industries.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: tied aid; corruption; top-down projects not suited to local needs; maintenance problems; dependency; short-term emergency aid does not address causes; conditions attached to loans.
questions.tip: Name different types of aid and their specific weaknesses.

questions.q: Assess the extent to which fair trade can reduce the development gap.
questions.answer: Fair trade guarantees farmers a minimum price, so they have more stable incomes, and the social premium funds schools, wells and clinics, improving quality of life. However only a small share of global trade is fair trade, and farmers may pay to be certified, so many of the poorest cannot join. It does little to change the structure of trade in primary products. Overall it improves life for participating communities but has only a limited effect on the global gap.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, well-developed points with accurate place-specific evidence; balanced discussion; clear, supported judgement where the command word asks for one.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points and some specific evidence; may be unbalanced or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little evidence or development; no judgement.

Indicative content: minimum price; social premium; community projects; empowerment; small share of world trade; certification costs; still primary products; consumers pay more; scale vs depth of impact; judgement.
questions.tip: Judge the scale of impact: local depth versus global breadth.

questions.q: 'Top-down strategies are more effective than bottom-up strategies in reducing the development gap.' Evaluate this statement. [9 marks]
questions.answer: Model Level 3 outline: Define top-down (large-scale, government or TNC-led: dams, industrial investment, debt relief) and bottom-up (community-led: intermediate technology, microfinance, fair trade). Top-down: large scale, infrastructure and jobs, e.g. TNC investment in Brazil; but may displace people, profits leave, benefits uneven. Bottom-up: cheap, sustainable, meets local needs; but small scale and slow. Judgement: bottom-up strategies are more effective for the poorest, top-down for national growth; the most effective approach combines both.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): thorough knowledge and understanding; detailed, accurate place-specific evidence (named places, dates, figures) used to support points; both sides weighed; a clear, well-substantiated judgement that answers the question directly.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): reasonable knowledge with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is asserted rather than supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): limited, generic knowledge; little evidence; descriptive with no clear judgement.
Indicative content: definitions; named examples; scale, cost, sustainability, who benefits, speed; supported judgement.
questions.tip: Define the terms at the start: it shows the examiner you understand the debate.

questions.q: Which trade group links Brazil with Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay?
ms: Mercosur is the South American trade bloc founded in 1991.
questions.tip: Know Brazil's two key groupings: Mercosur and BRICS.

questions.q: In 2019 a mining waste dam owned by Vale collapsed in Brazil, killing around 270 people. Where did it happen?
ms: The Brumadinho collapse (2019) followed the Mariana disaster (2015).
questions.tip: Two disasters, four years apart: do not mix them up.

questions.q: Fiat's car plant at Betim is located in which Brazilian state?
ms: Fiat's Betim plant is in Minas Gerais, near Belo Horizonte.
questions.tip: Case study precision is what earns Level 3.

questions.q: Brazil's exports of soybeans and iron ore to China grew rapidly in the 2000s. Which is the biggest risk of this pattern for Brazil?
options: It makes Brazil's economy dependent on primary product prices and Chinese demand
It reduces the size of the Amazon
ms: Reliance on primary exports to one buyer leaves the economy exposed to falling commodity prices, as in the 2014-16 recession.
questions.tip: Link changing trade to economic vulnerability.

questions.q: Give two examples of how Brazil is linked to the wider world.
questions.answer: Brazil is a member of BRICS. China is its largest trading partner.
ms: One link (1 mark).
