A second link (1 mark): e.g. Mercosur, hosting the 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympics, TNC investment, exports of soya and iron ore.
questions.tip: Give named groups, partners or events.

questions.q: Name one foreign TNC and one Brazilian TNC operating in Brazil.
questions.answer: Foreign: Fiat. Brazilian: Vale.
ms: Foreign TNC, e.g. Fiat, Ford, Nestlé, Volkswagen (1 mark).
Brazilian TNC, e.g. Vale, Petrobras, Embraer, JBS (1 mark).
questions.tip: Embraer is Brazilian; Fiat is Italian.

questions.q: Explain how manufacturing industry can stimulate economic development in Brazil.
questions.answer: Factories such as Fiat's plant at Betim create direct jobs, and the workers spend their wages locally, creating more jobs in shops and services: the multiplier effect. Component suppliers set up nearby, and the government gains tax revenue to spend on schools and roads. Manufactured goods are worth more than raw materials, so exports earn more.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: direct and indirect jobs; multiplier effect; suppliers and clustering; skills and training; tax revenue; infrastructure; higher-value exports; named example.
questions.tip: Use the multiplier effect as a chain, not a buzzword.

questions.q: Explain why development in Brazil has been uneven between regions.
questions.answer: The south east, including São Paulo and Rio, has ports, industry and investment from TNCs, so it has more jobs and higher incomes. The north east has a drier climate with frequent droughts, poorer infrastructure and a history of plantation farming, so fewer firms invest there. The north is dominated by the Amazon rainforest, which is remote and sparsely populated, so services are harder to provide.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: south east core: ports, industry, investment, finance; north east: drought, history, less investment, out-migration; north: Amazon, remoteness; cumulative causation; Bolsa Família targeting poorer regions.
questions.tip: Explain the reason for each region, not just describe the difference.

questions.q: Explain the role of international aid in Brazil's development.
questions.answer: Brazil has received loans from the World Bank to fund projects such as improving sanitation and protecting the Amazon, which improve health and the environment. Funds such as the Amazon Fund, supported by Norway and Germany, pay for projects to reduce deforestation. Aid has also helped fund education and poverty reduction, but as an NEE Brazil now relies mainly on its own economy, and it also gives aid to other countries.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: World Bank loans for infrastructure and social projects; Amazon Fund (Norway, Germany); environmental and health benefits; aid as small share of the economy; Brazil as a donor.
questions.tip: Note that aid in an NEE is relatively small compared with trade and investment.

questions.q: Explain how the Bolsa Família programme aimed to break the cycle of poverty in Brazil.
questions.answer: Poor families received monthly cash payments, so they could afford food and basic needs immediately. Payments were conditional on children attending school and having vaccinations and health checks, so the next generation became healthier and better educated. This means they are more likely to get better-paid jobs in the future, breaking the cycle of poverty rather than just relieving it.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: cash transfers to poor families; conditions on school attendance and health checks; short-term relief plus long-term human capital; paid mainly to mothers; criticisms: dependency, fraud, does not create jobs.
questions.tip: Explain short-term and long-term effects separately.

questions.q: Assess the effects of Brazil's changing relationship with China.
questions.answer: China became Brazil's largest trading partner in 2009, buying huge amounts of soybeans, iron ore and oil, which boosted export earnings and growth in the 2000s. Chinese investment has funded infrastructure and energy projects. However this has increased Brazil's dependence on primary exports, so when Chinese demand and commodity prices fell, Brazil's economy suffered, contributing to the 2014-16 recession. Soya expansion has also driven deforestation. Overall the relationship has brought growth but made the economy more vulnerable.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, well-developed points with accurate place-specific evidence; balanced discussion; clear, supported judgement where the command word asks for one.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points and some specific evidence; may be unbalanced or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little evidence or development; no judgement.

Indicative content: export growth; soybeans and iron ore; Chinese investment; BRICS; dependency on primary products; commodity price falls and recession; environmental impact (soya, deforestation); judgement.
questions.tip: Assess: weigh benefits against risks and reach a conclusion.

questions.q: 'TNCs have brought more advantages than disadvantages to Brazil.' Do you agree? [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: Model Level 3 outline: Advantages: jobs (e.g. Fiat in Betim), skills, technology transfer, multiplier effect with local suppliers, tax revenue; Brazilian TNCs such as Vale and Petrobras earn export income and invest abroad. Disadvantages: profits leave Brazil for foreign TNCs; wages can be low; environmental disasters such as the Mariana (2015) and Brumadinho (2019) dam collapses linked to Vale; deforestation by agribusiness; TNCs can relocate. Judgement: e.g. 'I agree to a large extent: TNCs drove industrialisation and growth, but weak regulation meant serious environmental and social costs, so the balance depends on how well they are controlled.'
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): thorough knowledge and understanding; detailed, accurate place-specific evidence (named places, dates, figures) used to support points; both sides weighed; a clear, well-substantiated judgement that answers the question directly.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): reasonable knowledge with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is asserted rather than supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): limited, generic knowledge; little evidence; descriptive with no clear judgement.
Indicative content: named foreign and Brazilian TNCs; economic, social and environmental advantages and disadvantages; Mariana and Brumadinho; profits repatriated; regulation; judgement.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate; grammar controls meaning; wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy; good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy; limited range of specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant content or errors seriously hinder meaning.
questions.tip: Use both foreign and Brazilian TNCs: it shows depth.

questions.q: Which sector of industry includes research and development and IT consultancy?
ms: The quaternary sector is knowledge-based: R&D, IT, consultancy.
questions.tip: Tertiary = services; quaternary = knowledge and research.

questions.q: The Northern Powerhouse is:
options: A wind farm in the North Sea
A government strategy to boost economic growth in northern England
A nuclear power station in Cumbria
ms: It was launched in 2014 to rebalance the UK economy towards northern cities.
questions.tip: Strategies to reduce the north-south divide: know at least two by name.

questions.q: Which change in UK employment since 1970 is correct?
options: Tertiary and quaternary employment have grown while manufacturing has declined
ms: Deindustrialisation cut manufacturing jobs; services and knowledge jobs grew.
questions.tip: Describe trends with direction and scale.

questions.q: A rural area's population fell from 26,500 to 25,100 while the share aged over 65 rose. What is the percentage change in population?
questions.tip: Show a fall with a minus sign and divide by the original value.

questions.q: Give two features of a science park.
questions.answer: Clusters of high-tech and research firms. Located near a university for research links and skilled graduates.
ms: One feature (1 mark).
Second feature (1 mark): near university, good road access, landscaped, high-tech or quaternary firms, attractive environment.
questions.tip: Science park = research-led; business park = offices and services.

questions.q: Name one UK government strategy to reduce the north-south divide.
questions.answer: The Northern Powerhouse.
ms: Northern Powerhouse / Enterprise Zones / devolution to city regions / relocating organisations such as BBC to MediaCityUK in Salford (1 mark).
questions.tip: Specific names score; 'government help' does not.

questions.q: Explain why the UK's economy has become post-industrial.
questions.answer: Manufacturing declined because it became cheaper to make goods in countries such as China, where labour costs are lower, and because older industries such as coal mining became uneconomic. At the same time, globalisation and improvements in ICT allowed the UK to specialise in finance, services and research, which add high value. Government policy, including privatisation in the 1980s, also favoured services over heavy industry.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: deindustrialisation; global competition and cheaper labour abroad; mechanisation; ICT and globalisation; growth of finance, services, creative and quaternary industries; government policy (1980s privatisation, closing mines).
questions.tip: Use the three causes the spec names: deindustrialisation, globalisation, policy.

questions.q: Explain the advantages of the UK's major port developments, such as London Gateway.
questions.answer: London Gateway is a deep-water port, so the largest container ships can dock, bringing more trade to the UK. It is close to London and linked to motorways and rail, so goods can be moved quickly to the biggest market. It creates jobs in logistics and attracts warehouses and distribution firms, adding to the multiplier effect.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: deep water for large ships; location near London and Europe; road and rail links; logistics park; jobs; trade capacity; reduced costs; multiplier effect.
questions.tip: Tie each advantage to a feature of the port's location or design.

questions.q: Explain the social and economic effects of population decline in a remote rural area such as the Outer Hebrides.
questions.answer: Young people move away for jobs and higher education, so the population ages and fewer children are born. School rolls fall and some schools, shops and bus services close because there are not enough users. Fewer workers means businesses struggle to recruit, which reduces the local economy, so even more people leave in a downward spiral.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: out-migration of young people; ageing; service closures (schools, shops, transport, health); skills shortages; declining economy; isolation; tourism and second homes.
questions.tip: Show a cycle of decline: one change causes the next.

questions.q: Explain how the development of HS2 might affect regional economies in the UK.
questions.answer: Faster links between London and Birmingham could attract businesses to the West Midlands, because they can reach London quickly but have lower costs. Construction creates jobs and new stations may lead to regeneration, such as around Curzon Street in Birmingham. However cancelling the northern leg to Manchester means northern cities will see fewer benefits, and better links could pull more economic activity towards London, widening the divide.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: faster journeys and capacity; investment and regeneration near stations; construction jobs; cancelled northern leg; risk of London drawing activity ('two-way road'); costs and environmental impacts.
questions.tip: A grade 9 answer notes that better links can strengthen the core as well as the periphery.

questions.q: Assess whether the UK's links with the wider world have strengthened or weakened since 2016.
questions.answer: Leaving the EU (formally in 2020) created new trade barriers, such as customs checks, which reduced some trade with the EU and added costs to businesses. However the UK has signed new trade deals and joined the CPTPP trade bloc, and remains strongly linked through finance, culture (the English language, media, music) and electronic communications via submarine cables. London remains a global financial centre. Overall links with the EU weakened, but global links remain strong, so the overall picture is mixed.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, well-developed points with accurate place-specific evidence; balanced discussion; clear, supported judgement where the command word asks for one.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points and some specific evidence; may be unbalanced or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little evidence or development; no judgement.
Indicative content: Brexit and trade frictions; new trade deals; CPTPP; Commonwealth; finance and London's global role; culture and media; transport hubs; submarine cables; judgement.
questions.tip: Weigh different types of link: trade, culture, transport, communications.

questions.q: Evaluate the extent to which modern industrial developments in the UK can be environmentally sustainable. [9 marks]
questions.answer: Model Level 3 outline: For: Torr Quarry uses rail to move stone and has restored land for wildlife; science parks are often landscaped with energy-efficient buildings; offshore wind industry (e.g. Hull's turbine factory) supports low-carbon energy. Against: quarrying still removes landscape and causes dust; business parks on greenfield sites encourage car use; manufacturing still uses energy and produces waste. Judgement: developments can be more sustainable than in the past, but rarely fully sustainable, as most still harm the environment in some way.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): thorough knowledge and understanding; detailed, accurate place-specific evidence (named places, dates, figures) used to support points; both sides weighed; a clear, well-substantiated judgement that answers the question directly.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): reasonable knowledge with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is asserted rather than supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): limited, generic knowledge; little evidence; descriptive with no clear judgement.

Indicative content: Torr Quarry: rail freight, landscaping, restoration plans (lake and nature reserve); green design, renewables; greenfield vs brownfield; transport emissions; judgement on 'extent'.
questions.tip: 'To what extent' needs a qualified answer: 'more sustainable, but not fully'.

questions.q: Which source supplies the largest share of the UK's renewable electricity?
ms: Wind, especially offshore wind, is the UK's largest renewable electricity source.
questions.tip: The UK has some of the world's largest offshore wind farms.

questions.q: Why does the UK import much of its food?
options: The UK cannot grow any crops
Imports always have fewer food miles
Demand for out-of-season and exotic foods and cheaper imports
ms: The UK climate cannot grow tropical crops or summer produce in winter, and imports are often cheaper.
questions.tip: Do not claim the UK grows nothing: it produces about 60% of the food it consumes.

questions.q: Which is a cause of water pollution in UK rivers?
options: Fertiliser runoff from farms leading to eutrophication
ms: Excess nitrates and phosphates feed algae, reducing oxygen in rivers.
questions.tip: Know the eutrophication chain: fertiliser, algae, less oxygen, fish die.

questions.q: A household of four uses 140 litres per person per day. Fitting a water-efficient system cuts use by 15%. How many litres per year would the household save?
ms: Annual use = 140 × 4 × 365 = 204,400 litres; 15% = 30,660 litres saved.
questions.tip: Find the total first, then the percentage.

questions.q: Give two reasons why demand for water in the UK is increasing.
questions.answer: Population growth, especially in the south east. People own more water-using appliances such as dishwashers and power showers.
ms: One reason (1 mark).
Second reason (1 mark): population growth, more households, appliances, lifestyle, industry and farming demand.
questions.tip: Population growth AND rising use per person.

questions.q: State two advantages of nuclear power for the UK.
questions.answer: It produces very low carbon emissions. It provides a reliable, constant supply of electricity unlike wind.
ms: One advantage (1 mark).
Second (1 mark): low carbon, reliable baseload, high output from small area, energy security, jobs.
questions.tip: Contrast with intermittent renewables to show understanding.

questions.q: Explain why water transfer schemes are controversial.
questions.answer: Transfers move water from areas of surplus, such as Wales or northern England, to areas of deficit in the south east, which helps meet demand. However they are expensive to build and maintain, and building reservoirs floods valleys, destroying farmland, homes and habitats. Moving water between river basins can affect wildlife and water temperature, and people in the source area may feel their resources are being taken.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: cost; flooding land for reservoirs; habitats; displacement; ecological impacts of transferring water between catchments; political issues (e.g. Wales); energy for pumping; alternatives such as reducing demand and fixing leaks.
questions.tip: Give both sides: why they are needed and why they are opposed.

questions.q: Explain why the UK's reliance on gas creates challenges for energy security.
questions.answer: North Sea gas production has declined, so the UK imports more gas through pipelines from Norway and as liquefied natural gas by ship. This means supply and prices depend on world markets, as shown when prices rose sharply after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Gas is also a fossil fuel, so relying on it makes it harder to meet net zero targets.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: declining North Sea output; imports from Norway and LNG; price volatility (2022 energy crisis); geopolitical risk; carbon emissions and net zero; need for storage.
questions.tip: Energy security means a reliable, affordable supply: link to that definition.

questions.q: Explain the economic and environmental issues of building new offshore wind farms in the UK.
questions.answer: Economically, offshore wind needs high upfront costs, but once built it has low running costs and creates jobs in ports such as Hull, where turbine blades are made. It also reduces the need to import gas. Environmentally it produces no carbon emissions while running, but construction can disturb seabed habitats and turbines can harm seabirds. Supply is intermittent, so backup or storage is needed.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: high capital cost, cheap running costs, falling price over time, jobs and supply chain (Hull), energy security; low carbon; seabed disturbance, birds, visual impact (less offshore), intermittency.
questions.tip: Keep economic and environmental points separate, as the question asks for both.

questions.q: Assess the benefits and costs of Hinkley Point C for the UK's energy future.
questions.answer: Benefits: when complete it will supply about 7% of UK electricity, providing low-carbon, reliable baseload power that supports net zero and reduces gas imports. It has created thousands of construction jobs in Somerset. Costs: it is far over budget and delayed, and electricity has a guaranteed high price for 35 years, so consumers will pay more. Nuclear waste remains dangerous for thousands of years, and building affects local habitats. Judgement: it improves energy security but at a very high price.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, well-developed points with accurate place-specific evidence; balanced discussion; clear, supported judgement where the command word asks for one.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points and some specific evidence; may be unbalanced or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little evidence or development; no judgement.

Indicative content: about 7% of UK electricity; low carbon; baseload; energy security; jobs; cost overruns and delays; strike price guaranteed for 35 years; nuclear waste; local environment; judgement.
questions.tip: Use specific figures where you are confident of them; avoid inventing costs.

questions.q: 'The UK should focus on reducing demand rather than increasing supply to manage its resources.' Evaluate this statement with reference to water and energy. [9 marks]
questions.answer: Model Level 3 outline: Reducing demand: water meters, fixing leaks, efficient appliances, insulation and smart meters; cheaper, quicker, more sustainable, reduces emissions. Limits: relies on behaviour change, population still growing. Increasing supply: reservoirs, transfers, desalination, new nuclear and wind; needed for growing demand and electrification of transport and heating, but costly and has environmental impacts. Judgement: reducing demand should come first because it is cheaper and more sustainable, but some new supply is unavoidable.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): thorough knowledge and understanding; detailed, accurate place-specific evidence (named places, dates, figures) used to support points; both sides weighed; a clear, well-substantiated judgement that answers the question directly.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): reasonable knowledge with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is asserted rather than supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): limited, generic knowledge; little evidence; descriptive with no clear judgement.
Indicative content: water: leakage, meters, transfers, reservoirs; energy: efficiency, insulation, renewables, nuclear, gas; costs, sustainability, timescales; judgement.
questions.tip: Cover both resources named in the question or you cap your level.

questions.q: What is meant by 'food supply'?
options: The amount of food a person eats
The amount of food available to a population
ms: Food supply is the food available for consumption, often measured in calories per person per day.
questions.tip: Supply is what is available; consumption is what is eaten.

questions.q: Drip irrigation increases food supply sustainably because it:
options: Delivers small amounts of water directly to plant roots, reducing waste
ms: Water goes straight to the roots, reducing evaporation and saving water.
questions.tip: Explain the mechanism that makes a technique sustainable.

questions.q: A farm used 6,500 m³ of water per hectare with flood irrigation and 3,900 m³ with drip irrigation. What is the percentage saving?
questions.tip: Divide by the original (flood) value.

questions.q: Give two reasons why global demand for food is increasing.
questions.answer: The world's population is growing. Rising incomes in NEEs such as China mean people eat more meat and dairy.
ms: Population growth (1 mark).
Economic development / rising incomes / change to meat-rich diets (1 mark).
questions.tip: Two distinct factors: number of people and what they eat.

questions.q: State two physical factors that can reduce food supply.
questions.answer: Drought or low rainfall. Pests and diseases that destroy crops.
ms: One physical factor (1 mark).
Second (1 mark): climate, drought, floods, pests and disease, poor soils, water stress.
questions.tip: Physical = natural; conflict and poverty are human factors.

questions.q: Explain how conflict can cause food insecurity.
questions.answer: Fighting can destroy crops, farms and irrigation systems, and farmers may flee, so less food is produced. Roads and markets are disrupted, so food cannot be transported and prices rise. Governments may spend money on war rather than farming, and aid agencies may not be able to reach people safely, which can lead to famine.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: destroyed crops and infrastructure; displaced farmers; disrupted transport and markets; rising prices; blockades; aid blocked; long-term damage (landmines); example such as Yemen or Sudan.
questions.tip: Link each impact of conflict to production, access or price of food.

questions.q: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of using GM crops to increase food supply.
questions.answer: GM crops can be made resistant to pests or drought, so yields increase and less pesticide is needed. Some are made more nutritious, such as golden rice with vitamin A. However seeds can be expensive and often need to be bought each year, which makes farmers dependent on large companies. There are concerns about cross-pollination with wild plants and reduced biodiversity.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: higher yields; drought and pest resistance; nutrition; less pesticide; cost of seed and dependence on TNCs; cross-pollination and biodiversity; consumer concerns; GM rules vary by country.
questions.tip: Balanced points are needed for top marks on advantage-and-disadvantage questions.

questions.q: Explain how undernutrition can affect a country's development.
questions.answer: Undernourished people have less energy and are more likely to get ill, so they can work less and earn less. Children who are undernourished may suffer stunting and do worse at school, which reduces skills in the future workforce. More people needing healthcare puts pressure on government spending, so less is available for development.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: less productivity; illness and disease; stunting; lower educational achievement; healthcare costs; cycle of poverty; reduced economic growth.
questions.tip: Show a cycle: hunger leads to low productivity which leads to poverty.

questions.q: Using an example, explain how a local scheme in an LIC or NEE can increase food supply sustainably.
questions.answer: In Bangladesh, floating gardens made from water hyacinth and bamboo allow farmers to grow vegetables during the monsoon floods, when normal fields are underwater. The materials are local and free, and the rotting rafts can be used as fertiliser, so the scheme is cheap and sustainable. It gives families food and income all year, reducing food insecurity without harming the environment.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: named scheme (e.g. Bangladesh floating gardens, Makueni sand dams in Kenya, Cuban organopónicos); how it works; local materials and skills; sustainability; benefits for food security and incomes; small scale.
questions.tip: Explain WHY it is sustainable, not just that it is.

questions.q: Assess the extent to which the Green Revolution improved food security.
questions.answer: The Green Revolution introduced high-yielding varieties of rice and wheat, fertilisers and irrigation from the 1960s, which greatly increased yields in countries such as India and helped prevent widespread famine. However it needed expensive inputs, so richer farmers benefited more than poor ones, widening inequality. Heavy use of water and chemicals caused soil degradation and falling water tables in places such as Punjab. Overall it increased food supply on a large scale, but its sustainability and fairness were limited.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, well-developed points with accurate place-specific evidence; balanced discussion; clear, supported judgement where the command word asks for one.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points and some specific evidence; may be unbalanced or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little evidence or development; no judgement.

Indicative content: high-yielding varieties; fertilisers, pesticides, irrigation; India and Punjab; yields up; famine averted; inequality between farmers; debt; soil, water and biodiversity damage; long-term sustainability; judgement.
questions.tip: 'Extent' answers need a qualified judgement, not yes or no.

questions.q: 'Technology is the most important way to achieve food security.' Evaluate this statement. [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: Model Level 3 outline: For technology: the Green Revolution raised yields; hydroponics at Thanet Earth grows food year-round; GM crops resist drought and pests; drip irrigation saves water. Against: technology is expensive and may not reach the poorest; food insecurity is often caused by poverty, conflict and waste rather than a lack of food; sustainable approaches such as permaculture, urban farming and reducing waste, and appropriate technology like floating gardens, matter more locally. Judgement: technology is important for supply, but access and distribution are the main problem, so technology alone cannot achieve food security.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): thorough knowledge and understanding; detailed, accurate place-specific evidence (named places, dates, figures) used to support points; both sides weighed; a clear, well-substantiated judgement that answers the question directly.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): reasonable knowledge with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is asserted rather than supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): limited, generic knowledge; little evidence; descriptive with no clear judgement.

Indicative content: Green Revolution, new green revolution, GM, hydroponics, aeroponics, irrigation, Thanet Earth; appropriate technology (floating gardens, sand dams); access vs availability; poverty, conflict, waste; sustainability; judgement.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate; grammar controls meaning; wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy; good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy; limited range of specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant content or errors seriously hinder meaning.
questions.tip: Distinguish availability (supply) from access: it is the key grade 9 evaluation point.

questions.q: A country's average daily calorie intake rose from 2,100 to 2,520. Calculate the percentage increase.
ms: Method (1 mark).
questions.tip: Check the answer is sensible: a 420 rise on 2,100 is a fifth.

questions.q: Which of these is an ECONOMIC factor when judging an option?
ms: Jobs and income are economic factors; habitat and air quality are environmental; wellbeing is social.
questions.tip: Use the SEE framework to classify each piece of evidence.

questions.q:
Resource summary: A town of 85,000 people on a river floodplain has a disused 12-hectare gasworks site. Figure 1: unemployment in the ward is 9.4% (national average 4.2%). Figure 2: 2,300 households are on the council housing waiting list. Figure 3: the site flooded in 2007 and 2020. Option 1: 600 private homes and a supermarket (developer pays). Option 2: 350 homes (50% affordable), a health centre and a riverside park with wetland (part council-funded). Option 3: a logistics warehouse employing 400 people next to the A-road.
Unemployment in the ward is how many times the national average (to 1 decimal place)?
ms: 9.4 ÷ 4.2 = 2.24, so about 2.2 times.
questions.tip: Divide, do not subtract, for 'how many times'.

questions.q: Resource summary: A town of 85,000 people on a river floodplain has a disused 12-hectare gasworks site. Figure 1: unemployment in the ward is 9.4% (national average 4.2%). Figure 2: 2,300 households are on the council housing waiting list. Figure 3: the site flooded in 2007 and 2020. Option 1: 600 private homes and a supermarket (developer pays). Option 2: 350 homes (50% affordable), a health centre and a riverside park with wetland (part council-funded). Option 3: a logistics warehouse employing 400 people next to the A-road. Which piece of evidence from the resource most strongly supports Option 2?
options: The site is next to an A-road
2,300 households are on the housing waiting list and the site has flooded twice
ms: Affordable homes address the waiting list and the wetland park reduces flood risk.
questions.tip: Pick evidence that links directly to a benefit of your chosen option.

questions.q: In an issue evaluation, Option 3 is a logistics warehouse employing 400 people on a floodplain site; the other options offer housing, a health centre and a wetland park. A student writes: 'Option 3 is best because it creates jobs.' What is the main weakness of this judgement?
options: It is not substantiated with evidence, ignores other factors and does not explain why other options are weaker
ms: A substantiated judgement uses specific evidence, weighs SEE factors and considers alternatives.
questions.tip: Every claim needs 'because' plus evidence from a figure.

questions.q:
Resource summary: A town of 85,000 people on a river floodplain has a disused 12-hectare gasworks site. Figure 1: unemployment in the ward is 9.4% (national average 4.2%). Figure 2: 2,300 households are on the council housing waiting list. Figure 3: the site flooded in 2007 and 2020. Option 1: 600 private homes and a supermarket (developer pays). Option 2: 350 homes (50% affordable), a health centre and a riverside park with wetland (part council-funded). Option 3: a logistics warehouse employing 400 people next to the A-road.
State two pieces of evidence that show the site has a flood risk.
questions.answer: It is on a river floodplain. It flooded in 2007 and 2020 (Figure 3).
ms: On a floodplain (1 mark).
Flooded in 2007 and 2020 / two floods in recent years (1 mark).
questions.tip: Lift the evidence from the resource: easy marks.

questions.q: Define the term 'stakeholder' and give one example from a regeneration issue.
questions.answer: A stakeholder is a person or group with an interest in, or affected by, a decision. For example, local residents.
ms: Definition (1 mark).
Valid example, e.g. residents, local council, developers, businesses, environmental groups (1 mark).
questions.tip: Stakeholders can be individuals or organisations.

questions.q:
Resource summary: A town of 85,000 people on a river floodplain has a disused 12-hectare gasworks site. Figure 1: unemployment in the ward is 9.4% (national average 4.2%). Figure 2: 2,300 households are on the council housing waiting list. Figure 3: the site flooded in 2007 and 2020. Option 1: 600 private homes and a supermarket (developer pays). Option 2: 350 homes (50% affordable), a health centre and a riverside park with wetland (part council-funded). Option 3: a logistics warehouse employing 400 people next to the A-road.
Explain why different stakeholders might disagree about the future of the site.
questions.answer: Unemployed residents might prefer Option 3 because it creates 400 jobs in a ward where unemployment is 9.4%. Families on the waiting list would support Option 2 because half its homes are affordable. The developer would favour Option 1 because private homes and a supermarket make the most profit, but environmental groups would oppose building homes on a floodplain that flooded in 2007 and 2020 and would support the wetland park.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: named stakeholders and their priorities; use of data (9.4% unemployment, 2,300 waiting list, flooding in 2007 and 2020, 400 jobs); conflicting social, economic and environmental priorities.
questions.tip: Link each stakeholder to an option and a piece of evidence.

questions.q: Explain why a decision-maker should consult local residents before choosing an option for a development site.
questions.answer: Local residents know the area and its problems best, such as which streets flood or where services are lacking, so their views improve the evidence used. Consultation means the chosen option is more likely to meet real needs, such as affordable housing, rather than what outsiders assume. People who feel listened to are more likely to support a scheme, which reduces conflict and delays, whereas ignoring them can lead to protests and legal challenges.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: local knowledge; meeting real needs; bottom-up planning; reducing conflict and delays; legitimacy and trust; inclusion of different groups; limits: some voices louder than others.
questions.tip: Explain the benefit of consultation, not just that it is fair.

questions.q:
Resource summary: A town of 85,000 people on a river floodplain has a disused 12-hectare gasworks site. Figure 1: unemployment in the ward is 9.4% (national average 4.2%). Figure 2: 2,300 households are on the council housing waiting list. Figure 3: the site flooded in 2007 and 2020. Option 1: 600 private homes and a supermarket (developer pays). Option 2: 350 homes (50% affordable), a health centre and a riverside park with wetland (part council-funded). Option 3: a logistics warehouse employing 400 people next to the A-road.
Option 2 provides 350 homes, of which 50% are affordable. Calculate the number of affordable homes and state what percentage of the waiting list this would house.
questions.answer: 350 × 0.5 = 175 affordable homes. 175 ÷ 2,300 × 100 = 7.6% of the waiting list.
ms: 175 affordable homes (1 mark).
7.6% (allow 8%) (1 mark).
questions.tip: Use the result to judge scale: 175 homes is only a small part of the problem.

questions.q:
Resource summary: A town of 85,000 people on a river floodplain has a disused 12-hectare gasworks site. Figure 1: unemployment in the ward is 9.4% (national average 4.2%). Figure 2: 2,300 households are on the council housing waiting list. Figure 3: the site flooded in 2007 and 2020. Option 1: 600 private homes and a supermarket (developer pays). Option 2: 350 homes (50% affordable), a health centre and a riverside park with wetland (part council-funded). Option 3: a logistics warehouse employing 400 people next to the A-road.
Evaluate the disadvantages of Option 1.
questions.answer: Option 1 builds 600 private homes on a floodplain that flooded in 2007 and 2020, so residents would be at risk and insurance costs could be high. Private homes may be too expensive for the 2,300 households on the waiting list, so it does little to solve local housing need and may cause gentrification. A supermarket creates some jobs but may take trade from local shops. However it costs the council nothing, which matters if budgets are tight. Overall its disadvantages are serious because it does not meet the main local needs.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, well-developed points with accurate place-specific evidence; balanced discussion; clear, supported judgement where the command word asks for one.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points and some specific evidence; may be unbalanced or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little evidence or development; no judgement.
Indicative content: flood risk with evidence; affordability and housing need; gentrification; impact on local shops; traffic; limited job quality; counterpoint: no cost to council; judgement.
questions.tip: Even on a 'disadvantages' question, a counterpoint and judgement lifts you to Level 3.

questions.q:
Resource summary: A town of 85,000 people on a river floodplain has a disused 12-hectare gasworks site. Figure 1: unemployment in the ward is 9.4% (national average 4.2%). Figure 2: 2,300 households are on the council housing waiting list. Figure 3: the site flooded in 2007 and 2020. Option 1: 600 private homes and a supermarket (developer pays). Option 2: 350 homes (50% affordable), a health centre and a riverside park with wetland (part council-funded). Option 3: a logistics warehouse employing 400 people next to the A-road.
Which option do you think should be chosen? Justify your decision. [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: Model Level 3 outline: Choose Option 2. Social: 175 affordable homes (7.6% of the 2,300 waiting list) and a health centre improve quality of life. Environmental: wetland park stores floodwater on a site that flooded in 2007 and 2020, reducing flood risk to homes and the town. Economic: some construction and health-centre jobs, though fewer than Option 3. Why not Option 1: private homes on a floodplain, unaffordable and high flood risk. Why not Option 3: 400 jobs help the 9.4% unemployment, but a warehouse on the floodplain adds hard surfaces and HGV traffic and offers no housing. Weakness of Option 2: council cost and fewer jobs, but long-term flood and health savings justify it. Conclusion: Option 2 is the most sustainable and best meets local needs.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): thorough knowledge and understanding; detailed, accurate place-specific evidence (named places, dates, figures) used to support points; both sides weighed; a clear, well-substantiated judgement that answers the question directly.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): reasonable knowledge with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is asserted rather than supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): limited, generic knowledge; little evidence; descriptive with no clear judgement.

Indicative content: clear choice; SEE evidence quoted from figures (9.4%, 4.2%, 2,300, 2007 and 2020 floods, 400 jobs, 600 and 350 homes); disadvantages of chosen option acknowledged; why rejected options are weaker; stakeholders; long term; sustainability.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate; grammar controls meaning; wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy; good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy; limited range of specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant content or errors seriously hinder meaning.
questions.tip: Any option can reach Level 3 if it is justified with evidence and the others are critically rejected.

questions.q: Explain why the most sustainable option is not always the one chosen by decision-makers.
questions.answer: Sustainable options often cost more at the start, so councils with tight budgets may choose a cheaper option paid for by a developer. Politicians may prioritise short-term benefits, such as jobs before an election, over long-term environmental gains. Powerful stakeholders, such as large companies, may have more influence than local residents, so their preferred option is chosen.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: upfront costs; budgets; short-term political priorities; influence of powerful stakeholders; legal and planning constraints; public opinion; uncertainty about long-term benefits.
questions.tip: Show awareness of power and money in decision-making: a grade 9 insight.

questions.q: An issue resource shows: Figure 4: a proposed solar farm would generate enough electricity for 15,000 homes and cover 60 hectares of farmland. Figure 5: a local survey found 58% of residents opposed it. Explain one social and one environmental issue raised by the proposal.
questions.answer: Social: 58% of residents oppose the scheme, perhaps because of visual impact on the landscape, which could cause conflict and lower wellbeing. Environmental: using 60 hectares of farmland reduces land for food production, although it provides low-carbon electricity for 15,000 homes, reducing emissions.
ms: Social issue identified with evidence (1 mark), developed (1 mark).
Environmental issue identified with evidence (1 mark), developed (1 mark).
questions.tip: Two issues, each identified then developed: 2 + 2.

questions.q: Which method would best record noise levels around Westfield Stratford City?
ms: A decibel meter measures sound level.
questions.tip: Match each instrument to what it measures.

questions.q: A field sketch is an example of:
ms: A field sketch is descriptive (qualitative) and collected by you (primary).
questions.tip: Classify every method twice: primary/secondary and qualitative/quantitative.

questions.q: Eleven pedestrian counts in Stratford were: 5, 9, 14, 18, 22, 27, 31, 40, 46, 58, 63. What is the interquartile range?
ms: LQ is the 3rd value (14), UQ is the 9th value (46); 46 - 14 = 32.
questions.tip: With n values, LQ is the (n+1)/4th value and UQ the 3(n+1)/4th.

questions.q: In a questionnaire, 86 of 200 people said regeneration had improved Stratford. To draw this on a pie chart, what angle is needed?
questions.tip: Fraction of total × 360.

questions.q: A student finds a strong negative relationship between distance from Stratford station and pedestrian count. Which conclusion is most valid?
options: Pedestrian flows are highest near the station and decline with distance in this sample, possibly because of shops and transport links
Distance from the station causes people to walk less everywhere in the UK
ms: Correlation in a sample supports a pattern but does not prove cause; conclusions should be limited to the area studied.
questions.tip: Correlation is not causation: avoid over-generalising.

questions.q: Which change would most improve the validity of an enquiry into whether regeneration has improved quality of life in Stratford?
options: Counting pedestrians at only one site
Comparing secondary data from before 2012 with current data and surveying long-term residents
ms: Validity means the method answers the question; before-and-after data and residents' views directly measure change in quality of life.
questions.tip: Validity is about measuring the right thing, not just measuring accurately.

questions.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using an environmental quality survey in an urban enquiry.
questions.answer: Advantage: it is quick and turns observations into scores that can be compared between sites. Disadvantage: it is subjective, so different people may give different scores.
ms: Advantage (1 mark).
Disadvantage (1 mark): subjective, affected by time of day or weather, limited categories.
questions.tip: 'Subjective' is the key word examiners look for.

questions.q: Temperatures at seven sites in Regent's Park were 18.4, 18.9, 19.6, 19.3, 20.4, 24.8 and 19.1 °C. The 24.8 °C reading was taken next to a café's air vent. Calculate the median and explain why the median is a better average than the mean for this data.
questions.answer: Ordered: 18.4, 18.9, 19.1, 19.3, 19.6, 20.4, 24.8. Median = 19.3 °C. The median is not affected by the anomalous 24.8 °C reading caused by the vent, whereas the mean (20.1 °C) is pulled upwards, so the median better represents typical temperatures.
ms: Median 19.3 °C (1 mark).
Median is not affected by extreme values / anomalies (1 mark).
Developed: the 24.8 °C anomaly from the air vent raises the mean (to about 20.1 °C) (1 mark).
questions.tip: Spot the anomaly in the stem and use it in your explanation.

questions.q: State one way of reducing a health and safety risk during fieldwork next to a busy road in Stratford.
questions.answer: Work in groups and stay on the pavement away from the kerb, wearing high-visibility vests.
ms: Any valid precaution linked to traffic, e.g. high-visibility clothing, stay on the pavement, use crossings, supervision (1 mark).
questions.tip: Link the precaution to the specific risk named.

questions.q: Infiltration test: 500 ml took 125 seconds on grass and 400 seconds on a path in Regent's Park. Calculate the infiltration rate for each in ml per second.
ms: Grass 4 ml/s (1 mark).
Path 1.25 ml/s (1 mark).
questions.tip: Rate = volume ÷ time.

questions.q: In an infiltration test in Regent's Park, 500 ml of water took 125 seconds to soak into grass (4 ml per second) and 400 seconds to soak into a path (1.25 ml per second). Compare the infiltration rates and suggest a reason for the difference.
questions.answer: Grass infiltrates 3.2 times faster than the path (4 vs 1.25 ml/s). The path is compacted by trampling, so there are fewer pore spaces for water to enter, whereas grass roots keep the soil loose.
ms: Comparison using data, e.g. 3.2 times faster or 2.75 ml/s faster (1 mark).
Reason: compaction / fewer pore spaces (1 mark).
Development: roots, organic matter, trampling by visitors (1 mark).
questions.tip: Manipulate the data (times faster) to show higher skills.

questions.q: Total environmental quality scores (each made up of eight criteria scored -2 to +2) at eight sites in Stratford were: 6, -2, 9, 3, 11, -4, 7, 2. Calculate the mean and explain why the mean might be misleading for this data.
questions.answer: Sum = 32; mean = 32 ÷ 8 = 4. The mean is affected by extreme values such as 11 and -4, and hides the wide variation between sites, so a median or range would also be useful.
ms: Correct sum 32 (1 mark).
Mean 4 (1 mark).
Explanation: affected by extreme values / hides spread (1 mark).
Suggests a better measure such as median, range or IQR (1 mark).
questions.tip: Always ask what an average hides.

questions.q: Explain why systematic sampling might be more suitable than random sampling for a transect from Stratford station into surrounding residential streets.
questions.answer: Systematic sampling places sites at regular intervals, such as every 100 m, so the whole transect is covered evenly and changes with distance can be seen clearly. Random sampling might cluster sites in one section and miss the transition between commercial and residential areas, so trends would be harder to identify.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: even coverage; shows change with distance; easy to repeat; random may cluster or leave gaps; bias risk if interval matches a pattern.
questions.tip: Link the method to the aim of the enquiry: change with distance.

questions.q: Suggest how a student could present data on land use along a transect in Stratford, and justify the choice.
questions.answer: A land-use map or annotated transect diagram, with colour-coded categories such as retail, residential and open space, would show where each land use occurs along the route. It is good because it keeps the geographical location of the data, so changes with distance from the centre are clear. A divided bar chart for each site could also show proportions for easy comparison.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: map, transect diagram, divided bar charts, pie charts located on a map; justification: spatial patterns, comparisons, categorical data suits bar or pie, not line graphs.
questions.tip: Justify by linking the graph type to the type of data (categorical, continuous, spatial).

questions.q: A student concluded that 'regeneration has benefited everyone in Stratford' from questionnaires completed by 40 shoppers in Westfield on a Saturday. Explain why this conclusion may be unreliable.
questions.answer: The sample of 40 is small, so it may not represent Stratford's population of tens of thousands. Asking only shoppers in Westfield is biased towards people who use and probably like the new development and may include visitors from elsewhere rather than local residents. Surveying only on a Saturday misses workers and people who do not shop there, so the conclusion over-generalises.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: small sample; location bias; time bias; visitors vs residents; leading questions; 'everyone' over-generalises; improvements: stratified sample, different locations and times, secondary data.
questions.tip: Explain the effect of each limitation on the conclusion.

questions.q: For your physical geography enquiry, evaluate the effectiveness of your data collection methods.
questions.answer: In my Regent's Park microclimate enquiry, I used digital thermometers and an anemometer at eight sites. They gave precise readings, and we took three readings at each site and calculated a mean, which improved reliability. However groups took readings at different times, and temperatures rose during the afternoon, which may have affected results. The anemometer was held at different heights, reducing accuracy. Overall the methods were partly effective: they showed the expected pattern near the lake, but simultaneous readings at a fixed height would make them more reliable.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, well-developed points with accurate place-specific evidence; balanced discussion; clear, supported judgement where the command word asks for one.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points and some specific evidence; may be unbalanced or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little evidence or development; no judgement.

Indicative content: named methods and equipment; sampling strategy; accuracy, reliability, validity; specific problems (timing, weather, human error, calibration); impact on results; improvements; judgement.
questions.tip: Refer to YOUR enquiry with real detail, not a generic one.

questions.q: For your human geography enquiry, assess how far your results supported your hypothesis.
questions.answer: Hypothesis: 'Environmental quality improves closer to the Olympic Park in Stratford.' Results: environmental quality scores were highest at sites in and next to the park, and the line graph showed a general decline with distance, supporting the hypothesis. However two sites near Stratford High Street scored low despite being close, because of traffic and litter, and one residential street further away scored highly. Overall the hypothesis was largely supported, but the anomalies show other factors such as traffic and land use also matter.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, well-developed points with accurate place-specific evidence; balanced discussion; clear, supported judgement where the command word asks for one.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points and some specific evidence; may be unbalanced or the judgement is weakly supported.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generic points; little evidence or development; no judgement.
Indicative content: hypothesis stated; results with data; pattern; anomalies and explanations; limitations affecting confidence; judgement of 'how far'.
questions.tip: Quote your own results to reach Level 3.

questions.q: 'The way I presented my data was the most important factor in reaching a valid conclusion.' Evaluate this statement using one of your enquiries. [9 marks]
questions.answer: Model Level 3 outline: Presentation: e.g. proportional symbols on a map of Stratford showed spatial patterns in pedestrian counts clearly; radar charts compared environmental quality; but poor choice (e.g. line graph for categorical data) can mislead. Other factors: data collection quality (sample size, sampling method, timing) is more fundamental, because poor data cannot be fixed by good presentation; analysis (averages, IQR, identifying anomalies) and the use of secondary data also shape conclusions. Judgement: presentation helped me see patterns, but data collection and analysis were more important for validity.
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): thorough knowledge and understanding; detailed, accurate place-specific evidence (named places, dates, figures) used to support points; both sides weighed; a clear, well-substantiated judgement that answers the question directly.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): reasonable knowledge with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is asserted rather than supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): limited, generic knowledge; little evidence; descriptive with no clear judgement.

Indicative content: named enquiry; presentation techniques and their strengths and weaknesses; data collection, sample, accuracy and reliability; analysis; secondary data; judgement on relative importance.
questions.tip: Questions about 'the most important factor' need you to compare it with other factors.

questions.q: 'Fieldwork in an urban area is more difficult to make reliable than fieldwork in a physical environment.' Using your two enquiries, to what extent do you agree? [9 marks + 3 SPaG]
questions.answer: Model Level 3 outline: Urban (Stratford): human behaviour varies by time and day, so pedestrian counts change; questionnaire responses depend on who agrees to answer and may be biased; environmental quality surveys are subjective. Physical (Regent's Park): measurements such as temperature and infiltration are quantitative and can be repeated, but weather changes during the day, equipment errors and site variation (e.g. trampling) also reduce reliability. Judgement: e.g. 'I largely agree, because urban data depends on people and their choices, whereas physical data can be controlled more easily, though both need repeat readings and careful timing.'
ms: Level 3 (7-9 marks): thorough knowledge and understanding; detailed, accurate place-specific evidence (named places, dates, figures) used to support points; both sides weighed; a clear, well-substantiated judgement that answers the question directly.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): reasonable knowledge with some specific evidence; some evaluation but may be one-sided or the judgement is asserted rather than supported.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): limited, generic knowledge; little evidence; descriptive with no clear judgement.
Indicative content: specific methods from both enquiries; sources of unreliability in each; ways reliability was improved; balanced comparison; judgement.
SPaG High (3 marks): spelling and punctuation consistently accurate; grammar controls meaning; wide range of specialist terms used precisely.
SPaG Intermediate (2 marks): considerable accuracy; good range of specialist terms.
SPaG Threshold (1 mark): reasonable accuracy; limited range of specialist terms. 0 marks if no relevant content or errors seriously hinder meaning.
questions.tip: Use both enquiries equally to reach Level 3.

questions.q: Figure 3 shows that Dhaka, Bangladesh, grew from about 0.3 million people in 1950 to over 20 million today, and that a large share of residents live in informal settlements. Suggest the challenges this growth creates for the city's government.
questions.answer: Growth this fast means the government cannot build enough housing, so many people live in informal settlements without legal land rights. Providing clean water, sewers and waste collection to so many new residents is very expensive, so disease spreads. Low tax revenue from the informal economy makes it harder to fund services, and roads become congested because public transport has not kept pace.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: scale and speed of growth; housing shortage and informal settlements; water, sanitation, waste; health; congestion; low tax base; flooding risk on low-lying land; application to Dhaka using figures given.
questions.tip: Use the figures in your answer to show you have applied your knowledge to the place.

questions.q: Compare the challenges of urban growth in Rio de Janeiro with those in London.
questions.answer: Both cities face housing pressure, but in Rio this has led to self-built favelas such as Rocinha on steep hillsides, whereas in London it shows as high prices, overcrowding and long waiting lists. Both have traffic and air pollution, though London has a larger public transport network and ULEZ to manage it. Rio's environmental challenges are more basic, such as untreated sewage in Guanabara Bay, while London's are about managing ageing systems, such as through the Tideway Tunnel.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: housing (favelas vs affordability); services and sanitation; transport and pollution; inequality in both; scale of management capacity; comparative language required for Level 2.
questions.tip: Comparison marks need comparative words in every point: whereas, both, more than.

questions.q: A country's infant mortality rate fell from 61 to 47 per 1,000 live births. Calculate the percentage decrease to 1 decimal place.
ms: Method: change ÷ original value × 100 (1 mark).
23.0% (1 mark). Do not accept 29.8% (divided by the new value).
questions.tip: The original value here is 61.

questions.q: An NEE's GNI per head rose from US$12,000 to US$16,000 over ten years. Calculate the percentage increase to 1 decimal place.
ms: Method (1 mark).
questions.tip: Round only at the end.

questions.q: Malawi is a landlocked LIC in southern Africa that relies mainly on exports of tobacco. Suggest why it has found it difficult to develop.
questions.answer: As a landlocked country, Malawi must transport exports through neighbouring countries to reach ports, which raises costs and makes its goods less competitive. Relying on one primary export, tobacco, means income falls when world prices fall or demand declines as fewer people smoke. Most people are subsistence farmers, so droughts or floods quickly reduce food and income, leaving little money for investment in education and infrastructure.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: landlocked: transport costs, dependence on neighbours; single primary export: price volatility, falling demand, little added value; climate hazards and farming; debt; limited investment; apply knowledge to the clues given.
questions.tip: Use every clue in the stem: landlocked, LIC, tobacco.

questions.q: Figure 4 shows that the percentage of UK workers in manufacturing fell from about 25% in 1980 to about 8% in 2020, while services rose from about 60% to over 80%. Describe the changes and suggest one effect on former industrial towns.
questions.answer: Manufacturing fell by about 17 percentage points, to roughly a third of its 1980 share, while services grew to over 80% of jobs. In former industrial towns, factory closures caused high unemployment, and many skilled manual workers found it hard to find new jobs, which led to deprivation and out-migration of young people.
ms: Describes the fall in manufacturing with data (1 mark).
Describes the rise in services with data (1 mark).
Effect identified, e.g. unemployment, deprivation, derelict land (1 mark).
Effect developed (1 mark).
questions.tip: Manipulate the data, e.g. 'fell by 17 percentage points'.

questions.q: Kenya's Makueni County is semi-arid and suffers frequent drought. Suggest how small-scale strategies could improve food security there.
questions.answer: Sand dams across seasonal rivers can store water in the sand after rains, giving water for drip irrigation in the dry season, so crops can be grown for longer. Drought-resistant crops such as sorghum reduce the risk of harvest failure. Because these methods use local labour and materials, communities can build and maintain them cheaply, making them sustainable.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.
Indicative content: sand dams; drip irrigation; drought-resistant crops; water harvesting; terracing to reduce soil erosion; community ownership; low cost; sustainability; apply to semi-arid context.
questions.tip: Link each strategy to the drought problem named in the question.

questions.q: Curitiba in Brazil is often described as a sustainable city. Using your knowledge of sustainable transport, suggest why its bus rapid transit system has been successful.
questions.answer: Buses run in dedicated lanes, so they are not slowed by car traffic, making journeys quicker and more reliable than driving. Raised tube stations where passengers pay before boarding cut stopping times. Because the system is cheaper to build than a metro, it could cover more of the city, so more people use it and car use and emissions fall.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: dedicated bus lanes; pre-boarding payment; frequency and reliability; low build cost vs metro; integration with land use planning; reduced congestion and emissions; apply BRT principles.
questions.tip: For an unfamiliar place, transfer what you know about strategies like BRT in Rio or bus lanes in London.

questions.q: A student investigating a river in an unfamiliar area measured channel width at five sites downstream. Explain one problem with measuring only five sites and how it could be overcome.
questions.answer: Five sites is a small sample, so one unusual site, such as where a bridge narrows the channel, could distort the pattern and make the conclusion unreliable. Increasing the number of sites, using systematic sampling at equal intervals and repeating measurements would give a clearer, more reliable trend.
ms: Problem identified: small sample (1 mark).
Developed: anomalies distort the pattern / unrepresentative (1 mark).
Solution: more sites / systematic sampling (1 mark).
Solution developed: repeat readings, mean, more reliable trend (1 mark).
questions.tip: Unfamiliar fieldwork questions test the same ideas: sample size, reliability, accuracy.

questions.q: Explain how the Elizabeth line has created economic opportunities for people in east London.
questions.answer: The line cuts journey times from places such as Abbey Wood and Stratford to the West End and Canary Wharf, so residents can reach more jobs within a reasonable commute. Better access raises the attractiveness of east London to businesses and developers, leading to new offices and housing around stations, which create construction and service jobs. However rising house prices near stations may push some residents out.
ms: Level 2 (3-4 marks): clear, developed explanation; points linked with cause and effect (because, so, which leads to); accurate geographical terms and specific detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, basic points with little or no development; may be generic.

Indicative content: faster journeys; access to jobs in central London, Canary Wharf, Heathrow; business investment and regeneration around stations; construction jobs; property values; gentrification risk.
questions.tip: Link transport to jobs via accessibility.

flashcards.back: A natural event or process that threatens people and property.
The probability or chance that a natural hazard will affect people.
Plates move apart; magma rises to form new crust. Gentle volcanoes, minor earthquakes. E.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
Denser oceanic plate subducts under continental plate. Explosive volcanoes and strong earthquakes. E.g. Nazca plate under South American plate (Chile).
Plates slide past each other. Earthquakes but no volcanoes. E.g. San Andreas Fault, California.
Two continental plates (Indian and Eurasian) push together, forming fold mountains (Himalayas) and earthquakes.
Focus: point underground where an earthquake starts. Epicentre: point on the surface directly above the focus.
Primary: immediate, caused directly by the hazard (buildings collapse). Secondary: result from primary effects, often later (disease, fires, loss of income).
Immediate: rescue, aid, shelter, food in the hours/days after. Long-term: rebuilding, improving resilience over months/years.
27 February 2010, magnitude 8.8, off the coast of central Chile (HIC case study).
About 500 people died.
